articles.title: From ban to boundaries: how 100 high-impact journals regulate AI-generated images after the 2026 policy shift
articles.authors: Shirley Yang
articles.abstract: Generative AI can draw explanatory figures and can also fabricate research images. We asked how the 100 highest-impact journals regulate AI-generated images and how those rules changed in a year. On 30 September 2026 we captured each journal’s author instructions and the publisher policies they cite. We retrieved archived versions from September–October 2025 and coded rules for five image types. At baseline, 79 journals belonged to publishers that prohibited AI-generated images. Between May and August 2026, Taylor & Francis, Elsevier and Springer Nature replaced these bans with rules that depend on image type. By September 2026, 55 journals explicitly permitted AI-generated explanatory illustrations and 58 permitted AI-assisted data visualisations, usually with disclosure or reproducibility conditions. For 89 journals, AI-created or AI-altered primary research images were prohibited; no journal permitted them. Rules for graphical abstracts and covers varied most. The Science journals, The Lancet family and JAMA Psychiatry still restricted illustrative uses. Twenty-seven journals gave instructions that contradicted or lagged behind their publisher’s current policy, including 20 of 31 Springer Nature journals. Authors need to check journal-level instructions, and publishers need to align them.

articles.title: Polyauthorship and Proportionate Authorship Transparency in Medical Research
articles.authors: Onder Canguven
articles.abstract: Large author groups can reflect legitimate collaboration, but author counts alone reveal little about individual contributions or accountability. Three recent articles in World Journal of Men’s Health illustrate the range: an editorial on authorship accountability lists 18 authors; a systematic review and meta-analysis that included five studies lists 28; and an international survey by Shah and colleagues lists nearly 200 named authors. These figures do not establish inappropriate authorship. They do raise a question: how can readers distinguish substantive authorship from other valuable contributions? We propose proportionate reporting requirements that increase with the size and structure of a collaboration, including specific individual contribution statements and, for very large groups, an account of how final manuscript approval and accountability were secured. Greater transparency would help readers interpret academic credit without imposing arbitrary limits on author numbers.

articles.title: Dawdling at Dusk: Affect and Bedtime Procrastination
articles.authors: Yijun Lin; Erin Corwin Westgate
articles.abstract: Why don’t people go to bed on time? Most research on bedtime procrastination has focused on individual differences (e.g., self-regulation, chronotype), potentially conflating between-person patterns with within-person processes. To address this, we examined whether affective valence and arousal predict bedtime procrastination within people, between people, or both. In Study 1, we replicated cross-sectional associations between negative affect and bedtime procrastination in a Chinese community sample. In Studies 2–3, we attempted to manipulate valence and arousal in separate week-long diary experiments; the manipulations produced limited shifts in affect and did not significantly change bedtime procrastination. Across both diary studies, however, analyses of self-reported affect revealed a consistent pattern: people who generally felt less positive were more likely to procrastinate, whereas evening-to-evening fluctuations in affect did not predict whether they procrastinated on a given night. Exploratory analyses in Study 2 suggested that this between-person association was partly indirect through feeling less able to go to bed. Taken together, these findings suggest that whether people put off going to bed may be more closely tied to how they typically feel than to how they feel on a given evening, highlighting the importance of separating between-person and within-person levels.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: ‘Clean Air for Everyone (CLAIRE): Ventilatie en luchtreiniging voor pandemische paraatheid’
articles.authors: Stefanie H Meeuwis; Amy Louise de Bruijn; Marloes Duijzings; Jennifer Mareen Becker; Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen
articles.abstract: Onderzoek toont aan dat luchtkwaliteit in binnenruimtes vaak ondermaats is. Dit kan leiden tot gezondheidsrisico's, zoals verergerde luchtwegproblematiek en een groter risico op infectieziekten. Luchtbehandelingstechnieken, waaronder ventilatie en (mobiele) luchtreinigers, zijn potentieel effectieve methoden om deze gezondheidsrisico's terug te dringen, maar het is niet duidelijk of stakeholders de inzet ervan aanvaardbaar en haalbaar achten. Dit rapport omvat de bevindingen uit een interviewstudie en een focusgroepen studie. Binnen deze onderzoeken zijn stakeholders uit basisscholen en ouderenzorg (beleidsmakers en gebruikers) geïnterviewd en gevraagd of zij bereid zijn ventilatie en luchtreiniging in te zetten en onder welke omstandigheden. Thema’s die een rol spelen bij de aanvaardbaarheid en haalbaarheid van de inzet van deze technieken worden in het rapport beschreven en geëvalueerd.

articles.title: Gaze semantics: A scoping review of how gaze conveys and constrains meaning in social contexts
articles.authors: Nikol Figalová; Anne Böckler; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: Humans rely on gaze to encode information and signal to others. Gaze may indicate where someone is attending, but its contribution extends beyond spatial orientation. Evidence is scattered across different research traditions. This scoping review synthesises 361 publications on gaze as a meaningful social cue. Gaze semantics describes the systematic contribution of gaze to conveying and constraining social meaning. A cross-domain synthesis identified four recurrent operations: gaze orients by making objects, people, or locations socially relevant; addresses by positioning people as recipients or interaction partners; qualifies by modifying how other cues are interpreted; and coordinates by organising participation and unfolding action. These functional contributions can co-occur within a single gaze event. Gaze interpretation is inferential, shaped by five categories of contextual factors: signal properties; interactional availability; multimodal and sequential embedding; cultural, social and activity frame; and gazer and observer states and interactional history. We propose a Gazer-Observer Model of Gaze Understanding that integrates these findings to describe the dynamic relation between gaze production and interpretation. The same gaze pattern may support different interpretations across situations yet allow a relatively specific interpretation within a particular encounter. Gaze can therefore systematically affect social interpretation while remaining semantically underdetermined to varying degrees.

articles.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles.title: Effort discounting of environmental and personal outcomes in a consequential decision-making task
articles.authors: Shiwei Yang; Ruth Krebs
articles.abstract: Effort investment is an important barrier that keeps individuals from engaging in pro-environmental behaviors and previous studies revealed that expected cognitive effort can reduce motivation for pro-environmental goals. The current study sought to investigate whether effort changes the shape of the cost-benefit analysis, and in particular whether it leads to stronger discounting of outcome value. The study employed a within-subjects experimental design through an online study (N = 400) using the Work for Environmental Protection Task (WEPT) featuring both pro-environmental and personal outcomes. We assessed participants' binary choice to accept or decline specific trial of a number identification task based on expected effort-reward-outcome combinations. Questionnaires were added to explore inter-individual characteristics. Overall, participants preferred trials with higher reward magnitude, lower effort requirements, and those benefiting them personally. Moreover, pro-environmental outcomes featured more pronounced effort discounting, or in other words, a weaker shielding of effort effects by outcome magnitude. Together, this provides experimental evidence for a general inferiority of pro-environmental outcomes (replicating previous data) and reveals a skewed costs-benefit analysis that prioritizes effort costs over outcome magnitude.

articles.title: Epistemic Stances in Humanoid Robot Evaluation: Evidence from the Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire and Morph-Based Perceptual Judgements
articles.authors: Ilaria Maria Antonietta Benzi; Francesca Ciardo
articles.abstract: Humanoid robots occupy an ambiguous position between social partners and artefacts, and people differ markedly in how they evaluate them. Research on individual differences in human–robot interaction has focused on personality, anthropomorphic tendencies and technology acceptance, leaving largely unexamined the processes by which people decide whether an artificial agent can be treated as a credible source of social information. The present study introduces epistemic stances, as conceptualised within the mentalizing tradition, to this literature. Seventy adults completed the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire, along with measures of generalized attitudes toward robots (Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire, Negative Attitudes toward Robots Scale, Robotic Social Attributes Scale), and a morph-based task in which robot faces varying in human likeness were rated for likeability, eeriness and human likeness. Epistemic stances were selectively associated with generalized social evaluations: Epistemic Trust predicted higher Robot Anxiety and lower attributed Warmth, whereas Credulity predicted higher attributed Warmth, with no associations for perceived Competence. At the stimulus level, morph condition strongly shaped all three judgements, whereas epistemic stances added little. Rather than a failure to extend person-level effects, this dissociation follows from the claim that epistemic stances operate on socially communicated information rather than on perceptual appraisal. Epistemic functioning may therefore shape the social meaning attributed to artificial agents, offering a testable framework for the design of robot communication.

articles.title: Holding up a mirror: The mental health and well-being of academic psychologists
articles.authors: Andrew Devendorf; David Disabato; Maya Nauphal; Jonathan Rottenberg; Sarah E. Victor
articles.abstract: The profession of psychology aims to improve societal mental health and well-being. Ironically, psychologists have neglected the study of mental health within the profession. We conducted the first comprehensive assessment of mental health difficulties across psychology disciplines in a sample (N = 1,261) of faculty and graduate students affiliated with U.S. doctoral degree granting institutions. Over 84% of respondents reported a lifetime history of mental health difficulties; 54% reported a lifetime diagnosis; 15% had clinically elevated current depression symptoms; 16% reported clinically elevated current anxiety symptoms; and 51% met Keyes’ “flourishing” criteria. The most common mental health concerns were depression, generalized anxiety disorder, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Across all outcomes, graduate students reported significantly greater frequency and severity of difficulties. Clinically elevated current depression and anxiety were 3-4 times higher in graduate students (21% and 22%, respectively) compared to professor-level faculty (6% and 7%, respectively). Rates of flourishing were lower in graduate students than faculty (OR = 2.65, p < .001). Clinical-area respondents (92%) were more likely to report a lifetime mental health difficulty than non-clinical area respondents (83%). Interestingly, while there were no field-level differences in rates of current elevated anxiety, clinical-area respondents had lower rates of clinically elevated depression. Academic psychology is not an exception to the mental health crisis in higher education. Particularly urgent action is needed to improve graduate students’ mental health. We discuss both systemic and practical recommendations for the profession of psychology.

articles.title: Peer Transmission of Mental Health Information Increases ADHD Self-Diagnosis
articles.authors: Tanay Katiyar; George Gillett; Adam Hunt; Amanda M Ferguson; Alessia Pascale; Alberto Acerbi; Nikhil Chaudhary; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Increased sharing of mental health information online has intensified public concern that social media may amplify mental health self-diagnosis rates. While much work has examined the types of mental health information available online, little attention is paid to the mechanisms governing how this information is created and consumed. Taking a cultural evolutionary perspective, we posit that social media facilitates peer-to-peer transmission of psychiatric information in novel formats and provides new motivations to transmit such information; this alters the information people see and their reactions to it. We investigate this through an adapted transmission chain paradigm where participants sequentially modify and transmit Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) explanations amongst each other, allowing us to examine how self-diagnostic tendencies evolve during this process. Across four studies, we find that such transmission increases participants’ tendency to diagnose themselves, and another individual with subclinical traits, with ADHD. Participants’ tendency to recommend this other individual to seek professional help also increases. Transmission format (i.e. generating an example list versus narrative summary) and motivation (i.e. making an explanation for maximising likes versus accuracy) moderate some effects. These results indicate that peer-to-peer transmission may play a key role in determining psychiatric diagnostic trends and shaping the public understanding of mental health.

articles.title: Heavy-Loaders and Light-Lifters: Individual Differences in Spontaneous Working Memory Use Are Stable Across Tasks in 6- to 10-Year-Old Children
articles.authors: Trevor Bissert; Candice Koolhaas; Zsuzsa Kaldy; Erik Blaser
articles.abstract: Naturalistic visuomotor tasks, like building a Lego model, allow one to trade off the use of external resources (here, looking at the instructions) versus internal resources (remembering steps in working memory). Prior work has revealed substantial individual differences in this sampling-remembering trade-off, with some individuals opting to sample less and remember more (‘heavy-loaders’) and others to sample more and remember less (‘light-lifters’). We hypothesized that these strategies are driven by subjective, but stable, assessments of the costs of sampling versus remembering. In this preregistered, developmental study, we tested this using two superficially different, but isomorphic tablet-based tasks: the Shopping Game and the Zoo Game. Children (N = 121, 60% female, age: 6.0-10.0 years) were shown icons of food items (or animals) and asked to select them in a store (or field) interspersed with distractors. Critically, children could not view the list and store/field simultaneously, but could toggle between them. List Study Time and Memory Use (correctly selected items), per visit, characterized strategy. As expected, we found substantial variability in Memory Use and Study Time between children that remained constant across age (0.5-5 items and 1-12 s, respectively), alongside significant, strong stability within children (>67% variance explained), both across the two tasks and over time (test-retest); heavy-loaders remained heavy-loaders and light-lifters, light-lifters. We also found that cognitive reflection (CRT-D) and age significantly predicted Memory Use. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explicitly characterize the individual differences and cognitive motivation predictors of children's spontaneous memory use.

articles.title: Metacognitive Skill Learning as a Mechanism of Advanced Meditation
articles.authors: Brendan Conway-Smith; Ruby Potash; Matthew Sacchet
articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in advanced meditation, the cognitive mechanisms underlying these capacities remain poorly understood. This paper develops a cognitive account of advanced meditation as a specialized form of metacognitive skill learning. Drawing on classic accounts of skill acquisition, we propose the automatization of metacognitive control as a mechanism through which meditative skill develops. Through sustained practice, practitioners become less reliant on explicit instructions as metacognitive control becomes increasingly automatic. This shift may allow meditative practice to become more effective, fluent, and less effortful. The resulting metacognitive control is directed toward well-defined phenomenological targets, including advanced absorption states and insight stages. By connecting cognitive mechanisms with neural findings and experiential descriptions, the account offers a testable framework for explaining the development of advanced meditative capacities.

articles.title: Multimodal Dynamics in Learning and Explaining Abstract and Concrete Concepts: A Triadic Interactive Task with Families
articles.authors: Chiara De Livio; Claudia Mazzuca; Francesca Bellagamba; Alessandro Gennaro; Giuliana Mazzoni; Silvia Mazzoni; Julian Zubek; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Studies have shown that learning abstract concepts (e.g., freedom compared to table) may be particularly challenging. To address concept learning, most studies use paradigms involving a single participant, such as lexical decision, match to sample, induction, and rating tasks. Here, we use an interactive task involving three family members—mother, father, and a 5-year-old child—and examine how concepts differing in abstractness are explained by the parents, either individually or together, and how the child learns and employs them. We investigate multimodal dynamics in interaction, studying gestures, movements of bodily parts, and movement coordination among interactors, in an effort to capture different embodied signatures characterizing concepts differing in abstractness. Results reveal that people gesture differently with abstract and concrete concepts, but in both cases tend to instantiate the conceptual referent, either metaphorically or iconically. Subtle differences in head movements and social touch suggest that people struggle more to understand the meanings of abstract concepts than concrete ones. Finally, with abstract concepts, coordination episodes are longer. Overall, the results provide support for the view that, with abstract concepts, people use more communicative signals and tend to converge more than with concrete concepts.

articles.title: Object Details Persist in Visual Working Memory Regardless of Category Sufficiency for Search
articles.authors: Ryan Williams; Joseph M. Saito; Keisuke Fukuda; Susanne Ferber
articles.abstract: When searching for objects in complex environments, performance often improves with more specific target representations. Yet, sometimes a more general representation may be preferable. For example, when repeatedly searching for unique exemplars from the same object category, a shared category-based representation could help alleviate the cognitive burden of constantly encoding and maintaining new exemplar representations. We therefore examined whether the format of target representations used for search is sensitive to the sustained preservation of object-category membership. Across two experiments, observers searched consecutively for images of real-world objects from the same basic-level category. We recorded contralateral delay activity (CDA), an electrophysiological marker of visual working memory (VWM) maintenance, to assess whether the encoding of object-specific details diminished across category repetitions in favor of more generalized representations. In Experiment 1, we manipulated whether object-category membership alone sufficiently differentiated each unique target from nontargets in the search array. In Experiment 2, we preserved category sufficiency but allowed the targets to additionally repeat at the level of the exemplar to examine how repeatedly searching for the same object differs from repeatedly searching for the same kind of object. We found that while fewer object-specific details were maintained in VWM when category membership was sufficient, the amount of detail only diminished across repetitions of the exact same object. Moreover, observers exhibited sensitivity to the sustained preservation of the target category in the form of perceptual and semantic expectancy violations following category switches, as indexed by N2pc and N400 ERP components. Together, we show that, even though the sustained preservation of a target object category does not continuously reduce the encoding of object-specific details, categorical information is nonetheless represented in parallel. We speculate that object-specific representations principally serve attentional guidance, while categorical representations benefit target-match decisions.

articles.title: The structure and degree of social connection is associated with the structure and idiosyncrasy of emotion perception
articles.authors: David Dodell-Feder; Tamar Galvin; Tara Augenstein
articles.abstract: Social connection is associated with broad aspects of social cognition. Here, we probe the nature of this association in two studies (Ns=305, 759) with college-aged samples in which we measured different aspects of social (dis)connection (e.g., loneliness) and performance on a measure of emotion perception. We find that intersubject differences in social connection mirrored intersubject differences in emotion perception, suggesting a shared fingerprint between the experience of one’s social relationships and the perception of emotion information. Further, greater levels of social disconnection were associated with greater idiosyncrasy in emotion perception, which was largely driven by task inaccuracy. This finding suggests that social disconnection may distort internal models of affective states in a way that pulls individuals from a canonical understanding of how emotions are expressed in faces. Although findings were specific to Study 2, these results provide important context to how social connection relates to emotion perception and highlights emotion perception as a potential intervention target for social disconnection.

articles.title: Using Large Language Models to Contextualize Smiling in Psychotherapy Research
articles.authors: Martin Lund Trinhammer; Stella Grasshof; Jana Volkert; Pia Rasche; Anna-Maria Weiland; Sami Sebastian Brandt; Uwe Altmann
articles.abstract:
The meaning of a smile during conversation depends on what is being
said, yet psychotherapy research has historically analyzed facial movements independently of
context. We introduce a methodology that links both partners’ smiling in a dyadic setting to
the sentiment of a speech turn (positive, neutral, negative). Using open-weight models on local
hardware only, we transcribed and diarized attachment interviews, annotated the sentiment of
the participant’s speech turns with a large language model (LLM), and analyzed individual smiling
 and smile synchrony as a function of that sentiment. We applied linear mixed models to
test for differences in smiling according to sentiment. Across 70 interviews and 1,294 speech
turns, only the interviewer’s smiling differed significantly according to the sentiment of what
the participant was saying (interviewer d = .51, q < .001; participant d = .05, q = .165); the
pair smiled simultaneously more often during positive than negative turns (d = .21, p < .001).
By conditioning smiling on what is being said — sentiment annotated from the conversation
as it unfolds rather than created by experimental instruction — our method enables the kind of
context-sensitive analysis contemporary theories call for. The pipeline is open and reproducible,
runs entirely on local hardware so that no data leave the site, and can be easily modified for any
annotation scheme or clinical setting.

articles.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles.title: Growing Up With Conversational AI: A Developmental Framework for Adolescent Agency Over Conversational AI Use
articles.authors: shanting chen; Mary Kate Koch; Renkai Ma; Cindy Liu; Natalie C. Ebner
articles.abstract: Conversational generative AI has rapidly reached majority adoption among U.S. adolescents. These systems now provide advice, emotional support, academic assistance, simulated social interaction, and opportunities for identity exploration at a critical phase in development when mental health needs are rising and capacities for self-regulation, autonomy, and social competence are still developing. Scholars and clinicians have raised urgent questions about what these systems do to adolescents, and early findings point to both benefits and risks. In this article, we ask what adolescents do with AI and introduce the concept of adolescent agency over conversational AI use: the degree to which adolescents purposefully direct, critically evaluate, and set limits on their engagement with conversational AI. Existing constructs such as AI literacy and AI self-efficacy describe what young people know or believe about AI and the risks associated with its use, but they do not capture how adolescents exercise agency across areas of their lives. We identify nine processes that arise at the intersection of conversational AI’s features and key developmental tasks during the period of adolescence, which we label AI-ERA: autonomy, identity, emotion regulation, relationships, and achievement. We distinguish this agency from existing constructs, including agentic engagement with AI and AI overreliance, and then propose how it is shaped by adolescents’ developing capacities, adult scaffolding, and peer influence. We conclude with implications for families, schools, clinicians, and researchers, as well as considerations regarding the design, regulation, and ethics of AI systems.

articles.title: People With Lower Well-Being Show Longer and Less Stable Smartphone Use: A Large-Scale Analysis of 12 Datasets
articles.authors: Anna M Langener; Philip Chow; Aurelio Fernández; Nicholas C. Jacobson; Martien Kas; Anne Milek; Rüdiger Pryss; Theda Radtke; Ramona Schoedel; David de Segovia Vicente
articles.abstract: Debate over whether smartphone use relates to poorer well-being is limited by self-reports, small single-country samples, and a focus on average use. We harmonized objective app-use from 12 studies  (2,945 participants; 37,229 person-days; 851,865 person-hours) across five countries to examine associations of well-being with smartphone use and its variability. Additionally, we examined variations in smartphone use across age, gender identity, and time-of-day and day-of-week. Daily, participants averaged 3.27 hours of use (SD = 2.28), accessed 15.9 apps (SD = 6.16), and were unstable (40.6% of the total variation accounted for by within-person changes). Poorer well-being was associated with longer, more variable use; a depressive symptom increase of 10% of the scale range corresponded to 7 additional minutes of daily use and 7.5% higher within-person variance. Overall, younger persons and women used their phones more frequently, and higher wellbeing was related to consistently lower smartphone usage.

articles.title: Remembering how events unfold: Emotion and memory consolidation for naturalistic events
articles.authors: Charline Colson; Arnaud D'Argembeau
articles.abstract: Although emotional content is known to strengthen memory consolidation, its influence on how the unfolding of events is retained over time has received little attention. Building on the finding that negative events are remembered with less temporal compression and richer detail than neutral events, this study examined whether this emotional advantage changes over time, as would be expected if consolidation contributes to it. Participants viewed a series of negative and neutral videos and, either immediately or after a 24-hour or 72-hour delay, mentally replayed each event and verbally described it. Temporal compression was indexed by the ratio of video duration to replay duration, memory richness by narrative length and linguistic measures of episodic detail, and the preservation of event content by embedding-based similarity to descriptions produced during viewing. At immediate recall, negative events were replayed with less compression and described with more words and episodic detail than neutral events, replicating prior findings. After a delay, the emotional advantage in narrative length and episodic detail increased, and similarity to the video descriptions declined for neutral but not for negative events, whereas evidence for a corresponding increase in the emotion effect on temporal compression was less conclusive. These findings show that the emotional advantage in memory content for naturalistic, dynamic events is not fixed at encoding but increases over time, pointing to a role for consolidation.

articles.title: How AI chatbots shape political attitudes when they are not prompted to persuade
articles.authors: Sayeh Yousefi; Jens Koed Madsen
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots to find information, including information about politicians and political issues. Given evidence that Large Language Models (LLMs) have high persuasive capacities, this has raised concerns about their potential to have undue influence on political attitudes. However, most existing research on AI persuasion explicitly prompts the LLM to persuade the user, which is not representative of how people typically engage with LLMs. Whether undirected political conversations with LLMs shift political attitudes, and whether personalisation amplifies any such effect, remains unclear. We address these questions across two studies. First, in a quota-matched survey of UK adults (N = 2,137), we find that political use of AI is already widespread and its outputs are generally perceived as being politically neutral. Second, in a pre-registered randomised controlled trial (N = 2,081), participants conversed with an LLM about either a politician or political issue, with the LLM not being prompted to persuade. We find that conversations about politicians increased favourability toward them, while conversations about policies modestly reduced support. Conversation personalisation did not amplify these effects. Our findings show that AI chatbots are already a meaningful source of political information in the UK, and that undirected chatbot conversations can influence political attitudes.

articles.title: Early caregiving adversities and parental context effects on adolescents’ momentary emotion differentiation
articles.authors: Lior Abramson; Anna Vannucci; Camila Vicioso; Daniela Juarez; Erin Joyce; Andrea Fields; Erica Niemiec; Lisa Gibson; Niall Bolger; Nim Tottenham
articles.abstract: Emotion differentiation—the ability to identify specific experienced emotions—associates with psychological health. Although theorized to develop through caregiving experiences, contextual effects on emotion differentiation in developmental populations have rarely been investigated, particularly among youth who have experienced disruptions in early caregiving. Here, we examined how adolescents’ momentary emotion differentiation varies across socioemotional contexts and whether these patterns differ following exposure to severe caregiving-related early adversities. Adolescents aged 10–17 with or without caregiving-related early adversities (N=81; mean age=13.49, SD = 1.97; 53% male/47% female, 9%-Asian American, 28%-black, 34%-white, 28%-other) completed 7-day ecological momentary assessment (4–5 surveys/day), reporting emotions and social contexts. At the trait level, there were no significant group differences in emotion differentiation. At the momentary level, negative momentary emotion differentiation decreased following negative parent-related contexts compared to other contexts. However, the momentary emotions’ standard deviation indicated also differentiated phasic intensification of a few negative emotions. Importantly, exposure to caregiving-related early adversities attenuated these contextual effects, L.Ratio(3) = 9.178 - 11.263. These findings provide initial evidence linking severe caregiving-related early adversities to affective dynamic processes and raise the hypothesis that early caregiving disruptions mitigate momentary parental modulation effects on emotion differentiation.

articles.title: Beyond Turing Equivalence:  The Human Premium in Human–AI Interaction
articles.authors: Ophelia Deroy
articles.abstract: Asking whether we can know whether a given text or output is coming from a machine or a human, which was at the core of the Turing test, is being progressively retired. This opens a new and no less interesting question: what happens when we know? This paper reviews evidence that when humans encounter exactly the same content, presented here as coming from a human and there from an AI, they do not behave similarly. The evidence across different kinds of interaction, advice giving, compliance, reciprocal interaction, and preferential choice, is that humans respect other humans more than they respect machines. This difference is often described as a 'machine penalty' where we distrust machines or lack familiarity with them, and predicted to decrease as AI becomes more prevalent. The paper offers a different interpretation, showing that we treat humans better for good reasons, including utility calculations, and that this human premium is likely to stay.

articles.title: A database of subjective evaluation ratings for decision-making research
articles.authors: Kianté Fernandez; Sumedha Goyal; Ian Krajbich
articles.abstract: Subjective value ratings guide everyday choices, and value-based decision-making research collects them in many experiments. Yet the field has no common method for eliciting them. Studies use different response scales, instructions, and stimulus sets, and their ratings are rarely shared in a form that allows them to be used together. We present the Liking Initiative, a curated database of 759,399 individual ratings from 38 studies (59 datasets) covering 2,217 items, rated by 5,377 participants summed across datasets. Each rating is provided along with dataset-level metadata documenting the response scale, the question asked, and the source publication. The database is available through a web application, versioned releases on Zenodo, and R and Python packages. Because many items were rated in more than one dataset, item-level ratings can be compared across samples, response scales, and laboratories.

articles.title: What Makes a Child Go Bad? Genes, Choice, and Punishment in Original Sin
articles.authors: Madelief Isabel Kuijper; Kassandra Pomper; Josefina Benita Bernardo; Selim Sametoğlu; Elsje van Bergen
articles.abstract: This review reflects on Kathryn Paige Harden’s Original Sin through discussions in our Educational Genetics lab. We consider the book’s treatment of behavioural genetics, responsibility, punishment, religion, and parenting, highlighting both the power of Harden’s personal perspective and the limitations of its strongly American Evangelical framing. We conclude by reflecting on what science can, and cannot, tell us about why individuals behave badly.

articles.title: Beyond problem solving: Adaptive reframing in human and artificial intelligence
articles.authors: Valerio Capraro; Antonio Lieto; Francesco Rea; Giulio Sandini; Alessandra Sciutti; Vittorio Gallese; Walter Quattrociocchi
articles.abstract: Research on human and artificial intelligence has largely focused on problem solving: given a predefined problem, can an agent produce an effective solution? Yet many real-world challenges cannot be captured by a fixed problem representation. They require agents not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when the original problem representation has become inadequate and must be revised to reflect new evidence or changes in the problem itself. We argue that this capacity, termed adaptive reframing, constitutes a fundamental but under-researched dimension of intelligence. We propose a multidisciplinary framework for studying adaptive reframing across neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, experimental economics and psychology, and complex systems. Adaptive reframing is defined as the capacity to revise the construction of a problem in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context. To support a systematic science of adaptive reframing, we introduce three complementary paradigms: the Dynamic Scenario Framing Task, the Perturbed Causal Model Task, and the Social-Affective Problem Setting Task. These paradigms provide a common framework for comparing humans and artificial agents in situations requiring problem reframing, and for building architecture-enhanced AI systems. We propose a shift from problem solving to adaptive problem framing as a central focus of intelligence research.

articles.title: What Fifty Years of Research on the Misinformation Effect Can Tell Us: A Meta-Analytic Review
articles.authors: Björn Alfons Edmar; Nathalie Shekila Anna Enquist; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: This meta-analysis examines the impact of misleading or incorrect information on subsequent reports of witnessed events, with the aim of identifying key moderators of the misinformation effect – defined as reduced accuracy following exposure to misinformation. We synthesized experimental studies using the three-phase misinformation paradigm published between 1975 and 2025. A three-level mixed-effects meta-regression model was used to account for effect size non-independence and to examine moderators, including retention interval, warnings, overall test performance, and study characteristics. Across 480 studies and 1,998 effect sizes (N = 59,079), the average misinformation effect was substantial (g = 0.694, 95% CI [0.259, 1.128]) and highly heterogeneous (σ2 = 0.697, I2 = 92.21%). Control condition accuracy was positively associated with the magnitude of the effect, and post-misinformation warnings significantly reduced it. In contrast to prior findings, post-event testing did not significantly moderate the effect. These findings support the robustness of the misinformation effect and suggest that it reflects a combination of memory-related and strategic processes. Given the substantial heterogeneity observed, the misinformation effect may be better conceptualized as a constellation of related phenomena rather than a single unified effect, with important implications for theory and applied settings such as eyewitness testimony.

articles.title: Latent Profiles on the Intelligence and Development Scales – 2 and their Relationship with Classifications of Dyslexia and ADHD
articles.authors: Linda Visser; Selma Anne José Ruiter; Marieke Timmerman
articles.abstract: Objectives: The aim of the current study was to get insight in intelligence and executive functioning profiles and their relation with gender and dyslexia and ADHD classifications. Methods: We performed a latent profile analysis on IDS-2 data from 3,954 Dutch, German and Italian children (7 – 21 years). Results: The results showed six profiles differing in overall cognitive level. Three profiles were relatively balanced (below-average, low-average, and average), one showed high-average scores with a clear strength in visual short-term memory and two showed only slight strengths and weaknesses. There were large gender differences between the profile, amongst which a clear overrepresentation of boys in the profile with balanced below-average scores. This profile, along with the one with low-average scores, had relatively high rates of classifications for both ADHD and dyslexia and scholastic skills in the low-average range. For the other profiles, the scholastic skills scores were largely comparable to those on intelligence and executive functioning. Conclusion: Our results do not support the idea that ADHD or dyslexia classifications are related to specific weaknesses in a cognitive profile. This highlights the need for individualized assessment that takes into account both acquired academic competencies and innate cognitive capacities.

articles.title: Cognitive Assessment Tools Developed or Adapted for Indigenous Populations in North America, South America, and Oceania: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Jaden Seligman; Marianne Galliez; Anne-Marie Ergis; Benjamin Boller
articles.abstract: Objective: Cognitive assessment tools are important for understanding cognitive performance and identifying cognitive impairment. However, many commonly used cognitive assessment tools were developed and validated within Western cultural and linguistic contexts, which may limit their validity and cultural appropriateness for Indigenous populations. This review examines the existing literature on cognitive assessment tools used with Indigenous populations and evaluates the methodological quality of these studies and the cultural adaptations made to these tools. Method: A systematic search was conducted across six databases and was limited to studies examining cognitive performance in Indigenous populations. Citations were imported into Covidence, where titles and abstracts were screened for relevance. Data were extracted by two independent reviewers; study selection was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram. Studies were evaluated for risk of bias and methodological rigour using the NOS-xs, NOS, and CCAT critical appraisal tools. Results: Sixty studies were included, from North America (n=21), South America (n=10), and Oceania (n=29). Studies demonstrating greater methodological rigour frequently employed community-based participatory research (CBPR) approaches, involving community consultation to develop, adapt, and administer tests in culturally appropriate ways. Methodological rigour varied across studies, largely because of limited sample sizes in these populations. Conclusions: Establishing appropriate normative data can provide more valid reference points for interpreting cognitive performance in Indigenous populations. Cognitive assessments should be adapted to reflect cultural and linguistic differences, and further research on diverse Indigenous populations globally is needed. Risk of bias scores should be interpreted with caution, as existing critical appraisal approaches may not adequately capture culturally relevant methodological considerations. Future research should aim to develop more appropriate tools for critically appraising research involving Indigenous populations. This systematic review was registered in the OSF registry, with registration number 10.17605/OSF.IO/436Q8.

articles.title: Development and Preliminary Psychometric Validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire: Associations with Social Networking Addiction and Nomophobia
articles.authors: Divyansh Pandey; Arnav Bhavsar; Alok Bajpai
articles.abstract:
Objective: This study aimed to develop and conduct preliminary psychometric validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire (G-SMCQ) and examine its associations with social networking addiction (SNA) and nomophobia (NMP) using the Triguna framework from Indian psychology.
Method: Participants were 106 Indian undergraduate students (86 males, 20 females; aged 16–20 years, M = 18.05, SD = 0.72). A cross-sectional design evaluated the preliminary psychometric properties of the G-SMCQ and its relationships with the Social Networking Addiction Scale and the Nomophobia Questionnaire.
Results: MCA provided some preliminary evidence that the G-SMCQ response patterns were characterised by a multidimensional structure. Mean scores for the three Gunas indicated that Sattvic consumption was 9.86 (SD = 4.24), Rajasic consumption was 5.97 (SD = 3.66), and Tamasic consumption was 1.17 (SD = 1.75). Internal consistency reliability coefficients for the three Gunas were reported to be .840, .776, and .697, respectively. The relationship between Sattvic consumption and social networking addiction and nomophobia was negative (SNA: ρ = −.530, p < .001; NMP: ρ = −.295, p = .002), while Rajasic consumption was positively correlated to both constructs (SNA: ρ = .463, p < .001; NMP: ρ = .284, p = .003). However, Tamasic consumption was correlated to SNA (ρ = .270, p = .005) only, but not with nomophobia (ρ = .157, p = .109).
Conclusion: The results provided some preliminary psychometric evidence that suggests the potential of the G-SMCQ as a culturally-grounded measure of the Triguna-based social media consumption patterns.
Keywords: Social Media Consumption; Social Networking Addiction; Nomophobia;
Triguna Theory; Digital behavior

articles.title: The Cultural Evolution of Analytic and Holistic Thought: How Informational Ecologies shape Bayesian Reasoning
articles.authors: Tian Chen Zeng; Ivan Kroupin; Rahul Bhui; Joseph Henrich
articles.abstract: A growing body of evidence suggests that human cognition is shaped by culture, affecting processes from attention and memory to causal inference and concept representation. Such psychological differences are often described in terms of the analytic-holistic spectrum of cognitive styles. However, a unified mechanistic account of this variation remains elusive. In this paper, drawing on concepts from computational cognitive science and cultural evolution, we propose that the analytic-holistic spectrum reflects cognitive adaptations to different information ecologies. Cultural traits such as social organization, communication norms and prevalent learning modalities determine how observations are sampled, thereby affecting how much people should weigh parsimony when building mental models. We propose that information ecologies associated with holistic thought produce observations that more loosely reflect underlying structure (``weak sampling''), whereas those associated with analytic thought produce more diagnostic observations (``strong sampling''). These regimes license weaker and stronger applications of Bayesian Occam's Razor, respectively, which we show can provide a unified mechanism for cognitive differences along the analytic-holistic spectrum. By offering a computational lens on one of the most prominent empirical patterns in cultural psychology, we pave the way toward further informational-ecological accounts of how culture shapes cognition.

articles.title: Strategi Keluarga Tangguh Menjalani Pernikahan Jarak Jauh
articles.authors: Dwi Hardani Oktawirawan
articles.abstract:
Pernikahan jarak jauh terjalin karena berbagai macam latar belakang. Alasan yang mendasari bisa terkait dengan pekerjaan, pendidikan, hingga tugas keluarga. Hubungan yang dijalin dengan adanya jarak ruang tentu memunculkan berbagai tantangan. Permasalahan yang muncul seperti keterbatasan komunikasi, rasa kesepian, pembagian tugas dalam berkeluarga, hingga adanya kecurigaan terhadap pasangan dan potensi terjadinya perselingkuhan. Tantangan-tantangan tersebut harus dihadapi dengan berbagai macam strategi.

Berbagai macam upaya dapat dilakukan untuk menjaga kualitas dan ketahanan hubungan pernikahan jarak jauh. Upaya yang melibatkan pasangan bisa seperti menjaga komunikasi, terbuka, pengertian, menjaga komitmen, mengelola pembagian tugas, dan memaksimalkan waktu bertemu. Secara pribadi masing-masing pasangan dapat berpikir secara positif, melakukan aktivitas pengalihan, menjaga pergaulan, hingga cara lain dengan pendekatan religius. Adanya dukungan orang lain seperti teman dan keluarga juga dapat menjadi salah satu cara menjaga ketahanan hubungan pernikahan jarak jauh. Jarak yang secara fisik memisahkan pasangan tidak menjadi penghalang bagi keluarga pernikahan jarak jauh untuk membangun hubungan secara maksimal seperti keluarga lainnya.

articles.title: Explicit affective inferences enhance behavioral sensitivity to naturalistic expressions
articles.authors: Doron Atias; Maria Gendron
articles.abstract: Emotion theories highlight the fundamental function of emotional expressions in regulating social behavior. Yet, this basic premise relies mostly on studies using posed expressions that may fail to capture the diversity of real-life emotional signals and invite explicit affective inferences due to their salient symbolic nature. Across three studies (N=1,529), we tested how naturalistic emotional expressions differentially shape affective judgments and prosocial behavior. Participants watched videos of distressed individuals expressing typical crying, atypical crying, typical laughter, or no vocalization, and either inferred the targets’ affect (Study 1) or donated real money to help them from a provided budget (Study 2). Perceivers were sensitive to the vocal crying variation when explicitly inferring affect, but not when making donation decisions. Importantly, when perceivers explicitly inferred affect before donating (Study 3), they donated nearly 40% more and showed increased sensitivity to vocal cue variation. These findings suggest that inferring other people’s affect when making behavioral decisions is not routine and can facilitate helping behavior and the sensitivity to others’ emotional signals. This also highlight the important role of explicit inferential processes in linking real-life emotional expressions to prosocial behavior in everyday life.

articles.title: Old Test, New Tricks: Using Large Language Models to Generate New Divergent Thinking Test Items
articles.authors: Averie Elizabeth Linnell; Simone A Luchini; Austin Swanson; Roni Reiter-Palmon; Roger Beaty; Antonio Laverghetta
articles.abstract: Automated item generation (AIG) using large language models (LLMs) is emerging as a promising solution for scalable creativity assessments, yet the potential of AIG to create psychometrically rigorous creativity items has thus far received little attention. In the present study, we evaluated the psychometric properties of LLM-generated items for the classic Consequences task of divergent thinking, comparing them to human-written items. A sample of 192 undergraduates completed six Consequences tasks—two human-written, two standard LLM-generated, and two genre-inspired LLM-generated, drawing on sci-fi and fantasy themes—along with measures of personality, cognitive ability, and creative behavior. We found that LLM-generated items elicited significantly higher fluency and flexibility. Genre-inspired items (fantasy and sci-fi) additionally elicited higher originality, enjoyment, and positive valence ratings; LLM-generated items were similar to human-written items. Genre-inspired items did not unfairly advantage participants with more exposure to genre content, demonstrating measurement invariance. Together, these findings suggest that LLMs can generate consequences items with psychometric properties comparable to those of human-written items. We discuss the implications for creativity assessment, item bank development, and best practices for AIG in creativity research, and we provide the prompts we used for item generation to enable researchers to generate new Consequences items at scale.

articles.title: Dynamic Semantic–Prosodic Integration in Emotional Speech Perception: From Channel Dominance to Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Yang Zhang
articles.abstract: Emotional speech is an important carrier of affective information in spoken communication. Its perception depends on the joint processing of emotional semantics and prosody, yet the relative contribution of these two information sources varies across individuals and contexts. However, a unified account is still lacking of why their processing weights change and how the brain dynamically adjusts them according to the reliability of incoming information. This review synthesizes evidence on emotional semantics and prosody, from relatively independent processing to interactive integration, and argues that their relationship is best understood in terms of dynamic weight allocation. On this basis, we propose a Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding Model (PW-PC), which integrates Bayesian inference, cue precision, and prediction error within a unified framework. The model assumes that semantic and prosodic information are continuously reweighted according to current evidence and its estimated precision, while incorporating sensory reliability, experience-based expectations, contextual diagnosticity, and reweighting flexibility. This framework shifts the focus of emotional speech research from identifying which channel dominates to explaining when, why, and how the brain dynamically reallocates weight across multiple affective information sources, thereby providing a unified theoretical perspective linking behavioral performance, neural dynamics, and computational mechanisms.

articles.title: Functional Neuroanatomy of Sign Language Production: An ALE Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Lydia Wiernik; Angela D. Friederici; Karen Emmorey; Patrick C. Trettenbrein
articles.abstract: Sign languages are natural languages expressed by a distinct set of linguistic articulators: the hands, face, and body. Several neuroimaging studies of the neural substrates underlying sign production have observed the recruitment of brain regions previously identified as being involved in speech production, despite the difference in production channels. However, no prior work has provided a statistical synthesis of this available literature. Here, we report a pre-registered meta-analysis of the published positron emission tomography (PET) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) literature on sign language production (N experiments = 15, N participants = 168). Combining an Activation Likelihood Estimation (ALE) approach with jackknife re-sampling to validate the robustness of our findings, we identify four clusters consistently associated with the production of single signs across studies in the literature located in (1) left inferior frontal gyrus including BA 45 and extending into (2) left anterior insula, (3) the left superior frontal gyrus, and (4) the medial and right cerebellum. Meta-analytic connectivity modelling using data from a large-scale database of neuroimaging studies confirmed that the IFG, insula, and SFG clusters observed for sign language production are also recruited for spoken language production and comprehension. Moreover, our results also highlight the importance of the cerebellum during sign production and indicate modality-dependent convergence patterns in cerebellar subregions. In sum, our findings complement prior work on sign language comprehension and spoken language production, suggesting substantial overlap in the neural substrates of language processing and production-related mechanisms between sign and spoken language.

articles.title: Beyond speed and beyond prediction: The multi-faceted nature of speech processing in preschoolers and how it relates to language development
articles.authors: Meg Cychosz; Sonia Patrizi; Amy Martinez
articles.abstract:
Efficient language processing requires both prediction and flexible revision. Studies show young children can predict during online language processing, but less is known about their ability to quickly revise interpretations when initial predictions are infelicitous. We examined four- and
five-year-olds’ (N=60) phonological revision using an eye-tracking paradigm that captured children’s initial interpretation of a word and their subsequent revision and recovery. On average, word mispronunciations slowed children’s looks to the target object. But that average hid different responses: some children initially treated the mispronounced word as a new word before settling on the target one, while others treated it as the target word from the start. Standard analyses of children’s looking data often capture how quickly and completely looks converge on a target, not a trajectory that involves hypothesis and revision. We therefore characterized each child’s looking trajectory along numerous dimensions spanning mispronunciation sensitivity, rejection, recovery, and word-recognition efficiency. Children whose processing profiles showed the least rejection and revision had modestly lower vocabulary and phonological awareness scores, consistent with Bayesian inference and error-driven learning accounts in which the probabilistic prediction and resolution of mismatches may drive language development. Overall, preschoolers vary widely in how flexibly, not just how quickly, they interpret unexpected pronunciations, with implications for language development.

articles.title: A Biosocial Approach to Molecular Research in Perinatal Mental Health: Insights from Allopregnanolone
articles.authors: Gabriella Mayne; Luwam Ghidei; K Joseph Hurt; Wei Perng; David P. Tracer
articles.abstract: Pregnancy requires dynamic physiological adaptation across multiple biological systems implicated in perinatal mental health. Researchers increasingly recognize the importance of social and structural determinants of maternal mental health, yet integrating these conditions with molecular research remains challenging. A biosocial approach builds on these efforts by asking what conditions – both biological and social – contribute to the molecular variation we observe. In this Perspective, we use allopregnanolone (ALLO), a progesterone-derived neuroactive steroid implicated in perinatal mental health, to illustrate this approach. Evidence reviewed here shows that ALLO is patterned across social and physiological contexts, while associations between ALLO and depression, anxiety, and psychosocial distress during pregnancy remain heterogeneous. These observations highlight two priorities for biosocial molecular research: better characterization of the contexts in which molecular variation occurs and direct testing of what those contexts contribute to our understanding of ALLO in perinatal mental health. A biosocial approach does not replace biological explanation with social explanation; it asks whether better characterization of both changes what we observe. This means measuring social experiences alongside physiological characteristics, then asking whether these conditions contribute to ALLO variation or shape its associations with psychosocial distress. Such approaches can investigate how adversity becomes biologically embodied and how supportive conditions may promote maternal adaptation and well-being. Recognizing biological plasticity is central to this work: molecular variation can reflect dynamic responses to ongoing conditions rather than fixed characteristics of individuals or populations. Molecular variation should not be treated as the endpoint of inquiry, but as a starting point.

articles.title: Repetition increases belief more for trivia statements than news headlines
articles.authors: Raunak M Pillai; Steven Yang; Qiwenjing Jiang; Lisa Fazio
articles.abstract: Repetition increases belief in true and false statements. This “illusory truth effect,” has been documented across dozens of experiments using materials ranging from trivia statements to claims about consumer products to political news. Further, current theories of the effect focus on low-level psychological cues like processing fluency that arise spontaneously and that should affect judgements of truth uniformly for all such types of statements. In contrast to this picture, we find that the size of the illusory truth effect varies for different types of statements, with larger effects occurring when people see banal trivia statements as opposed to political or viral, health-related news headlines. We report six studies (total N = 1,749 US MTurkers) demonstrating this effect or testing potential explanations. We find that these differences appear to be driven by the overall context of the type of statements participants encounter rather than features of each individual statement. These findings speak to the malleable nature of the link between repetition and belief, with repetition being more a more impactful contributor to beliefs in contexts where people are saying some kinds of statements (e.g., trivia statements) than others (e.g., political or health-related news).

articles.title: No evidence of phonosymbolic effects in Polish echoic reduplications with sr-
articles.authors: Antonio Benítez-Burraco; Mingshan Xu; Monika Lisowska
articles.abstract: Expressives (i.e. linguistic items used for conveying emotions) can be phonosymbolic in nature or culturally-motivated. In Polish, echoic reduplicated sequences with the formant sr- are frequently used to convey contempt. We conducted an online survey to determine whether sr- is universally associated with this emotion. We tested speakers of Polish, but also of 2 other Indo-European languages (English and Spanish), and 3 non-Indo-European languages (Hungarian, Turkish and Indonesian). Findings suggest that only Polish speakers associate sr- with contempt, but less than expected. This suggests that this association does not result from any phonosymbolic effect or is typical of Indo-European languages generally. But is confined instead to Polish language, seemingly because sr- is the onset of one derogatory term in this language (srać). Still, the effect is stronger when concerning real words compared to pseudowords.

articles.title: Real-Time Associations Between Emotional Responses to Social Media and Mood Differ By Adolescent: Implications For Risk and Resilience
articles.authors: Melissa J Dreier; Jennifer Susan Silk; Evan Kleiman; Jessica L. Hamilton
articles.abstract: Adolescents differ in their vulnerability to social media’s mental health effects. Some may experience stronger links between emotional reactions to social media (ERSM) and mood, increasing risk for subsequent mental health problems. In the current study, 131 adolescents (ages 14–17) completed baseline assessments and eight weeks of ecological momentary assessment (3x/day). A dynamic structural equation model tested group-level and person-specific relationships between negative ERSM and depressed mood, controlling for prior mood. Adolescents showed substantial heterogeneity in ERSM-mood relationships. Stronger coupling was associated with baseline depression, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and nonsuicidal self-injury, but not suicide attempts. Throughout the study, stronger coupling was associated with higher depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, and mood volatility. It was not associated with the frequency or intensity of negative ERSM or in-person experiences or emotion regulation strategies. Taken together, adolescents whose mood is more strongly tied to ERSM may be at heightened risk for mental health problems.

articles.title: What beliefs are most debunkable?
articles.authors: Esther Boissin; Thomas H Costello; David Gertler Rand; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can persuade people to revise their beliefs, but it is unclear which beliefs are most "debunkable," and why. Across three pooled studies, participants (N = 3,341 online U.S. adults) discussed a self-reported conspiracy or other epistemically suspect belief with GPT-4, instructed to debunk it using facts and evidence. An LLM classified each belief by content domain (i.e., conspiratorial, paranormal/supernatural, pseudoscience, political, religious, other) and evidential status, from strong counterevidence to supported by evidence. Confidence decreased in every domain, but belief updating tracked evidential status rather than domain: reductions were substantial wherever the belief was open to counterevidence — strong, weak, or uninvestigated — and small for non-falsifiable and supported beliefs. Domain no longer predicted change once evidential status was accounted for, and the counterevidence the LLM deployed partially mediated the gradient. AI debunking appears most effective for falsifiable beliefs resting on weak evidence.

articles.title: Redundancy Protects Human Collaborations from Failure
articles.authors: Elizabeth Mieczkowski; Rachit Dubey; Natalia Vélez; Thomas L. Griffiths
articles.abstract: In the name of efficiency, organizations and governments around the world are increasingly trimming redundancy---personnel or overlapping capabilities beyond what routine operations require. Drawing on distributed computing and cognitive science, we challenge this view. Using queueing simulations and a preregistered multiplayer experiment (N = 832 in 187 teams of 3–6), we show that redundancy improves performance through two distinct routes. Adding collaborators to a team improves resilience, with larger teams completing more tasks when members became temporarily unable to contribute. Giving team members overlapping capabilities also improved efficiency, with teams in which collaborators could perform multiple roles completing substantially more work. These findings suggest that efforts to improve short-term efficiency by reducing redundancy may come at a cost, quietly eroding a team’s capacity to withstand unexpected failures.

articles.title: Multiple neural signatures of serial order access in verbal working memory
articles.authors: Giulia Cristoforetti; Yangwen Xu; Simone Viganò; Jean Philippe van Dijck; Roberto Bottini; Wim Fias
articles.abstract: Serial order working memory allows information to be maintained as structured sequences, yet the neural formats supporting access to serial position remain unclear. Behavioral evidence suggests that temporal order can be recoded into spatial representations, but serial order may also rely on representations that generalize beyond the spatial configuration of encoding. Here, participants memorized digit sequences presented either left-to-right or right-to-left, thereby reversing the mapping between ordinal position and external space while keeping retrieval cues centrally presented during fMRI. Behaviorally, spatial coding during retrieval was modulated by encoding direction. Multivoxel pattern analysis revealed direction-specific decoding in lateral parietal cortex: left inferior parietal cortex encoded serial position after left-to-right encoding, whereas right inferior parietal cortex did so after right-to-left encoding. In contrast, cross-direction decoding revealed direction-invariant effects in left supramarginal and precentral regions, suggesting serial-position information that generalized across spatial layouts. Finally, univariate parametric modulation revealed activity scaling with serial position in bilateral posterior parietal cortex, left anterior hippocampus, and action-control regions. Together, these findings indicate that serial order access in working memory relies on multiple neural signatures, including spatially context-dependent representations, direction-invariant ordinal codes, and graded process-related activity.

articles.title: Nonverbal Cognition is Associated with Discourse Production in Persons with Aphasia: Evidence from Expository and Picture Description Tasks
articles.authors: Hana Kim; Manaswita Dutta
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Spoken discourse analysis has gained empirical and clinical attention, yet current practice predominantly relies on picture-based tasks which may not fully capture the language impairments experienced by persons with aphasia (PWA) in more complex contexts. Expository discourse, though more cognitively demanding and structurally complex, remains under-researched in aphasia despite its ecological relevance. This study aimed to (1) compare nonverbal cognitive abilities in PWA and neurologically healthy adults (NHA); (2) examine the effects of discourse task by comparing expository and picture description performance in PWA; and (3) investigate associations between nonverbal cognitive abilities and discourse outcomes. 
Method: Participants (PWA = 24; NHA = 13) completed nonverbal cognitive tasks that assess processing speed, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. They also completed expository discourse tasks (expressing opinions on the healthcare system and homeschooling). Discourse samples were analyzed using six variables (MATTR, Percent CIU, Verbs per utterance, syntactic complexity, local and global coherence) selected to represent linguistic, propositional, and macrostructural domains in discourse.
Results: Significant group differences were found in cognitive flexibility task accuracy, and response times on tasks measuring cognitive flexibility and processing speed. In expository discourse, PWA performed worse than NHA across the linguistic, propositional, and macrostructural domains. Notably, task comparisons revealed that expository discourse elicited greater performance in syntactic complexity but poorer coherence than the picture description task in PWA. Cognitive influences on discourse differed by tasks and groups: in PWA, cognitive flexibility generally showed strong associations with all discourse domains across both tasks, with fewer correlations for the picture description task. Also, the pattern of associations varied across cognitive tasks and discourse measures for the picture description task. No significant associations were observed among controls. 
Conclusion: Findings highlight the unique interplay between cognitive and linguistic skills in the expository task. This finding supports the potential use of expository discourse in aphasia assessment.

articles.title: Cognitive constraints govern collective outcomes in strategic network formation
articles.authors: Hicham DAHMOU; Frédéric Moisan; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Social networks are built through local decisions, yet the value of a connection depends on paths that individuals cannot fully observe. How such bounded information shapes collective efficiency remains unclear. Here we develop a computational model in which agents revise links using a limited view of the network, an expectation about connections beyond that view, and stochastic choice. Starting from an inefficient empty network, the model reaches near-efficient structures within an intermediate regime: agents must value unseen opportunities enough to initiate connectivity, but not so strongly that continued linking prevents the removal of redundant ties. This favorable regime narrows as groups grow, although broader visibility partly restores it and agent heterogeneity preserves its qualitative form. Earlier action or link receipt is associated with eventual hub status, while stable agent-level decision parameters are associated with persistent payoff ranks across repeated networks. Introducing one agent that forms links without considering payoffs reduces welfare in small groups but increases it in larger groups, while concentrating costs on the builder. These results identify a scale-dependent balance between exploration, local representation and value-sensitive pruning through which bounded individual decisions can generate collective efficiency and structural inequality.

articles.title: Comprehenders’ Error Correction Mechanisms are Finely Calibrated to Language Production Statistics
articles.authors: Peng Qian; Roger Philip Levy
articles.abstract: An essential feature of human communication is robustness to errors: even when speakers and writers make mistakes, listeners and readers can usually determine the intended meaning. A leading hypothesis is that comprehenders achieve robust error correction by internally deploying a "noisy-channel" model of the language production process. Crucially, to best achieve error robustness, a comprehender's noisy-channel model should be finely calibrated to the environmental statistics of language production, incorporating not only prior expectations about communicative intents but also structure-sensitive likelihoods of different types of speaker error. This environmentally-calibrated noisy-channel hypothesis has been difficult to test, because the rates of most types of language production errors are hard to estimate. Here we test this hypothesis by experimentally investigating comprehenders' interpretations of subject-verb agreement errors, for which context-contingent language production error rates are feasible to estimate. In a novel free-form error correction task,  participants edited sentences with subject-verb agreement mismatches to indicate what they think was intended. Bayesian analysis of the resulting data shows that comprehenders' interpretations reflect both item-specific prior expectations and structure-sensitive error likelihoods that closely correspond to error rates in language production. These results provide quantitative evidence that humans closely track prior statistics over linguistic forms and deploy a noisy-channel model finely calibrated to statistics of the linguistic environment to achieve robust language understanding.

articles.title: Green Against the Machine: Natural Environment Exposure Attenuates Subjective and Physiological Responses to Technostress Across Levels of Agency
articles.authors: Simone Di Plinio; Claudia Greco; David Perpetuini; Massimo De Acetis; Miriam D'Ignazio; Arcangelo Merla; Daniela Cardone; Sjoerd Ebisch
articles.abstract: Urban living often limits routine contact with nature, while digital technologies have become deeply embedded in everyday life and cognition. Yet technological malfunctions, intrusions, and diminished user agency can elicit technostress, raising the question of whether exposure to natural environments can buffer its effects. This study examined whether exposure to a natural (green) environment, compared with a built urban (gray) environment, attenuates psychophysiological responses to technostress. Fifty-two healthy adults were assigned to either a green (garden-like) or gray (built urban) environment. Before and after two outdoor walking sessions in the assigned environment, participants completed a word-selection task manipulating technology-induced stress and sense of agency. High-resolution infrared thermal imaging was used as a contact-free method to monitor facial temperature dynamics, providing indirect indices of peripheral autonomic regulation during task performance, while heart rate variability (HRV) was monitored as an index of cardiac autonomic activity during task performance.
