Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Advancing Global Social Science through Cross-Societal Online Behavioral Economic Games (CoBEx): Lessons Learned and A Practical Guide
articles.authors: Shuxian Jin; Vanessa Christina Clemens; Laura Carlotta Hoenig; Carsten De Dreu; Angela Rachael Dorrough; Catherine Molho; Marina Orifici; Angelo Romano; Shaul Shalvi; Ayse K. Uskul
articles.abstract: Understanding human behavior across diverse cultural settings is essential for advancing theories that address pressing global social challenges. Recent advances, which use an innovative methodology—cross-societal online behavioral economic games (CoBEx)—have revealed key insights into cross-cultural differences and similarities in the mechanisms and functions of human behavior. To foster this emerging field, we discuss the key successes and lessons learned from ten years of experience in designing and conducting CoBEx studies. We illustrate the theoretical and methodological benefits of CoBEx, and offer practical recommendations on key design considerations, study materials preparation, ethics and funding, as well as analysis, interpretation, and dissemination processes. This paper aims to equip researchers around the globe with the necessary tools to conduct methodologically rigorous and culturally informed CoBEx studies, ultimately advancing the field of psychological science and beyond.

articles.title: Who can re-enter the loop? A scoping review on cognitive abilities and task re-engagement in human-AI interaction
articles.authors: Han Zhang; Bianca Done; Stefanie Schneider; Nithya Rajan; Manhua Wang
articles.abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) promise a near future in which humans and AI systems work together to solve complex problems. Although offloading tasks to AI reduces immediate cognitive demands, the system may later require human input or decision-making, at which point the human must “re-enter the loop” by redirecting attention, reconstructing the task state, and responding appropriately. Whether individual differences in cognitive ability predict the capacity to re-enter the loop remains unclear. Here, we conducted a scoping review of studies relating cognitive ability to loop re-entry performance. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Among them, most studies examined conditionally automated driving, and none examined interactions with generative AI systems. Working memory capacity was the most frequently studied ability and was generally associated with better loop re-entry performance, whereas results for attentional control were mixed. The evidence was further limited by small samples, single-task measures of cognitive abilities, and inconsistent outcome measures. As human oversight becomes increasingly central to AI safety, understanding who can re-enter the loop effectively remains an important open question. We offer concrete recommendations to guide future research.

articles.title: Conversation as data: Extracting features from naturalistic conversation datasets
articles.authors: Emma Templeton; Luke J. Chang
articles.abstract: In this chapter, we outline important considerations for designing and analyzing conversation studies. We first advocate for the use of representative designs to ensure that datasets adequately reflect the complexity inherent in conversation. We then focus on how behavior in conversation recordings can be quantified through a process of feature extraction, and discuss strategies to assess the validity of feature extraction pipelines. Finally, we discuss analytical considerations specific to working with conversation data. Being able to rigorously collect, operationalize, and analyze natural conversation data will lead to robust results that the entire field can build upon, advancing our understanding of exactly how conversation allows us to achieve our social goals.

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, in nearly all cases, one must register in order to vote—yet, a substantial portion of the eligible electorate remains unregistered. Despite this, relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that a voter registers. Here, we tested the impact of 10 expert-crowdsourced, theoretically-based psychological interventions on a sample of eligible, yet unregistered, U.S. voters ahead of the 2024 presidential election (N = 12,896). Eight of the interventions increased intentions to vote, and five led individuals to click on the voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, which sequentially employed several social pressure strategies, was the strongest intervention across these outcomes. However, none of the interventions had a significant effect on actual voter registration or voter turnout. The results highlight a substantial disconnect between voters’ intentions and their ultimate behaviors. We discuss potential structural and psychological barriers that undermine the translation of intent into action.

articles.title: Validity, Diagnostic Accuracy, and Feasibility of Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality for Mild Cognitive Impairment
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Antonia Ioakeimidou; Myrto Dimakopoulou; Christina Anastasopoulou; Maria Roussou; Petros Roussos; Chrysanthi Nega; Ion Beratis
articles.abstract:
Background: Immersive virtual reality (VR) adaptations of neuropsychological tests change how participants respond and must be validated in each clinical population. We evaluated the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze version of the paper-and-pencil Trail Making Test (hereafter, TMT) that records completion times and wrong-target selections automatically, in older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
Methods: In this case–control evaluation, 84 adults aged 60–89 years (42 with clinically diagnosed MCI, 42 healthy comparison participants) completed the TMT-VR, the TMT and the Mini-Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (M-ACE), with pre- and post-exposure cybersickness ratings. Planned analyses examined feasibility, convergence, group differences and diagnostic accuracy for all 26 TMT-VR scores against their TMT counterparts and the M-ACE, with demographic adjustment, multiplicity correction, bootstrap validation and education-matched sensitivity analysis.
Results: All participants completed both TMT-VR parts, and cybersickness ratings decreased over the session. Part B completion times correlated positively across formats within both groups. Participants with MCI were slower and made more wrong-target selections on TMT-VR Part B but not Part A. Score for score, the TMT-VR matched the TMT on Part B completion time and discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B, total and B−A error scores and every Part B-specific derived score; these effects persisted after demographic adjustment and widened in the education-matched subsample. The TMT's advantage lay in Part A completion time, and its error scores carried little discriminatory information. With education equalised, the TMT-VR B−A scores gave balanced operating characteristics and approached the M-ACE, which every TMT score remained below. The M-ACE discriminated more accurately than any single trail-making score of either format.
Conclusions: The TMT-VR is a feasible, well-tolerated adaptation with convergent validity against the TMT and known-groups validity for MCI. Because it discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B-specific and error-based scores that carry the test's executive demand, it emerges as the preferable Trail Making Test format within neuropsychological batteries for MCI; whether it adds diagnostic information beyond global screens such as the M-ACE must be established in consecutive clinical referrals, together with age- and education-stratified normative cut-offs.

articles.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
articles.authors: Brian W. L. Wong; Arthur G. Samuel; Efthymia C Kapnoula
articles.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

articles.title: Mapping Behavioural and Psychological Factors Associated with Engagement in Online Activism: A Critical Scoping Review
articles.authors: Benjamin Gibson; Jekaterina Schneider; Mark J. Forshaw
articles.abstract: Online activism can be a powerful means of supporting social and political engagement. However, there are genuine concerns that online behaviours do not translate into social and political action, while nascent research suggests that online activism may affect well-being and feelings of identity more negatively compared to traditional (i.e., in-person) forms of activism. This scoping review attempted to map out the evidence so that the reader may better understand the psychological and behavioural factors associated with engagement in online activism. A search of academic databases and registers identified 24 articles comprising 28 studies and examined various forms of online activism including hashtag campaigns, online petitions, and social media engagement. Online engagement was shown to support a range of (further) online and offline activist behaviours, to foster collective identities, and to provide psychological benefits such as increased self-efficacy and feelings of empowerment (which in turn encouraged further political action). However, contextual and individual factors likely influence both behaviours and opportunities for psychological benefits. This review highlights the blurred boundaries between online and offline activism, while evidencing that even “passive” digital engagement may serve as a gateway to broader civic participation.

articles.title: “Who Will Marry a Mad Doctor?”: A Qualitative Study of Associative Stigma Among Mental Health Professionals in India
articles.authors: Deepti Dilip Moar; Rajat Kanti Mitra; Sunil Mittal
articles.abstract: Mental health professionals (MHPs) can experience stigma through their professional association with mental illness and mental healthcare. Existing studies have often focused on particular professions, service populations, or specific aspects of associative stigma, making it difficult to identify recurring patterns across professions and beyond the workplace. This study explored associative stigma among MHPs in India across professional, family, and wider social contexts. Semi-structured interviews with 22 MHPs, including psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counsellors, psychiatric social workers, and psychiatric nurses, were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist framework. Eight themes were developed, spanning misconceptions about MHP roles and abilities, mistrust of expertise and motives, concerns about how mental health work might affect them, devaluation of mental health work, exclusion involving social distancing and concealment, role expectations extending beyond work, ambivalent responses in which admiration or reliance coexisted with misunderstanding, avoidance, or devaluation, and differences in professional standing. Across the analysis, experiences that might otherwise appear separate were connected by recurring meanings attached to mental illness and mental healthcare. The study broadens understanding of the social and professional reach of stigma surrounding mental illness. Through professional association, these meanings can shape how MHPs, their expertise, and mental health work are understood and valued.

articles.title: When the Same Leader Helps and Harms: Inconsistent Leadership Behavior in Team Meetings
articles.authors: Amelie Verena Güntner; Kai N. Klasmeier; Catrin Millhoff; Nora Gosch; Simone Kauffeld
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The same leader often displays constructive and destructive behaviors at once, a
phenomenon known as inconsistent leadership. Inconsistency has been linked to negative
follower outcomes, yet it has almost exclusively been studied as a follower perception. This
study examines inconsistent leadership as enacted behavior, asking how and under what
conditions the co-occurrence of instrumental and destructive leadership shapes team behavior in
meetings.
Design/methodology/approach: Using a multilevel moderated mediation model, we tested our
model on 30 videotaped team meetings (5,430 coded behaviors), rating leaders' instrumental and
destructive behavior and coding leaders' action planning and team members' conflict-related
communication.
Findings: Instrumental leadership was associated with more action planning, which in turn
reduced conflict-related communication, but only when destructive leadership was low. When
leaders behaved destructively alongside instrumental leadership, this indirect effect disappeared.
Practical implications: Occasional destructive behavior can undo the benefits of otherwise
constructive leadership, so what matters for teams is not only what leaders do well but whether
they do it consistently. Organizations can address this through leadership development that helps
leaders recognize and reduce inconsistent behavior in meetings.
Originality/value: Inconsistency has almost always been studied as a follower perception. This
study extends its consequences beyond follower attitudes to observable team communication and
to the leader's own planning, showing that inconsistency also shapes the enacting leader. It offers
a behavioral, micro-level operationalization that complements existing perception-based
measures.

articles.title: Perceptions of Profit Motive: For-Profit Companies are Judged Less Favourably Than Non-Profits Even When the Societal Benefits of Profit-Seeking are Made Salient
articles.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Martin Harry Turpin; Alexander C. Walker; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Derek J. Koehler
articles.abstract: People tend to view profit-seeking businesses more negatively than otherwise equivalent non-profit businesses or organizations. This tendency puts people at risk of missing out on the potential societal benefit that can emerge when profit-seeking motivations are aligned with prosocial goals. When making judgments about firms and businesses, people may simply neglect the possibility that profit-seeking could result in gains for society. The current research finds that people’s attitudes are more ambivalent (as opposed to strictly negative) when they consider, in a broader sense, examples of how profit-seeking companies could positively or negatively affect society (e.g., consumer and employee welfare, technological advances, etc.). Study 1 (N = 101) showed that people are open to endorsing both general (pro-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially beneficial outcomes and general (anti-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially harmful outcomes. In Study 2 (N = 301), we examined whether exposure to such statements highlighting the potential positive (or negative) societal impacts of profit-seeking affected participant’s judgements of for- and non-profit firms. Exposure to pro-profit and anti-profit statements did not impact people’s judgments of profit-seeking businesses. Instead, people consistently exhibited a tendency to judge for-profit companies as having a less positive societal impact in comparison with their non-profit counterparts. This anti-profit bias persisted even among participants who had expressed agreement with general statements about the ways in which profit-seeking companies can deliver societal benefits.

articles.title: THE EVOLUTION OF DYSLEXIA AS A MEDICAL, EDUCATIONAL, AND SOCIAL CONCEPT: A CONCEPTUAL ANALYSIS OF DYSLEXIA
articles.authors: Tyler Ogata
articles.abstract: Phenomena relating to reading difficulties assume many names but none more controversial than dyslexia. Previous historical accounts of the so-called “dyslexia debates” (Elliott & Grigorenko, 2024b; Kirby, 2020) focus on definitions of dyslexia that incorporate the assumption that dyslexia results from some specific, albeit not completely understood, neurobiological etiology of specific reading challenges. Similar disagreements appear presently in the form of competing conceptualizations of dyslexia (Elliott, 2020; Odegard et al., 2024) and their influence on the International Dyslexia Association’s 2025 definition of dyslexia. The ensuing conceptual analysis examines dyslexia according to its past, present, and possible future conceptualizations by highlighting the varied contexts in which dyslexia evolved, namely the fields of medicine, education, and disability. The analysis reveals that the concept of dyslexia has become entangled in paradigmatic differences between these contexts. It is suspected that these differences will continue to subject dyslexia to the same old debates and limit the translation of developing thought on dyslexia into meaningful service delivery systems. A sketch of an integrative framework is proposed to guide dyslexia’s future.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure and Symptom Profiles of the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS): A Meta-Analytic Mean and Covariance Structure Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Johanna Einsiedler; Timo Gnambs
articles_hidden.abstract: The Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) is one of the most widely used clinician-rated instruments for assessing depressive symptom severity, particularly in pharmacological intervention studies. Despite its widespread use, evidence on the dimensional structure of the MADRS remains inconsistent. In this Registered Report, we propose a meta-analytic mean and covariance structure analysis of the MADRS to examine (a) which latent structure best represents MADRS responses and how reliably its factors are measured, (b) whether items or symptom dimensions function differently across clinical (diagnostic group, pharmacological treatment, assessment time point within treatment) and measurement-related (language version) moderators, and (c) whether diagnostic groups, pharmacological treatment regimens, and treatment stages are associated with distinct latent symptom profiles.

articles_hidden.title: Eye-gaze dynamics reveal the adaptive nature of real-time noisy-channel inference in speech comprehension
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel Anna Ryskin
articles_hidden.abstract: To understand spoken language, listeners must extract meaning from acoustic input that is variable and noisy. The noisy-channel framework posits that listeners overcome this uncertainty by rationally inferring the speaker's intent, combining prior expectations with a model of how the message may have been corrupted during transmission. However, the exact nature of this noise model and its sensitivity to context (e.g., speaker or acoustic environment) remain unknown. Here, I use eye-tracking to measure human speech processing as it unfolds on the millisecond timescale, and I use the representational geometry of a self-supervised speech model (HuBERT) to estimate the noise model. I show that spoken word comprehension is well captured as real-time Bayesian belief updating. Further, listeners flexibly tune their expectation of noise to the specific acoustic environment. These results extend the noisy-channel framework to the moment-by-moment comprehension of speech. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that the human language system continuously adapts its internal model to the statistical structure of the communicative environment. By linking noisy-channel inference with real-time perceptual dynamics, this work highlights the remarkable flexibility of human cognition in navigating uncertainty and opens the door to investigating internal representations in human and artificial speech recognition systems through their fine-grained temporal dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Profiles in aesthetic engagement: A new survey and a snapshot of behavior in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Eileen R. Cardillo; Hannah Meghan Merseal; Raphael Englander; Anjan Chatterjee
articles_hidden.abstract: The measurement of art engagement, typically relies on narrow views of engagement, emphasizing attendance at fine arts institutions. Such approaches underestimate the variety of aesthetic participation and likely underrepresent groups who experience barriers to access or engage with aesthetics outside traditional art venues. The rise of digital modes of participation further challenges the adequacy of conventional assessments. To address these gaps, we developed the Assessment of Aesthetic Participation, a new survey that builds on the strengths of nationally administered National Endowment of the Arts surveys, and captures a broader spectrum of aesthetic behaviors, including everyday aesthetic activities, religious and heritage embedded practices, and digitally mediated engagement. To establish its utility for experimental research, we validated the Assessment of Aesthetic Participation against commonly used measures in empirical aesthetics—the Revised Aesthetic Fluency Scale and the Aesthetic Responsiveness Assessment. Results from a nationally representative U.S. sample (N=1501) replicate previously observed demographic trends related to age and education, while suggesting a more complex pattern for race and gender. An exploratory latent profile analysis suggested five distinct styles of engagement, differentiated by frequency and preferred activities: low participation by the Disengaged, intermediate but distinguishable patterns of the Spectator, the Fan, and the Enthusiast, and the highly engaged Aesthete. The Assessment of Aesthetic Participation offers a flexible, inclusive tool that addresses limits in existing measures of arts engagement, bridges the measurement needs of population-level and experimental researchers, and can advance future research on the benefits of aesthetic experiences.

articles_hidden.title: Growing Beyond Traits: A Skill-Based Approach to Volitional Personality Change
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher J. Soto; Christopher Napolitano; Madison Nicole Sewell; Heejun Roy Yoon; Tommaso Feraco; Nathan W. Hudson; Brent Roberts
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent research suggests that individuals can intentionally change their personality traits. This article proposes a complementary, skill-based approach to volitional change, arguing that social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills—defined as learned capabilities rather than dispositional tendencies—represent more direct and intuitive targets for intentional development. We introduce the Cumulative Practice Model (CPM), a framework that integrates principles from the personality development, clinical intervention, managerial coaching, and cognitive science literatures. This model proposes that the volitional development of SEB skills can occur most effectively through a repeating cycle of motivation, instruction, opportunity, practice, feedback, and skill change. We then review preliminary evidence supporting this model. This evidence indicates that individuals generally find developing SEB skills to be more desirable and feasible than changing personality traits. It further shows that skills exhibit plasticity across the lifespan, with both normative age trends and individual-level changes linked to relevant life experiences. Crucially, it suggests that interventions centered on deliberate practice can facilitate SEB skill development, and that gains in these skills are linked with positive life outcomes including academics, occupational interests, social relationships, health, and well-being. Thus, the Cumulative Practice Model offers a promising framework for individuals who wish to improve their SEB skills, practitioners who wish to facilitate skill development and growth, and researchers who wish to better understand the antecedents, process, conditions, and outcomes of volitional change. This skill-based approach to volitional change also highlights open questions and promising directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: What makes up the moral domain? Theory must answer to data
articles_hidden.authors: Meltem Yucel; Amrisha Vaish
articles_hidden.abstract: Jambon et al. (in press) seek to evaluate Yucel et al.’s (2022) proposal that fairness may be psychologically distinct from other, prototypical moral norms, and, in line with Social Domain Theory (SDT), to reassert fairness’ place within the moral domain. Here, we show that Jambon et al.’s own data and arguments, alongside a reanalysis of Yucel et al.’s (2022) data, undermine rather than support Jambon et al.’s claims. Across studies, fairness reliably differs from harm on the very measures (criterion judgments, justifications) the authors treat as diagnostic for establishing moral status. This pattern goes unaddressed by Jambon et al. in part because of inconsistent evidentiary standards as well as circular reasoning that assumes the very conclusion it seeks to demonstrate. These findings raise a more fundamental question: As currently conceived under SDT, to what extent does the “moral domain” constitute a psychologically coherent category?

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual Cues Can Influence Curiosity, Metamemory, and Memory Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Ashley Chen; Matthew Rhodes; Alan Castel
articles_hidden.abstract: Important information is often presented in large fonts, a tactic used to direct individuals’ attention and emphasize relevance. In a series of experiments, we tested whether font size, a perceptual cue that may communicate relative importance, may influence one’s curiosity, judgments of learning (JOLs), and recall. Participants were presented with lists of word pairs consisting of rare English words and their more commonly known synonyms. After being shown the rare word in small (12-point) or large (48-point) font, they rated how curious they were to learn its synonym, studied the synonym, and judged how likely they were to remember it at a later time before completing an immediate cued-recall test. We found that individuals exhibited greater curiosity towards large versus small items (Experiments 1a and 1b), but JOLs were unaffected by font size (Experiments 1a and 1c), perhaps due to a reliance on other perceptual cues (e.g., word structure, mental imagery) during encoding (Experiment 1c) or opportunities for pretesting attenuating the font-size JOL effect (Experiment 1d). Moreover, although large items were rated as more important to learn (Experiment 2), the positive relationship between font size and recall (Experiments 1 and 2) was only mediated by curiosity and not perceived importance (Experiment 2). Overall, our findings provide insight into how perceptual cues may influence how individuals select, process, and remember information, contributing to our understanding of how curiosity and memory are shaped by perceptual processes.

articles_hidden.title: Towards a Cognitive Science of Practical Wisdom for Ill-Defined Decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Abhishek Dedhe; Samuel Gregory Blane Johnson; Igor Grossmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Many challenges we face as individuals and collectives are ill-defined: What are the probabilities for different courses of action? How to compare distinct outcomes? Under such radical uncertainty, conventional optimization solutions fail, prompting calls for wisdom. Yet, the science of wisdom remains fragmented across disciplines. To fill this void, we reconstruct practical wisdom through the lens of cognitive science, asking what wisdom is for, how it works, and how it develops and evolves. Guided by criteria that make a cognitive science concept empirically tractable, formally precise, and continuous with broader theories of mind, we develop a two-level functional cognitive architecture of practical wisdom, in which evoked, higher-order metacognitive processes regulate a culturally-transmitted repertoire of object-level decision strategies. We outline formal elements of this architecture and examine its implications across persons, groups, societies, and natural and artificial intelligences. Finally, we derive testable predictions and close by asking what such a science offers back to the disciplines it draws on.

articles_hidden.title: The 2024 U.S. Election, Sexual and Gender Minority Adults’ Moving Plans, and Mental Health Symptoms: A Mixed-Methods Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Briana Shiri Last; Nguyen Tran; Dane Rivas-Koehl; Devin Hursey; Juno Obedin-Maliver; Mitchell Lunn; Annesa Flentje
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Since the 2024 U.S. Presidential election, the rights of sexual and gender minority (SGM) people have been at risk. The purpose of this mixed-methods study was to describe SGM people’s thoughts, plans, and decisions to move following the election and to examine whether these thoughts, plans, and decisions differed by participants’ sociodemographic characteristics and mental health symptoms. 
Methods: Participants completed an online survey between November 5, 2024 and September 20, 2025 for The PRIDE Study, a national, prospective, community-engaged cohort study of SGM adults. Participants responded to closed-ended questions about their: thoughts, plans, and decisions to move; sociodemographic characteristics; and mental health (anxiety, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder) symptoms. Participants responded to open-ended questions about their moving destinations and moving reasons. 
Results: The sample included 3,301 participants (48.1% identified as transgender or nonbinary [TNB]). Most participants (85%) thought about, planned to, or decided to move to another state or country. Moving considerations differed by participants’ sociodemographics (e.g., participants with moving thoughts, plans, and decisions were more likely to be TNB than cisgender, ps<.05) and mental health symptoms (e.g., participants with moving thoughts, plans, and decisions had more symptoms than those with no moving thoughts, ps<.05). Participants’ reasons for moving included the increasingly hostile and anti-SGM sociopolitical conditions in their states and the country. 
Conclusions and Policy Implications: Following the 2024 election, many SGM U.S. adults made plans to or decided to move due to the changing policy environment. Psychological distress from anti-SGM policies may be driving individuals to move.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the eight-week convention: A rapid review of assigned program architecture and temporal change in mindfulness-based programs
articles_hidden.authors: Barry Tse
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Mindfulness-based programs (MBPs) are commonly organized around eight weeks, yet direct experimental evidence on the consequences of varying this architecture is sparse. In a contextual inventory of 39 established programs, 11 of the 15 with an unqualified fixed-week structure used eight weeks.

Methods: This rapid review examined direct evidence on assigned program length, session intensity, pacing, outcome and mechanism trajectories, and postprogram maintenance. APA PsycINFO was searched through Ovid from inception to September 3, 2026. The review used one database and one reviewer, and no protocol was prospectively registered. All 301 records were screened and 81 full texts were assessed. Risk of bias was appraised with tools matched to study design, and certainty was assessed for eight synthesis claims using an adapted Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach.

Results: Fifty-two reports representing 47 studies were included. Five reports directly compared assigned architectures that varied different dimensions; the remainder mainly described trajectories under one assigned program. Randomized length comparisons did not demonstrate reliable between-length differences, but none was designed to establish equivalence. In the largest controlled trajectory, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction first showed statistically detected separation from usual care at session 2 for sleep, 4 for physical function, 6 for pain intensity, 7 for pain interference, and 8 for depression; these were power-dependent statistical crossing points, not minimum effective durations. The session of first detected separation also differed across mechanisms, mechanism-outcome coupling changed across sessions, and postprogram maintenance varied by outcome. No included estimand was judged at low overall risk of bias, and of the eight synthesis claims, two were of low certainty and six of very low certainty.

Discussion: The literature supports neither universal abbreviation nor preservation of eight weeks as an empirically optimized standard. The main conceptual advance is to separate evidence about change during a program from evidence about the consequences of changing the program: calendar length, contact, spacing, outcome timing, mechanism timing, individual heterogeneity, and durability are distinct design questions. Well-powered randomized architecture comparisons with aligned repeated measurement and prespecified noninferiority or optimization criteria are needed.

articles_hidden.title: Through the PRISM: Reinterpreting Psychedelic Cognition as Motivational Reallocation
articles_hidden.authors: Orchid2022*
articles_hidden.abstract:
Classic psychedelics such as psilocybin and LSD are known to acutely disrupt executive function, producing impairments in response inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. Paradoxically, these compounds often lead to lasting improvements in cognitive flexibility, insight, and goal-directed behavior in the days and weeks following administration. This apparent contradiction has traditionally been interpreted as a biphasic modulation of control capacity—initial impairment followed by compensatory enhancement.
An alternative account is proposed in the PRISM model (Psychedelic Recalibration of Internal Salience and Mental Effort Costs), which reframes cognitive outcomes not as shifts in capacity, but as changes in motivation for cognitive control. According to this framework, psychedelics may reduce the perceived cost of cognitive effort during acute states by disrupting habitual internally directed processes, such as Default Mode Network activity. Post-acutely, increased salience of emotionally or personally meaningful goals may enhance the willingness to engage in effortful, goal-directed cognition.
Rather than a global increase in executive ability, observed changes in performance may reflect a dynamic reallocation of motivational resources, explaining both acute dissociations and post-acute improvements in specific cognitive domains. This model integrates recent behavioral, neuroimaging, and pharmacological findings to offer testable predictions for future research. New experimental paradigms are outlined for dissociating motivational engagement from cognitive capacity, providing a mechanistic bridge between subjective psychedelic experiences and enduring adaptive outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Perceived error climate in elementary school classrooms: A multidimensional perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles_hidden.abstract: The error climate in the classroom captures the extent to which errors are positively perceived and treated as constructive learning opportunities by teachers and students. It has been conceptualized as comprising eight subdimensions organized under a single second-order factor among secondary school students (Steuer et al., 2013). However, this structure has not yet been investigated in younger students. Consequently, we examined the error climate’s structure in elementary school classrooms while additionally proposing a novel and more differentiated second-order structure distinguishing between emotional and instructional support following errors. Among 2,628 elementary school students from 187 classrooms across two domains (maths and German), multilevel multigroup confirmatory factor analyses at the individual and classroom level were conducted. Results revealed a multifaceted error climate perception already in elementary school, with eight subdimensions loading onto the two proposed second-order factors. These, in turn, were also positively related to students’ individual adaptive reactions to errors.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct Patterns of Reward-Related Neural Activation and Dopamine Neurophysiology in Adolescent Depression with and without Mixed Manic Features
articles_hidden.authors: Stefanie Fraga Gonçalves; Amar Ojha; Morgan Lindenmuth; Helmet Talib Karim; Teague R Henry; Rasim Diler; Cecile D. Ladouceur
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents with depression are at elevated risk for maladaptive risk behaviors, underscoring the importance of understanding neurobiological alterations in reward function in this population. However, reward function alterations associated with depression, particularly in the presence of co-occurring manic symptoms (i.e., mixed manic features), remain poorly understood. In this study, 154 12–18-year-olds (ndepression without mixed manic features = 65; ndepression with mixed manic features = 56; nhealthy controls = 33) and their primary caregiver completed questionnaires, clinical interviews, and fMRI during the monetary incentive delay task. Neural response during monetary reward anticipation, as well as tissue iron concentrations, important for dopamine neurophysiology, were derived from the striatum and used to predict group membership and severity of mixed manic features. Exploratory whole brain functional activation analyses were also conducted. Lower caudate activation (in the outlier-excluded analysis) was associated with membership in the depression with mixed manic features group. Across both depression groups, higher caudate and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) activation was associated with greater mixed manic feature severity. In addition, lower tissue iron concentration in the putamen and higher tissue iron concentration in the caudate were each associated with membership in the depression without mixed features group. These findings suggest that reward-related neural activation differentiates mixed manic features, whereas alterations in tissue iron characterize adolescent depression more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: When to Use Mixed Models and When RM-ANOVA - An Argument for Statistical Parsimony
articles_hidden.authors: Henrik Singmann
articles_hidden.abstract: When should researchers use linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) versus repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA) for analysing repeated-measures data? I first outline the conceptual and statistical differences between the two approaches: RM-ANOVA operates on aggregated difference scores, whereas LMMs model trial-level data using fixed and random effects to account for dependencies among observations. I then describe the key limitations of RM-ANOVA: its inability to handle missing data, partially within-participants factors, continuous within-participants covariates, and complex dependency structures such as crossed random effects designs. I also discuss the conceptual and computational challenges associated with LMMs, such as model specification and convergence issues. Using two simulation studies, I then demonstrate that when both methods are appropriate, RM-ANOVA -- especially with Greenhouse-Geisser correction -- generally provides better control of Type I error rates and statistical power equal to or greater than that of LMMs. Consequently, I recommend using RM-ANOVA in designs where RM-ANOVA is appropriate. LMMs should be reserved for cases that require the additional flexibility, such as complex designs, missing data, or advanced modelling goals.

articles_hidden.title: iTemplate2: An Open-Source Python Toolbox for Automatic Eye-Movement Analysis of Dynamic Facial Stimuli
articles_hidden.authors: Naiqi G Xiao; Rafael Román-Caballero; Wei Fang; Sara Ripley; Danyang Han; Laurel Trainor
articles_hidden.abstract: Template-based gaze-to-face registration enables standardized analysis of eye movements by mapping gaze coordinates onto a canonical facial template, reducing variability introduced by manual area-of-interest (AOI) definition across heterogeneous stimuli. However, existing implementations are largely restricted to static images, rely on semi-manual landmark annotation, and depend on proprietary software, limiting scalability and reproducibility. These constraints become increasingly problematic as research shifts toward dynamic stimuli, wearable eye-tracking, and open-source workflows. We present iTemplate2, a fully open-source Python-based redesign of the original system. The framework introduces four key advances: (1) support for dynamic stimuli via frame-wise coordinate transformation, including a normalization module for wearable and scene-based eye-tracking data; (2) integration of MediaPipe’s Face Landmarker for automated detection of 478 facial landmarks per frame, with multi-face tracking and identity persistence mechanisms that reduce manual annotation requirements; (3) a complete Python reimplementation using NumPy, pandas, OpenCV, PyQt6, and Apache Parquet, providing a cross-platform graphical interface without commercial dependencies; and (4) expanded visualization and analysis tools, including interactive heatmaps, snap-to-landmark AOI definition, and extraction of facial blendshape parameters for concurrent expression analysis. The system is applicable across diverse domains, including infant face scanning, cross-cultural gaze research, clinical screening, and naturalistic social interaction paradigms using wearable eye-tracking. It robustly processes complex multi-face video datasets that are difficult to analyze using conventional template-based methods. iTemplate2 modernizes the template-based registration framework for contemporary behavioral research, converting idiosyncratic visual data into a unified, reproducible analytical space. The software is freely available as an open-source tool at https://osf.io/54v9e/overview?view_only=5ac289558a3d4897a02336124ae409a1.

articles_hidden.title: Co-STARS: A Participatory Action Research Approach to Co-Producing Culturally Responsive Mental Health Literacy Training with Young Black People
articles_hidden.authors: Milan Antonovic; Megan A. Pope; Gerald Jordan; Balachandran Kumarendran; Luke Brown; Nadia; Ayan Mahamud; Lowri Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Young Black people in the UK face disproportionate mental health inequalities driven by stigma, racism, and structural exclusion. Although mental health literacy can promote early recognition and help-seeking, most interventions do not reflect Black communities’ lived realities. This study used Participatory Action Research (PAR) to co-produce a peer-led community mental health literacy training package with young Black people, alongside an e-learning resource to support culturally responsive practice among mental health and allied professionals.

Method: Eight young Black participants (M age = 24.5; five female) with lived experience of mental ill health from diverse cultural, religious, and gender backgrounds took part in four peer-led workshops and three refinement sessions. Guided by an anti-oppressive framework, participants identified priorities, developed content, and shaped the training. Data were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Results: Four interconnected themes emerged: (1) Navigating Cultural Silences and Systemic Exclusions (stigma, cultural taboos, intergenerational trauma, and racialised experiences in education and healthcare); (2) Fighting to Be Heard (dismissal, misrecognition, and delayed care); (3) Reimagining Care Through Cultural Proximity and Community Anchoring (relational, culturally grounded, community-based models); and (4) Embedding Accountability and Cultural Reflexivity in Training (youth-led recommendations for train-the-trainer programmes emphasising structural competency, experiential learning, and supervision).

Conclusions: Co-production elevated young Black people’s expertise and produced a culturally responsive training package grounded in lived experience and structural realities. The findings highlight the need for preventative, relational, and equity-focused mental health approaches and support community-led, culturally grounded interventions to reduce disparities among Black and racialised youth.

articles_hidden.title: Weak Distributive Inference in Language Acquisition
articles_hidden.authors: David Barner; Dimitrios Skordos; Elena Pagliarini; Alan Clinton Bale
articles_hidden.abstract: We find that children compute distributive inferences, and thus that they are capable pragmatic reasoners when alternatives can be derived without lexical substitution. This provides further evidence that they are not limited by other factors like working memory or pragmatic tolerance. In addition, we find evidence that children consistently computed weak distributive inferences. In the spirit of Fox’s (2007) grammatical account, such inferences require double application of Exh, one scoping above the universal quantifier and another below. Thus, not only do children compute implicatures, but they appear to adopt the more complex parse—embedding one operator inside another—rather than relying on the simpler, global option that generates a strong distributive inference.

articles_hidden.title: The validation of cognitive ability constructs: A theoretically motivated user’s guide
articles_hidden.authors: Kristof Kovacs; John Protzko; Andrew R. A. Conway
articles_hidden.abstract: How do we validate tests of cognitive abilities? We argue that the validation process depends fundamentally on the nature of the construct under investigation. There are two the different traditions in the study of validity: one emphasizes a realist approach, asserting that variations in an underlying attribute must causally produce variation in measurement outcomes, while the other prioritizes the utility and predictive value of test scores. We distinguish between reflective constructs, which represent real entities with causal properties, and formative constructs, which serve as useful statistical summaries. We propose that seemingly conflicting conceptions of validity are not mutually exclusive but rather represent appropriate approaches for different types of constructs; reflective constructs warrant a causal-realist interpretation of validity, while a predictive-utilitarian approach is sufficient for the validation of formative constructs. Specifically, for reflective constructs, a reductionist approach is appropriate, and researchers should aim to ground their validation efforts in an understanding of the withinperson cognitive processes that underlie individual differences. Conversely, formative constructs are best validated through their predictive utility. By providing a typology of constructs and a guide for validation, this paper aims to help researchers apply the appropriate criteria for cognitive ability constructs.

articles_hidden.title: Mental health consequences of extremely vivid mental imagery: A qualitative investigation of managing anxiety with hyperphantasia
articles_hidden.authors: Nicole McGowan; Reshanne R Reeder
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental imagery is the ability to mentally simulate sensory experience in the absence of an external stimulus, with individual vividness ranging from extremely weak or absent (aphantasia) to superlative and hyper-realistic (hyperphantasia): these ends of the spectrum are called “imagery extremes”.  Though most imagery extremes research is focused on aphantasia, given that mental imagery is thought to play a critical role in the presentation of mental health disorders, as well as being central to many therapeutic interventions, this study aimed to explore the lived mental health experiences of hyperphantasics with anxiety. Eight hyperphantasics were recruited from a database for those interested in taking part in mental imagery research. All participants had a diagnosed anxiety disorder, and experience of accessing mental health services within the UK. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis was used to analyse their semi-structured interviews. Three Group Experiential Themes were identified for all participants: 1) Blurred Boundaries with Reality, 2) Limitless Imagination, and 3) Pathways to Managing Anxiety. The multisensory and emotional intensity of hyperphantasic imagery experiences related to anxiety created a realness of experience which was difficult for participants to describe and manage. Limitless imagination could be perceived as a threat when participants were not in control of their imagery; however, it was a source of great joy and calmness when participants were in control. Participants managed their anxiety by disconnecting from their mental imagery and engaging in the world around them, or by finding ways to use their abilities to support themselves. Research and clinical implications are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Strengths and Weaknesses: Early word learning skills and profiles of vocabulary development
articles_hidden.authors: Laia Fibla; John P Spencer; Larissa K. Samuelson
articles_hidden.abstract: Early vocabulary development predicts later cognitive functioning and school success. We sought to examine how processing differences across several skills that contribute to early word learning relate to variability in children’s vocabulary development. Building on recent direct measures of early vocabulary and language learning processes, we collected data from 166 children between 15- to 27-months in a single eyetracking task measuring lexical speed of processing, comprehension, novelty bias, word mapping and new word retention. We found clear differences in responding across the different measures and robust patterns of developmental change. Children’s comprehension grew over development, and across word classes they showed clearly distinct looking patterns, reflecting fundamental differences in word type processing and more efficient noun recognition compared to adjectives and verbs. Speed of processing and online comprehension showed strong relationships with concurrent vocabulary, similar to previous reports. Children also showed a strong improvement in referent selection over development, but as found in previous literature, they did not show evidence of retaining new word-object mappings formed on earlier trials of the task. Data driven classification found two robust clusters of children. One group showed faster speed of lexical processing, better comprehension and were better at linking new nouns to novel objects. Numerically, this group had the highest parent-reported concurrent productive vocabulary scores. Data are discussed in relation to similar work in the literature, what concurrent measurement of multiple word learning processes reveals about the system of multiple processes supporting early vocabulary development, and children’s individual trajectories of word learning.

articles_hidden.title: Take it personally: Promoting a personalised neuroscience informed approach to cognitive rehabilitation following psychopathology.
articles_hidden.authors: Marie-José van Tol; Ernst H. W. Koster; Matthias Pillny; Ivan Grahek; Lisette van Der Meer
articles_hidden.abstract:
People suffering from schizophrenia, depression and other severe mental illnesses often suffer from cognitive problems. In most people, these problems persists after the major symptomatic episode is over, and in some cases cognitive problems also preceded an episode. Unfortunately, even after symptomatic remission, full recovery of cognitive functions often does not occur, thereby severely and enduringly impeding daily life functioning. Although it’s recognized in the field of psychiatry and psychology that these cognitive problems persist, there is little mechanistic understanding of how these problems arose and persist. We believe that this lack of a mechanistic understanding severely hampers mitigation of these residual problems and limits the ability for stable remission and potential for rebuilding a fulfilling live. 
In this perspective paper, we introduce a model inspired by behavioural economics that focuses on the decision making process underpinning cognitive control allocation. With this model we conceptualize the situational inability to engage in enduring and/or demanding cognitive daily life tasks, as a consequence of aberrant/maladaptive decision-making. We integrate insights from cognitive psychology, cognitive neuroscience, clinical psychology with practices of cognitive remediation in the field of severe mental illness. With this multidisciplinary approach, we offer hypotheses on how widely available therapies could be used to boost cognitive functioning following mental illness.

articles_hidden.title: A Step-by-Step Tutorial on the Stochastic Cusp Model in R
articles_hidden.authors: Renaud Mabire-Yon; Raoul P P P Grasman; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract: People facing similar circumstances may function very differently. The stochastic cusp model offers one possible explanation: the same conditions may support two stable levels of functioning. This tutorial shows how to understand, fit, and interpret the model in R, assuming familiarity with regression and basic R. Simple illustrations explain how stable states emerge and how changing conditions can alter them. A synthetic example links personal resources and acute stress to adaptive functioning. Readers learn to specify the model, check the fit, interpret coefficients and uncertainty, and examine its predictions. At average resources, the fitted distribution changes from one peak at low stress to two separated peaks at higher stress. The tutorial also explains which further observations would help distinguish a cusp hypothesis from competing explanations. Publicly available data, code, and archived output allow readers to reproduce the example.

articles_hidden.title: Co-Production and Development of ‘Resilience Rucksacks’: A Whole-School Preventative Approach to Support Young People’s Resilience
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Tupitsa; Clea Desebrock; Agnes Tait; Megan Devereux; Nevena Harris; Oluwatoyosi Alake; Asnea Tariq; Stella Chan
articles_hidden.abstract: The rising prevalence of mental health difficulties in young people, along with increased demands on mental health services, highlights an urgent need for developing effective preventative interventions. Whole-school approaches offer timely and accessible support; however, existing interventions show mixed efficacy, with many excluding the involvement of key stakeholders, especially young people with lived experience. This paper reports the development of a co-produced, whole-school intervention, ‘Resilience Rucksacks’, which aimed to equip young people with knowledge and practical skills to promote general resilience during a pivotal transition period from primary to secondary school. Project development comprised three phases: (i) a literature review to identify key factors that support youth mental health and resilience, (ii) stakeholder consultation via 7 steering group meetings with young people, school staff, and parents (n = 6-20 representatives per session) and a follow-up online survey (n = 197), and (iii) 20 co-production workshops with young people (n = 2-9 attendees per workshop) to develop evidence-based well-being tools. This process identified four biopsychosocial factors (sleep, physical activity, self-compassion, and social relationships) to be focused on due to their strong research evidence base and resonance with everyday experiences. The subsequent co-production workshops produced 7 main well-being tools designed to increase young people’s knowledge, skills, and confidence around mental health. This study critically highlights the value of co-production with young people to identify intervention targets and to design effective and accessible tools that support resilience and well-being development in their own environment.

articles_hidden.title: Parental ethnic-racial socialization in Europe: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Ymke de Bruijn; Jana Vietze
articles_hidden.abstract: Objectives: Children in Europe grow up in societies with high ethnic-racial diversity. It is therefore imperative to understand how they learn about ethnicity and race (ethnic-racial socialization). Knowledge on parental ethnic-racial socialization, however, is very heavily based on U.S. research, and sociohistorical and -political differences limit generalizability. Therefore, the aim of the present study is to create an overview and synthesis of research on parental ethnic-racial socialization in the European context. Methods: A preregistered scoping review was conducted following the PRIMSA-ScR guidelines. Three electronic databases (PsychInfo, ERIC, Web of Science) were searched for papers published up and till 2024. After two rounds of screening, 32 out of 1431 papers were deemed eligible and included for data extraction and synthesis. Results: The findings display an overrepresentation of Northern/Western European countries, families of immigrant or minoritized backgrounds and quantitative research on adolescence. Cultural socialization by families or immigrant or minoritized backgrounds has received the most attention. Qualitative study results furthermore describe how parental ethnic-racial socialization is shaped by developmental timing, reactive and reciprocal processes, intersecting identities, and selective engagement with cultural “others. Conclusions: The findings of this scoping review underscore both the promise and current limitations of research on parental ethnic-racial socialization in Europe. To further this research agenda, we need more systematic inclusion of underrepresented populations, greater investments in qualitative and mixed-methods designs, openness to diverse and self-identified ingroup boundaries and identity meanings, and the development of conceptualizations and measures that reflect Europe’s distinctive sociohistorical trajectories, demographic diversity, and linguistic practices.

articles_hidden.title: The effect of alcohol-specific episodic memories and alcohol cue exposure on value-based decision-making and ad libitum alcohol consumption
articles_hidden.authors: Amber Copeland; Tom Stafford; Cameron Crook; Michelle Pun; Aaron Bornstein; Lee Hogarth; James Murphy; Hanna Pickard; Frank Ryan; Justin Charles Strickland
articles_hidden.abstract: Background and Aims: Alcohol choice is governed by its subjective value, which can be experimentally modified. However, less is known about the moment-to-moment dynamics through which experimental manipulations of value influence observable choice behaviour. We tested whether an experimental manipulation intended to elevate alcohol value would alter computational parameters of value-based decision-making (VBDM) and alcohol choice, and whether these outcomes would mediate ad libitum alcohol consumption. Design: Pre-registered, randomised between-subjects experiment comparing two personalised experimental conditions: alcohol value (exposure to alcohol memories and multisensory alcohol cues) vs. control (exposure to non-alcohol memories and multisensory soft-drink cues), conducted over two separate sessions with baseline measures included as covariates. Setting: University laboratory in the United Kingdom (UK). Participants: 129 adults (63% male; mean age = 44 years; mean Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test [AUDIT] score = 16) who regularly consume alcohol (mean Estimated Weekly Alcohol Consumption [EWAC] = 42 UK units/week), randomised to alcohol value (n = 65) or control (n = 64) conditions. Measurements: At baseline and post-exposure, participants completed self-reported measures of alcohol craving and a value-based decision-making (VBDM) task where they chose between pairs of previously rated alcohol-related and non-alcohol images. A drift-diffusion model was fitted to behavioural data to estimate evidence accumulation rates (value sensitivity) and response thresholds (response caution). Participants also completed a concurrent choice task (alcohol vs. non-alcohol) that measured percentage alcohol relative to non-alcohol reward (enlargement; index of relative alcohol value), and a taste test to measure alcohol consumption. Findings: Some indices of subjective craving were responsive to the experimental manipulation, but there were no significant between-group differences at post-manipulation (ps ≥ .17). Baseline-adjusted analyses showed that response thresholds for non-alcohol decisions were higher in the alcohol value condition compared to control (p = .03, d = 0.40); however, Bayesian analysis quantified only anecdotal evidence for this effect (BF10 = 1.84). Other VBDM parameters, percentage alcohol choice, and alcohol consumed were unaffected by the manipulation (ps ≥ .19, BF10s ≤ 0.40). Furthermore, no value indices (computational or percentage choice) mediated the effect of the experimental manipulation on alcohol consumed. Conclusions: A personalised experimental manipulation intended to elevate alcohol value had modest effects on self-reported craving, but did not alter computational parameters of VBDM, relative alcohol choice, or ad-libitum alcohol consumption.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting dropout from psychotherapy with routine measurement-based care data: Which patients benefit from more complex prediction models?
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Athan McAleavey; Hans Jacob Westbye; Christian Moltu
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Treatment discontinuation in mental health care represents a significant individual and systemic challenge, with considerable associated costs. Machine learning (ML) may be able to accurately predict risk of dropout, which could be useful in psychotherapy. Methods. Data on 26,877 individual patients were extracted from the electronic encounter records and self-report databases of mental healthcare settings in Norway. We predicted risk of early treatment termination after attending one psychotherapy session, using data that would be available at (or shortly after) the first treatment session. We compared eXtreme Gradient Boosted decision trees (XGBoost) to penalized regression and standard logistic regression models. Results. Dropout prevalence was estimated at 19.7% of the sample. Of the tested models, XGBoost achieved very slightly better accuracy than the other models in AUC ROC (0.620 vs. 0.611-0.613 for the regression-based models). Exploratory analyses indicated that the small average increase in predictive accuracy was primarily due to better performance at the high end of the prediction scale. Discussion. While complex models only modestly improved overall prediction accuracy, exploratory analysis indicated that this small benefit may mask a strength of complex models for individuals with uncommon presentations and high or low risk for dropout. A stepped approach to model complexity may be appropriate in practice: many patients may only benefit from simple data collection and simple modeling strategies, while more detailed analysis could be useful when simple models identify unusual responses.

articles_hidden.title: Temporal Binding between Stimulus and Response
articles_hidden.authors: Takumi Tanaka; Kazuma Takada
articles_hidden.abstract: Temporal binding—the perceived compression of time between successive events—has been studied primarily between voluntary actions and their sensory outcomes and is often interpreted as an implicit marker of the sense of agency. A broader alternative is that temporal binding reflects the reconstruction of subjective time in accordance with inferred causal structure. Motivated by this account, we asked whether a similar distortion also arises between an imperative stimulus and the response it elicits. Across three preregistered experiments, we found converging evidence for temporal binding between stimulus and response (TBSR). In Experiment 1, a Libet clock task revealed the hallmark bidirectional attraction pattern: relative to baseline judgments of each event in isolation, imperative tones were perceived later and stimulus-triggered responses earlier. Experiments 2a and 2b then assessed interval perception directly using psychophysical two-alternative forced-choice judgments. In Experiment 2a, stimulus–response intervals were judged shorter than physically matched stimulus–stimulus intervals. In Experiment 2b, the same compression emerged relative to a physically matched passive button press baseline, indicating that the effect cannot be reduced to overt sensory sequence or temporal contingency alone. Together, these findings show that temporal binding is not confined to action–outcome episodes but also arises in stimulus–response episodes. More broadly, the findings are consistent with accounts in which subjective time is shaped by inferred causal structure and pose a challenge to the view that temporal binding serves as a selective marker of the sense of agency.

articles_hidden.title: Reading and writing anxiety in Finnish school children aged 9-15: Associations with gender, grade level, and reading competence
articles_hidden.authors: Rosa Salmela; Santeri Holopainen; Tomi Rautaoja; Emilia Nordenswan; Katarina Alanko; Pekka Räsänen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: This study examined the level of reading and writing anxiety in a cross-sectional sample of Finnish school children and the moderating roles of gender, grade level, and reading competence. 

Method: We used a reading and writing anxiety questionnaire (RWAQ) that consists of three factors: workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety. Linear regression modeling was used to analyze how gender, grade level, and reading competence moderate different dimensions of reading and writing anxiety. Participants were 9,723 Finnish-speaking children in grades 3–9, including 4,832 girls and 4,891 boys.

Results: Finnish school-age children showed relatively low reading and writing anxiety overall, but it increased with age (lowest in grades 3–5, highest in grades 7–9). This was especially evident in girls’ social and evaluation-related anxiety, while boys reported higher workload-related anxiety across grades. Lower reading competence was linked to higher reading and writing anxiety, but this effect varied by gender. Math anxiety and general anxiety were controlled in the models, and both anxiety types predicted reading and writing anxiety strongly.

Conclusion: Together the results suggest that workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety are distinct dimensions of reading and writing anxiety, and that future research could benefit from accounting that grade level, gender, and reading competence may influence these dimensions differently.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Virtue: Courage's Associations with Aversive Intentions and Behaviors and Dark Triad Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Grzegorz Pajestka; Katarzyna Skałacka
articles_hidden.abstract: Individual differences associated with aversive behavior have been linked primarily to antagonistic personality traits. Less is known about whether characteristics typically regarded as adaptive also contribute. Courage is traditionally viewed as a virtue, yet theoretical accounts suggest it may also facilitate socially aversive behaviors. This study tested whether two operationalizations—psychological courage (PC) and courage as a character strength (VIA-C)—predict aversive intentions and behaviors beyond Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy). A community sample of 711 Polish adults completed measures of PC, VIA-C, the Short Dark Triad, and aversive intentions and behaviors. Variable-centered analyses (hierarchical regressions, two-part models) controlling for age, gender, and Dark Triad traits revealed domain-specific effects: both courage measures predicted higher aggressive intentions and greater frequency of aggressive behaviors; VIA-C additionally predicted aggressive and sex-/drug-related behaviors. Neither courage measure related to theft, reckless driving, or self-destructive behaviors, and PC showed a small protective association with self-destructive intentions. Latent profile analysis identified four classes defined primarily by Dark Triad levels rather than courage; no high-courage/low-antagonism profile emerged. Overall, findings challenge unqualified valorization of courage and underscore the need to pair courage-building with ethical frameworks, empathy training, and prosocial goal setting to reduce iatrogenic risk.

articles_hidden.title: Psychiatric Overdiagnosis as Diagnostic Stretching in Response to Clinical Need
articles_hidden.authors: Awais Aftab
articles_hidden.abstract: I define psychiatric “overdiagnosis” as the observation that there has been a rapid rise in the rate of mental health diagnoses in recent decades, combined with the suspicion that a substantial proportion of these diagnoses are illegitimate or unwarranted. I propose that a major and under-recognized contributor to both the rise and the suspicion is diagnostic stretching: the application of a specified diagnostic category to a presentation that does not meet its official criteria but is accompanied by clinically significant distress or impairment, to make that presentation legible to the institutions that organize care. Since the 1990s, specified categories such as major depressive disorder, ADHD, bipolar disorder, and autism have been stretched in clinical practice to cover patients who have the relevant symptoms and clinically significant distress or impairment but whose presentations are subthreshold or phenomenologically adjacent. Increased awareness of mental health problems has lowered the help-seeking threshold, so that the population that comes to clinical attention is converging on the population that meets a burden threshold independent of help-seeking. Stretching is a response to genuine clinical need interacting with official classifications that are too narrow, not too broad. The overdiagnosis backlash correctly perceives a mismatch between official criteria and diagnostic practice but misidentifies its source, reading as laxity what is better understood as unmet need routed through official categories that are not adequate to the task.

articles_hidden.title: Making Sense of Sensory Differences: Identifying Sensory Processing Phenotypes and Their Relationship to Social and Executive Functioning in Neurotypical Children.
articles_hidden.authors: Adrianna M Molenaar; Natalia Van Esch; Nichole Scheerer
articles_hidden.abstract: Sensory processing varies substantially across individuals, yet research on distinct sensory phenotypes has focused primarily on neurodivergent populations. We examined whether comparable sensory phenotypes could be identified in 200 children aged 4-12 years with no known neurodevelopmental or psychiatric diagnoses, and whether phenotype membership was associated with executive functioning, social competence, mental health, alexithymia, and neurodivergent traits. K-means clustering of parent-reported sensory processing identified four sensory phenotypes: Sensory Adaptive, Generalized Sensory Differences, Under-responsive/Filtering Differences, and Sensory Sensitive. Children in the Sensory Adaptive group showed fewer executive functioning difficulties than children in all other groups and higher social competence than those in the Generalized Sensory Differences and Sensory Sensitive groups. In contrast, phenotypes did not differ significantly in autistic or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder traits, alexithymia, anxiety, or depression. These findings demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in sensory processing among children without diagnosed conditions and suggest that sensory phenotypes may be meaningfully related to everyday cognitive and social functioning. Future transdiagnostic work should directly examine the extent to which these phenotypes are shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children.

articles_hidden.title: A Transposed Bock–Aitkin EM Algorithm for Item Response Models with Many Items and Few Subjects
articles_hidden.authors: PRESTON DAVID BOTTER; Christopher Stewart
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language model benchmarks often contain many more items than evaluated systems. We develop a transposed Bock–Aitkin EM algorithm for 1PL and 2PL random-item models, including correlated difficulty and log discrimination. Capabilities are structural parameters; item effects are integrated over a normal population. We derive posterior-averaged scoring equations and distinguish exact marginal-likelihood theory from the implemented Laplace–cubature moment iteration, which can stabilize without solving the likelihood score. A simulation comparison uses 100 replications in each of 16 conditions. Capability recovery improves with more items for the transposed procedures, but population-correlation bias persists in small model cohorts. All variational fits in this comparison reached their iteration cap, limiting cross-framework conclusions. In an application to 98,032 WILD items, numerically eligible correlated transposed 2PL and variational 2PL have similar predictive performance, with log loss and Brier score favoring different procedures. JML 2PL has the lowest test Brier score but does not meet its numerical eligibility rule. The simulation and application use different fitting implementations and baseline settings, so they do not jointly validate a single numerical procedure. These exploratory findings concern point estimation and random-cell prediction, not calibrated parameter uncertainty or generalization to new models.

articles_hidden.title: Everyday Encounters with Economic Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Carla Moccia; Matthew John Easterbrook; Matthias S Gobel
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on economic inequality has traditionally relied on macro-level indices, though a growing body of work examines how economic inequality is perceived in everyday life. Whether different forms of everyday encounters carry different political and psychological consequences remains unclear. Across four studies with London-based samples (N = 1,554), we used a situation-sampling approach to identify forms of real-world inequality encounters and test how they relate to appraisal, redistribution support, and psychological distress. Study 1 identified two forms of inequality: Structural Inequality, describing disparities in essential goods and institutions, and Lifestyle Inequality, involving differences in consumption, leisure, and social participation. Study 2 showed that Structural situations were perceived as more unequal and unfair and elicited stronger redistribution support than Lifestyle Inequality situations. Study 3a, reported in Supplementary Materials, showed that greater redistribution support for Structural Inequality situations was largely carried through greater perceived unfairness. Study 3b modelled Structural and Lifestyle Inequality content continuously: Structural Inequality was linked to redistribution support and distress through unfairness, whereas Lifestyle Inequality was linked to distress through upward social comparison. The political and psychological consequences of inequality therefore depend on the form of encounter, not only on its perceived magnitude.

articles_hidden.title: Statistical Inference Regularized with Neural Networks and its Application in Psychometrics
articles_hidden.authors: Dmitry I Belov; Oliver Lüdtke; Esther Ulitzsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Likelihood-based methods such as marginal maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) are widely used for estimating item response theory (IRT) models and perform well in large samples. In small samples, however, these approaches may yield unstable estimates due to insufficient information in the likelihood, unless strong prior distributions are imposed. We address this problem by turning to the fundamentals of estimation via decision theory, showing that small-sample estimation can be viewed as an ill-posed decision problem in the sense that the decision function is sensitive to small changes in the data and, therefore, may not be continuous. We discuss how such ill-posed decision problems—both in IRT estimation and more broadly—can be regularized using neural network (NN)-based approaches that build a continuous map from observations into parameters. We formalize this approach within a general framework termed regularized decision theory and apply it to IRT models. Focusing on the 3PL, we study its properties via simulations.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional and Well-being Consequences of Discrimination and Collective Action Engagement
articles_hidden.authors: Shahrzad Goudarzi; Riana M. Brown; Ashley L Berkebile-Weinberg; Maureen A. Craig
articles_hidden.abstract: Inequality and collective struggles against it are psychologically taxing. Yet to be successful, social movements must persist through sustained action despite their toll on the participants, and many do. While the negative affective determinants of collective action, particularly outrage, are extensively studied, less is known about the accompanying positive psychological states.
