Using cross-sectional and experience-sampling methodologies, we find that engaging (and intending to engage) in collective action is marked by heightened subjective well-being and a range of positive feelings. Nonetheless, the positive consequences of engagement (but not mere intention) may only emerge when action is coupled with experiences of discrimination targeting outgroups (but not the self, personally, or ingroups) or in the absence of discrimination. This suggests that some psychological distance from discrimination supports the psychological benefits of collective action in grappling with inequality. Overall, this work can provide insight into a psychological mechanism contributing to sustained mobilization.

articles_hidden.title: Questions about Generative Language Models for Human Resources Decision Making
articles_hidden.authors: Dev K. Dalal; Gaurav Malhotra; Gregory Edward Cox; Adam T. Weber
articles_hidden.abstract: In this chapter, we discuss the gaps in the current understanding of how generative large language models (LLMs) make person judgments. Person judgments refer to inferences about someone's standing on a psychological construct, particularly when the judgment is made under uncertainty. We extend this concern to the application of LLMs to inform human resources (HR) decision making. We consider the ethical and legal implications of using LLMs to make person judgments to inform HR decision making. Finally, we outline a set of general research questions centered on  unstudied and understudied questions as it pertains to the use of LLMs in HR decision making.

articles_hidden.title: Co-STARS: A Participatory Action Research Approach to Co-Producing Culturally Responsive Mental Health Literacy Training with Young Black People
articles_hidden.authors: Milan Antonovic; Megan A. Pope; Gerald Jordan; Balachandran Kumarendran; Luke Brown; Nadia; Ayan Mahamud; Lowri Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Young Black people in the UK face disproportionate mental health inequalities driven by stigma, racism, and structural exclusion. Although mental health literacy can promote early recognition and help-seeking, most interventions do not reflect Black communities’ lived realities. This study used Participatory Action Research (PAR) to co-produce a peer-led community mental health literacy training package with young Black people, alongside an e-learning resource to support culturally responsive practice among mental health and allied professionals.

Method: Eight young Black participants (M age = 24.5; five female) with lived experience of mental ill health from diverse cultural, religious, and gender backgrounds took part in four peer-led workshops and three refinement sessions. Guided by an anti-oppressive framework, participants identified priorities, developed content, and shaped the training. Data were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Results: Four interconnected themes emerged: (1) Navigating Cultural Silences and Systemic Exclusions (stigma, cultural taboos, intergenerational trauma, and racialised experiences in education and healthcare); (2) Fighting to Be Heard (dismissal, misrecognition, and delayed care); (3) Reimagining Care Through Cultural Proximity and Community Anchoring (relational, culturally grounded, community-based models); and (4) Embedding Accountability and Cultural Reflexivity in Training (youth-led recommendations for train-the-trainer programmes emphasising structural competency, experiential learning, and supervision).

Conclusions: Co-production elevated young Black people’s expertise and produced a culturally responsive training package grounded in lived experience and structural realities. The findings highlight the need for preventative, relational, and equity-focused mental health approaches and support community-led, culturally grounded interventions to reduce disparities among Black and racialised youth.

articles_hidden.title: Autobiographical Editing Questionnaire: Measuring personally motivated distortion of shared memories and its relationship with the Dark Triad and dissociation
articles_hidden.authors: Noboru Matsumoto; Satoru Kiire; Rie Kubota; Hinako Kojima
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory distortions motivated by interpersonal manipulation are frequently observed in clinical and forensic contexts among individuals with borderline and narcissistic personality disorders. However, experimental studies (e.g., DRM paradigm) have provided limited evidence of increased false-memory susceptibility in personality disorders, possibly because laboratory tasks fail to capture personally motivated memory distortions. We developed the Autobiographical Editing Questionnaire (AEQ), a self-report measure of the deliberate reporting of distorted memories driven by personal motivations, in Japanese and English, and examined its associations with personality traits and dissociation. Across four studies, we confirmed the factorial validity of a 20-item cross-classified nested model, in which each item was jointly defined by four distortion-type dimensions (Maximization, Minimization, Concealment, and Fabrication) and five functional dimensions (Understanding, Empathy, Positive Impression, Negative Impression, and Self-Interest). Except for grandiose narcissism in the English version, the Dark Triad, the Vulnerable Dark Triad, and dissociation correlated positively with the functional dimensions. Consistent patterns emerged across both language versions: vulnerable narcissism was selectively associated with Maximization, Machiavellianism with Minimization, psychopathy with Concealment and Fabrication, and dissociation with Fabrication. These findings suggest that memory distortions observed in personality pathology are not entirely unconscious and can be meaningfully assessed by self-report.

articles_hidden.title: Deciding with muscles
articles_hidden.authors: Edouard Dendauw; Nathan J. Evans; Emma Michel; Axel Garnier-Allain; thibault gajdos; Mathieu Servant
articles_hidden.abstract: Sequential sampling models have a rich tradition in psychology and play a central role in our understanding of human decision-making. According to these models, decisions arise from the gradual accumulation of noisy evidence over time until a decision threshold is reached. This framework accounts for both choice behavior and reaction times and is further supported by neurophysiological evidence: neural activity in various brain regions exhibits accumulation-to-bound dynamics consistent with model predictions. Recent empirical findings extend this view, revealing that similar accumulation-like signals can also be observed in the electrical activity of response muscles, suggesting that decision signals may propagate continuously from perceptual processing through motor execution. This raises a fundamental theoretical question: How are effortful actions initiated when sensory evidence is weak, particularly under time pressure? We hypothesized that evidence-independent urgency signals provide the additional drive needed for the translation of decision signals into muscle activation in such contexts. To formalize this hypothesis, we extended the gated cascade diffusion model, a computational framework that links decision formation, motor preparation, and motor execution. We tested this model extension against behavioral and neuromuscular data from two experiments manipulating sensory evidence quality and required response force, with speed pressure additionally manipulated in Experiment 2. Model fits and formal comparisons with alternative accounts provided strong support for our hypothesis. These findings enhance our understanding of the interface between decision-making and motor systems, particularly in contexts that require effortful actions, which are common in everyday behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Spirituality Matters in Deconstructive Meditation: Comparing Secular and Buddhist-Based Mechanisms of Change in Depressive Vulnerability
articles_hidden.authors: Céline Stinus; Sophie Berjot
articles_hidden.abstract: This exploratory study extends a previously implemented randomized protocol to examine whether incorporating Buddhist-based spiritual and philosophical components into deconstructive meditation is associated with different patterns of psychological change. We compared secular deconstructive meditation (S-SI; n = 49), Buddhist-based deconstructive meditation (B-SI; n = 53), and a waitlist control condition (WL; n = 50) on depression-related outcomes (dysfunctional attitudes, identity threat, and depressive symptoms) and selflessness-related processes (connectedness to humanity, connectedness to nature, and cognitive decentering). Participants completed pre- and post-intervention assessments, and changes across conditions were examined using repeated-measures MANOVA. Within-subject mediation analyses further explored whether changes in selflessness-related processes were associated with changes in depression-related outcomes. Both active conditions showed greater reductions in depressive symptoms than the waitlist condition. Compared with S-SI, B-SI showed greater reductions in dysfunctional attitudes and identity threat, as well as larger increases in connectedness to humanity, connectedness to nature, and cognitive decentering. Within B-SI, changes in cognitive decentering and connectedness to nature showed significant indirect effects on changes in dysfunctional attitudes, whereas changes in connectedness to humanity showed significant indirect effects on changes in identity threat in both active conditions. None of the examined processes showed significant indirect effects on changes in depressive symptoms in either active condition. These findings suggest that the Buddhist-based condition may engage a broader range of self-related processes associated with depressive vulnerability. Given the exploratory, nonconcurrent design, these findings require confirmation in prospectively randomized comparisons.

articles_hidden.title: Give one way or another? Choosing between public goods and private transfers under inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Natalie Struwe; Yixuan Shi; Anwesha Banerjee
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals who care about the well-being of others can act through voluntary contributions to public goods (e.g. education, health, social protection), or through private monetary transfers as redistributive measures, as seen in informal community support networks, and formal unconditional cash transfer (UCT) programs. This paper studies the strategic relationship between these two simultaneous channels of giving in unequal groups. Building on a model of altruistic preferences, we conduct a pre-registered, between-subjects experiment (n=478) that varies income inequality and the availability of simultaneous private transfers in a repeated, two-person, and non-linear public good game. We identify a significant reduction of public good contributions in the presence of private transfers at all levels of inequality, with individuals substituting between the two strategies regardless of endowment type. Notably, poorer group members also send transfers, and transfers occur even when initial endowments are equal. Exploratory analysis reveals that this behavior can be explained by positive reciprocity motivations. Importantly, allowing for transfers in highly unequal groups need not reduce aggregate earnings. Despite the substitution in the considered setting, transfers improve the income of the poorer individuals without harming the wealthier group members. Our results speak to the behavioral micro-foundations of public goods and private transfers as complementary instruments for reducing within-group inequality.

articles_hidden.title: Triangulating Careless Responding: Quantitative Models Meet Qualitative Insights on Response Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Malin Müller; Dominique Maciejewski; Leonie Schorrlepp; Tanja Lischetzke; Leonie V. D. E. Vogelsmeier
articles_hidden.abstract:
Detecting careless responding in experience sampling methodology (ESM) is essential for ensuring data quality. Although quantitative detection methods are increasingly available, their low alignment raises questions about what they capture. Evaluation is constrained by the lack of ground truth in real-world data, while simulations require assumptions about the form of careless responding. This methodological catch-22 leaves disagreements among methods unresolved. We demonstrate how qualitative information about response processes (i.e., cognitive processes involved in rating items) can triangulate quantitative classifications and provide insight into what different methods capture. Using 4,175 measurement occasions from 41 participants in a 28-day ESM study, we compared a measurement-model-based mixture model using five emotion items and an indicator-based mixture model using four careless responding indices within a mixture continuous-time latent Markov framework. The models classified 35% and 15% of occasions as careless, respectively, with moderate overlap (Jaccard similarity = .37). Across models, careless occasions had more coded response processes and longer descriptions than attentive occasions. A qualitative analysis of 350 occasions showed how inductively derived classifications and response behavior codes provide complementary information about convergence and divergence between quantitative approaches. Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential value of triangulation for understanding what careless responding detection methods capture.
Keywords: experience sampling methodology, careless responding, response processes, qualitative triangulation, latent Markov model

articles_hidden.title: Mesmer’s error: Beliefs reverse the rubber hand illusion (a Registered Report)
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Lush; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: In the rubber hand illusion (RHI), participants report ownership of a fake hand which is stroked in synchrony with their own concealed hand, with lower ownership ratings for asynchronous stroking. This effect has been historically attributed to multisensory integration. However, such a pattern of results is consistent with experimental demand characteristics, and an alternative theory proposes that the RHI is an effect of phenomenological control (the trait ability to change experience to satisfy goals). To date, support for a phenomenological control theory of the RHI has been limited to correlational evidence. Here we conduct a pre-registered causal test of the relative contribution of these two proposed mechanisms in RHI effects. 25 high phenomenological control participants (top 15%) were tested in an RHI procedure and the classic effects of greater response for synchrony than asynchrony were replicated. The procedure was then repeated following imaginative suggestions for a reversal of the classic effect (i.e. greater synchrony than asynchrony effects). Ratings of ownership and proprioceptive drift were modulated by suggestion. Effects for ownership and drift were reversed. Exploratory analysis showed the same pattern of results for referred touch ratings. Participant beliefs arising from demand characteristics dominated over multisensory mechanisms in RHI ownership of a fake hand and proprioceptive drift. Multisensory synchrony was not necessary to produce the classic effects, falsifying the theory that the illusion requires multisensory integration. Claims of an illusion beyond that attributable to demand characteristics and phenomenological control require experimental evidence from controlled experiments.

articles_hidden.title: Moving beyond single-shot studies  toward cumulative research
articles_hidden.authors: Balazs Aczel; Eiko I Fried; Sabine Hoffmann
articles_hidden.abstract: In this perspective, we argue that single-design, single-analysis studies leave too much uncertainty unresolved to provide sufficiently informative answers to research questions. Such single-shot studies remain common across many disciplines, yet they reflect numerous explicit and implicit design and analytical decisions. Yet without systematically examining the consequences of these choices, researchers cannot determine the extent to which empirical findings depend on them. We contend that uncertainties arising from variability in research design and analysis are an unavoidable feature of empirical inquiry and a major source of the persistent replication problems, conflicting and seemingly irreconcilable findings, and limited cumulative knowledge observed across many fields. To address this challenge, we present a unifying framework for existing methodologies that allow researchers to systematically explore, reduce, and integrate these often-overlooked uncertainties underlying empirical claims. We argue that many of the necessary methods already exist across disciplines, but their broader impact has been limited by a lack of a shared conceptual framework and interdisciplinary integration. By balancing hypothesis testing with exploration and theory building, and by systematically incorporating Space Analysis tools into research practice, scientific fields can move beyond isolated single-shot studies toward systematic research programmes capable of producing more reliable, robust, and cumulative scientific knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Chronic pain and relationship satisfaction, social support, and social network size in chronic pain couples
articles_hidden.authors: Karolin Teichmüller; Gudrun-Karin Kindl; Heike Rittner; Andrea M.F. Reiter
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Chronic pain has detrimental effects on patients’ social integration and also affects patients’ significant others. This study asks if chronic pain patients, their spouses and pain-free couples differ in their self-reported relationship satisfaction and the quality and quantity of their social relationships with others.
Methods: Self-report data on relationship satisfaction (Partnership Questionnaire, PFB-K), perceived social support (Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, MSPSS), and social network size (Social Network Index, SNI) were collected online from 136 individuals, representing 34 chronic pain and 34 pain-free couples, matched on age and relationship duration. Chronic pain patients were recruited from a tertiary pain centre and presented with various pain conditions, mainly non-specific back pain, musculoskeletal pain and neuropathy. Pain-free couples were recruited from the general population.
Results: Linear mixed model analyses showed lower relationship satisfaction in chronic pain patients, and couples with longer relationship duration. The presence of chronic pain and longer relationship duration were particularly associated with reduced satisfaction on the PFB-K Tenderness subscale, assessing physical closeness. Moreover, patients perceived lower social support from friends but did not have fewer social contacts. Descriptively, chronic pain patients’ partners ranged between patients and controls regarding relationship satisfaction and perceived social support.
Conclusions: Chronic pain seems to complicate partnership, especially intimacy, and the quality of friendships for chronic pain patients, but not necessarily for their spouses. Our results highlight the need for multidimensional pain management strategies, which include assessing and targeting aspects of social functioning in romantic relationships and beyond.

articles_hidden.title: Extreme Response Style Generalizes Across Likert-Type and Visual Analogue Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik Vollbracht; Malin Müller; Tanja Lischetzke; Mirka Henninger
articles_hidden.abstract: Response styles, such as the tendency to prefer extreme or midpoint response options, are a systematic source of variance in self-report data. Individual differences in response styles are largely consistent across traits and over time, but it is unknown whether they generalize across Likert-type scales and visual analogue scales (VAS). In a preregistered within-subjects study, N = 501 participants completed the HEXACO-PI-R, with two content-balanced item subsets presented on a 7-point Likert-type scale and on a VAS. We modeled extreme and midpoint responding as opposite poles of a single dimension, referred to as extreme response style (ERS), using conceptually aligned models: a partial credit model for the Likert-type items and a beta item response model for the VAS items, each extended by a person-specific ERS parameter. Estimating both models jointly in a Bayesian framework, we found that ERS on Likert-type scales and on VAS was substantially correlated (ρERS = .76, 95% CrI [.68, .83]). Individual differences in ERS thus generalized to a considerable extent across response formats. Choosing VAS instead of Likert-type scales therefore does not avoid the influence of response styles, which should be modeled in VAS data as well.

articles_hidden.title: The Effects of Group-Based Community Interventions on Social Reintegration of Marginalized Adults with Mental Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Thorup Dalgaard; jakob Kaarup Jensen; Jasmin Sami Adada; Maya Christiane Flensborg Jensen; Elizabeth Bengtsen; Mikkel Helding Vembye; Elizabeth Tipton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background 
Adults with mental illness who also experience social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, yet scalable interventions addressing both dimensions of recovery remain limited.

Aims 
To evaluate the effects of group-based community interventions on social reintegration and mental health among socially marginalized adults with mental illness.

Methods 
We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions delivered in OECD countries. Searches identified 28,980 records; 62 studies met the inclusion criteria and 49 studies, contributing 349 effect sizes, were included in the meta-analysis. Outcomes were classified as social reintegration or mental health. Meta-analytic models accounted for dependent effect sizes within studies.

Results 
Group-based community interventions improved social reintegration (g = 0.195, 95% CI [0.122, 0.268]) and mental health (g = 0.215, 95% CI [0.090, 0.340]) relative to control conditions, corresponding to effects approximately 2.3 and 1.4 times larger, respectively, than the typical improvements under treatment as usual. Effects varied substantially across studies and outcomes, while measured moderators explained little of this heterogeneity. Effects on social reintegration and mental health were positively associated. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses and showed little indication of publication bias. Nearly half of studies were preregistered and contributed approximately two-thirds of all effect sizes. Preregistered studies yielded smaller social reintegration effects than non-preregistered studies, although the average effect remained statistically significant and substantively meaningful.

Conclusions 
Group-based community interventions can improve both social reintegration and mental health among marginalized adults with mental illness, suggesting that they may support multidimensional recovery. Their potential value therefore extends beyond scalability and lower delivery costs to substantively meaningful improvements in outcomes. However, substantial unexplained heterogeneity indicates that benefits are unlikely to be uniform across populations, interventions, and settings.

What is already known on this topic
Adults experiencing both mental illness and social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, while existing systematic reviews on group-based interventions have largely focused on specific diagnoses, intervention types, or psychiatric symptoms.

What this study adds
Across 49 studies contributing 349 effect sizes, group-based community interventions produced positive average effects on both social reintegration and mental health. Effects in the two domains were positively associated, but substantial heterogeneity remained largely unexplained.

articles_hidden.title: Profiling the Chinese Participants in Psychological Science: Non-WEIRD but Not Representative
articles_hidden.authors: Lei Yue; Zhangweiwei; Chunxiao Wang; Xi-Nian Zuo; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological science aims at understanding the human mind and behavior, but it primarily relies on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic regions, i.e., the WEIRD problem. This lack of diversity and representativeness of participants compromises the generalizability of psychological science. To address this issue, large-scale international collaborative projects have been initiated, and more data have been collected from non-WEIRD regions. However, it is unknown whether participants from non-WEIRD regions can represent their local population. In this preregistered report, we depicted the demographic profile of Chinese participants reported in 1, 000 empirical studies (n = 554, 794) published in five mainstream Chinese psychological journals and in 27 large-scale international collaborative projects (n = 29, 006, accounting for 2.12% of all participants). We found that age and sex were the most reported demographic variables, and other aspects of participants were less reported. The available demographic information revealed that Chinese participants were not representative of the population: most were young, well-educated, and resided in East China. Also, Chinese participants in large-scale international collaborative projects are less representative than those from Chinese journals in terms of geographical distributions. The demographic profile of Chinese participants in psychology is similar to their counterparts in many other countries and regions, suggesting the globalization of young and highly educated participants in psychological science. Together, our findings indicate that problems of representativeness are deeply entrenched in global psychological science and require coordinated cross-sector efforts.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Regression Effect: Investigating Time-Order Effects on the Cross-Modal Correspondence of Brightness and Loudness Within the Global Psychophysical Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Naumann; Annemarie Oelert; Jürgen Heller
articles_hidden.abstract:
This exploratory experimental study investigates the contribution of stimulus
presentation order to the regression effect in cross-modal matching of brightness and
loudness. Previous research has largely relied on the magnitude production paradigm to
obtain individual cross-modal matches, which induces distinct stimulus roles (i. e., a
fixed standard vs. an adjustable comparison). The cross-modal matches typically
exhibit a role-dependent regression effect, that is, they gravitate toward the mean of the
adjusted stimulus’ range. This regression effect can be explained by the theory of global
psychophysics via role-dependent internal references. However, stimulus role and
presentation order were often confounded in previous experiments. To decouple these
variables, this study employed a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm. Participants
judged whether a noise sound or an achromatic disk appeared more intense. To hide
explicit stimulus roles and level selection across the luminance and sound pressure
spectra, several adaptive staircases were run interleaved, balancing presentation order
across a high number of trials. Results showed an order-dependent regression effect in
three of the seven subjects, suggesting these individuals used the first stimulus in a trial
as an implicit standard. The remaining four subjects did not seem to exhibit this
strategy. Irregularities in the adaptive staircases, deviations from the global
psychophysical model, and future directions are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking a “core moral concept” in infancy: A relationship account of infants’ responses to resource distributions
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Mackiel; Amanda Woodward
articles_hidden.abstract: Infants’ responses to resource distributions are commonly interpreted as evidence of early fairness expectations and evaluations. We systematically review and meta-analyze this literature and propose an alternative, the relationship account: infants may use allocations to infer how distributors are connected to recipients and whether they are available as potential social partners. Our meta-analyses of the reviewed literature identify an overall reliable tendency for infants to look longer at unequal outcomes and preferentially engage with equal distributors. However, we argue that the current body of evidence does not uniquely establish fairness reasoning. Instead, infants’ responses may stem from preferences, expectations, and predictions grounded in reasoning about relationships. We propose that infants treat a distributor’s allocation as evidence about their relationships with recipients and use this information to assess the potential for themselves seeking relationships with the distributors. We outline experiments that could distinguish between fairness and relationship interpretations of infants’ responses and conclude by highlighting the generative potential of a relationship-focused framework for understanding infant social cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Generalizable experiment agents threaten online behavioral experiments
articles_hidden.authors: Talha Özüdoğru; Andrey Chetverikov; Richard Huskey; Leendert van Maanen; Christoph Strauch
articles_hidden.abstract:
Online behavioral experiments rely on the assumption that participants are human. Advances in large language models
(LLMs) challenge this assumption, but previous demonstrations have largely focused on surveys or agents built for individual
experimental tasks. Here, we introduce the Artificial General Experiment Agent (AGEA), a general-purpose agent developed
entirely through natural language prompting using a consumer-level LLM subscription. Without custom training for any
specific task, AGEA completed twenty-six online behavioral experiments across seven hosting platforms, independently
inferring each task’s structure. Benchmark comparisons across three cognitive domains, using the N-back, Tower of London,
and Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, showed performance within typical human ranges, including changes in accuracy and
response time with experimental conditions. It further completed, with human-like behavior, seven held-out studies prepared
in the spirit of adversarial collaboration between the co-authors. These findings show that agent participation can extend
across experimental paradigms and platforms. As general-purpose agents become cheaper and more capable, they pose a
growing risk to the integrity of online behavioral research, and safeguards must keep pace.

articles_hidden.title: Pleasurable beliefs and hedonic belief-based utility
articles_hidden.authors: Stephen Gadsby
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans are consistently biased towards pleasurable beliefs, for example, that we are better than average regarding desirable traits and that our futures will be brighter than statistically plausible. According to an influential theory within psychology, neuroscience, and behavioural economics, we are biased towards these (and other) pleasurable beliefs because they maximise hedonic belief-utility. I challenge this theory and suggest alternative explanations for pleasurable beliefs and the psychological processes that produce them. According to the view I present, such beliefs stem from processes that have little to do with maximising belief-utility.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Defeating Utilitarianism:  Laypeople Think that Aiming to Maximize Societal Welfare Will Backfire
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Zev Berman; Stefan Schubert; Lucius Caviola
articles_hidden.abstract: Utilitarianism holds that morally right actions are those that maximize aggregate welfare. One might therefore expect a society that adopts utilitarianism as its guiding moral code to flourish. However, across five preregistered studies (plus one preregistered supplemental study; total N = 2,626), we find that laypeople view utilitarianism as being self-defeating. Participants expect a society that adopts a welfare-maximizing moral code to contain less happiness and more suffering than a society that adopts a moral code based on fixed rules or duties. While individuals endorse welfare maximization as a societal aim and believe that promoting moderate versions of utilitarianism’s implications—especially greater impartiality and personal self-sacrifice—would advance this aim, they view utilitarianism as promoting these implications to an extreme and ultimately self-defeating degree. This yields a fundamental paradox in lay moral reasoning: the moral philosophy explicitly designed to maximize welfare is expected to fail to do so at scale.

articles_hidden.title: AI or Human Support for Suicide Prevention?  Examining Help-Seeking Intention in Suicidal Crisis
articles_hidden.authors: Daisuke Nakamura; Hajime Sueki; Jiro Ito
articles_hidden.abstract:
This preprint has now been published in the peer-reviewed journal Suicide Policy Research. Please read and cite the published version:

Nakamura, D., Sueki, H., & Ito, J. (2026). AI or human support for suicide prevention? Examining help-seeking intention in suicidal crisis. Suicide Policy Research, 5(1), 1–12.

The published article is freely available at:
https://jscp.or.jp/assets/img/SPR_5-1_1_Nakamura.pdf


Background:
Chat-based crisis support is a common strategy for suicide prevention, and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have the potential to improve the low response rates to such support. Although AI chatbots are technically feasible for crisis support, it remains unclear whether individuals experiencing suicidal ideation intend to use them.

Aims:
To examine the intentions of adults with depressive symptoms experiencing suicidal ideation to use chat-based crisis support (human vs AI) and explore how these intentions relate to their background characteristics.

Methods:
A cross-sectional web-based survey was performed, recruiting participants aged 18–69 with a Kessler-6 score ≥13 from an internet research company’s database in Japan. Participants completed a questionnaire assessing their intention to use chat-based crisis support when feeling suicidal, sociodemographic factors, and suicide-related characteristics. Subsequently, participants were categorized into four groups: (1) those intending to use both human and AI-based chats, (2) AI chat only, (3) human chat only, and (4) neither. We calculated the proportions of each group and used the chi-square, Kruskal–Wallis, and Fisher’s exact tests to compare group differences.

Results:
Overall, 1,024 participants completed the survey, and we determined that 19.5% intended to use AI chat support and 21.3% intended to use human chat. The proportions of participants who intended to use both human- and AI-based chat, AI chat only, human chat only, and neither option were 15.6 %, 3.9 %, 5.7 %, and 74.8 %, respectively. Significant differences were observed in gender (p = 0.028), history of crisis support use (p <0.001), and current issues (financial problems [p = 0.002)] and sexuality-related concerns (p = 0.006) across the groups.

Conclusion:
In this web-based survey, approximately 20% of individuals with depressive symptoms feeling suicidal were willing to seek help, even if it was provided by AI.

articles_hidden.title: How Does Child Maltreatment Affect Prosocial Behavior? Disentangling the Unique Contributions of Abuse, Neglect and Emotional Maltreatment
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Berger; Marian S. Schulz; Tyler Colasante; Georg von Polier; Kai von Klitzing; Andrea Schlesier-Michel; Lars O. White; Tina Malti; Jan Keil
articles_hidden.abstract: Child maltreatment is a well-established risk factor for mental health problems and maladaptive developmental outcomes. However, beyond its well-documented links to psychopathology, child maltreatment can also disrupt social functioning and erode social support, further increasing vulnerability to adverse outcomes across development. Prosocial behavior—voluntary actions intended to benefit others—is a core component of social functioning and supports the formation and maintenance of positive relationships. Although child maltreatment has been consistently linked to lower levels of prosocial behavior in children and adolescents, findings regarding the unique contributions of specific maltreatment dimensions (i.e., abuse, neglect and emotional maltreatment) remain mixed. The present preregistered study therefore aimed to examine the unique contributions of abuse, neglect and emotional maltreatment to the development of prosocial behavior across childhood and adolescence. To this end, we applied structural equation modeling (SEM) to fine-grained and multisource dimensional assessments of maltreatment to examine their unique associations with self- and caregiver-reported prosocial behavior in a large sample (N = 812) of German children and adolescents aged 3 to 16 years. Results indicate that experiences of abuse - but not neglect or emotional maltreatment – were uniquely associated with lower levels of both self- and caregiver-reported prosocial behavior. For caregiver-reported prosocial behavior, these associations further varied by gender and age group: the negative association of abuse was more pronounced in boys, and neglect was additionally associated with lower prosocial behavior among adolescents. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between dimensions of child maltreatment, as abuse appears to play a particularly salient role in undermining prosocial development. Accounting for developmental stage and gender may further refine our understanding of risk pathways in social functioning to ultimately inform more tailored prevention and intervention strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Virtue: Courage's Associations with Aversive Intentions and Behaviors and Dark Triad Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Grzegorz Pajestka; Katarzyna Skałacka
articles_hidden.abstract: Individual differences associated with aversive behavior have been linked primarily to antagonistic personality traits. Less is known about whether characteristics typically regarded as adaptive also contribute. Courage is traditionally viewed as a virtue, yet theoretical accounts suggest it may also facilitate socially aversive behaviors. This study tested whether two operationalizations—psychological courage (PC) and courage as a character strength (VIA-C)—predict aversive intentions and behaviors beyond Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy). A community sample of 711 Polish adults completed measures of PC, VIA-C, the Short Dark Triad, and aversive intentions and behaviors. Variable-centered analyses (hierarchical regressions, two-part models) controlling for age, gender, and Dark Triad traits revealed domain-specific effects: both courage measures predicted higher aggressive intentions and greater frequency of aggressive behaviors; VIA-C additionally predicted aggressive and sex-/drug-related behaviors. Neither courage measure related to theft, reckless driving, or self-destructive behaviors, and PC showed a small protective association with self-destructive intentions. Latent profile analysis identified four classes defined primarily by Dark Triad levels rather than courage; no high-courage/low-antagonism profile emerged. Overall, findings challenge unqualified valorization of courage and underscore the need to pair courage-building with ethical frameworks, empathy training, and prosocial goal setting to reduce iatrogenic risk.

articles_hidden.title: Self-identity in anorexia nervosa
articles_hidden.authors: Stephen Gadsby
articles_hidden.abstract: Anorexia nervosa is widely characterised as a disorder of the self, in which sufferers come to identify with their illness. Yet what such identification amounts to remains poorly understood. I argue that there are two distinct forms of self-identity involved, individual identity and group identity. These emerge at different time points, stem from different factors, and bear different clinical consequences. By unpacking this distinction, I provide a pluralistic and psychologically plausible account of self-identity in anorexia—one that illuminates the disorder’s tenacity and points to new ways of understanding it.

articles_hidden.title: Day-to-day fluctuations in craving and the value of drugs and food in daily life
articles_hidden.authors: Sergej Grunevski; Emmanuel E. Alvarez; Emma M. Schweitzer; Julia Kong; Sahar Hafezi; Anna B. Konova
articles_hidden.abstract: Craving is a powerful urge for a specific target (e.g., food, drugs) that prompts decisions directed at satisfying craving. While prior laboratory studies suggest craving biases behavior by amplifying target-specific value, the real-world generalizability of this mechanism remains unknown. We validate and extend these findings in a 28-day naturalistic smartphone-enabled study in patients with opioid use disorder (N=67) and community controls (N=49) who reported on their food (savory, sweet) and drug (opioid) urges and willingness-to-pay values. Despite person-level (mean) covariation, food and drug urges fluctuated largely independently within individuals while maintaining target-specific relationships with value. Using dynamics in drug urge and value and computational modeling, we isolated a distinct, ecologically relevant craving “state” tied to drug cue exposure and drug use in daily life. This research shows craving acts on normative valuation processes in real-world decision making and offers a novel approach to infer clinically vulnerable moments for behavior change.

articles_hidden.title: When do intentions predict action? The temporal dynamics of the intention–action gap
articles_hidden.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Luisa Leonelli; Yijun Lin; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Procrastination is defined as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action, yet the gap between intention and action is rarely measured directly, and little is known about how it unfolds over time. We gave 127 adults seven days to complete 180 units of a self-paced online reading task and recorded the timestamp of every completed unit. Before the task began, 67 of them reported how many units they intended to complete on each of the seven days, so that intended and actual work were expressed in the same units on the same days. Among those who finished, work was concentrated 0.59 days later than intended, although the day people finished did not differ from the day they had planned. The gap widened through Day 4, stopped growing on Day 5, and narrowed over the final two days. Intentions predicted when people started but not when they finished, and their influence faded after the first half of the task. Trait procrastination showed the opposite pattern, predicting actual but not intended work and shaping the timing of work throughout the task, most strongly in the middle.

articles_hidden.title: Shared and Divergent Multisensory Emotion Perception Deficits across Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer’s Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia: A Systematic Review and Hierarchical Bayesian Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Yi Lin; Yangfan Lu; Enze Tang; Yang Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to decode others’ emotions from multisensory cues is central to social functioning. However, findings remain inconsistent regarding the extent to which this capacity is compromised in neurodegenerative diseases, leaving the underlying mechanisms unclear. This study aimed to delineate the shared and divergent patterns of multisensory emotion perception (MEP) deficits among clinically distinct populations of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We conducted a systematic review on 51 studies identified from Web of Science, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES to synthesize research trends in this field between 2001 and 2025. We applied a hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis (1,511 patients and 1,151 healthy controls) to quantify the deficits and their moderators. Meta-analytic results demonstrated a differential magnitude of MEP impairment across groups (FTD > AD > MCI), reflecting distinct socio-emotional vulnerabilities rather than a single disease continuum. Moderator analyses of 15 participant- and study-related factors showed that impairment magnitude was more strongly associated with age, sex, education, global cognitive functioning, publication year, and emotion category, and less strongly with region, paradigm, language, and modality. Sensitivity analyses indicated that these patterns remained robust to potential publication bias, though the results were less stable within the FTD cohort. We propose a Hierarchical Socio-Emotional Disintegration and Compensation Framework to explain the dynamic interplay between neurodegeneration-driven deficits and compensatory mechanisms. This framework advances mechanistic insight into the relationship between emotion and cognition, informing future clinical efforts to support the interpersonal well-being of aging populations.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of the Visual Perspective Questionnaire: Measuring Individual Differences in Own-Eyes and Observer-Like Perspectives in Autobiographical Memories
articles_hidden.authors: Peggy L. St. Jacques; Claudia Morales Valiente
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual perspective is a core feature of autobiographical remembering, yet relatively little is known about stable individual differences in the tendency to remember events from own-eyes (OE) and observer-like (OB) perspectives. The present study evaluated the psychometric properties of the Visual Perspective Questionnaire (VPQ), a brief four-item measure of OE and OB tendencies. Data were drawn from 15,043 undergraduate students, with convergent validity analyses conducted in a subsample of 1,712 participants. Reliability analyses supported scoring the VPQ as separate OE and OB dimensions. Simulation-based comparisons further revealed that the observed joint distribution of OE and OB more closely resembled a relatively independent framework than continuum or mutually exclusive alternatives. Extreme-profile analyses identified all four combinations of OE and OB, including high OE-high OB and low OE-low OB configurations that are difficult to accommodate within a strictly bipolar account. In the validation sample, OE and OB showed modest associations with object and spatial imagery, providing additional evidence of convergence with broader imagery tendencies. Together, the findings provide initial support for the VPQ as a brief measure of individual differences in visual perspective in autobiographical memory, and suggest that OE and OB are better represented as separate, coexisting dimensions than as opposite ends of a single continuum.

articles_hidden.title: Modality-Independent Core Brain Network for Language as Proved by Sign Language
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick C. Trettenbrein; Nina-Kristin Meister; Ksenija Slivac; Thomas A. Finkbeiner; Markus Steinbach; Angela D. Friederici; Emiliano Zaccarella
articles_hidden.abstract:
The human brain has the capacity to automatically compute the grammatical relations of
words in sentences, be they spoken or written. This species-specific ability for syntax lies at
the core of our capacity for language and is primarily subserved by a left-hemispheric fronto-
temporal network consisting of the posterior inferior frontal gyrus (pIFG), as well as the
posterior middle temporal gyrus and superior temporal sulcus (pMTG/STS). To date, it
remains unclear whether this core network for syntactic processing identified for spoken and
written language in hearing people also holds for the processing of the grammatical structure
of a natural sign language in deaf people. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, a
sign language paradigm that systematically varied the presence of syntactic and lexical-
semantic information, and meta-analytically defined functional regions-of-interests derived
from a large dataset of syntactic processing in hearing non-signers, we demonstrate that deaf
native signers of German Sign Language (DGS) also recruit left pIFG and pMTG/STS for
computing grammatical relations in sign language—indicating the universality of the core
language network. These findings suggest that the human brain evolved a dedicated neural
network for processing the grammatical structure of natural languages independent of
language modality, which flexibly interacts with different externalization systems depending
on the modality of language use.

articles_hidden.title: How should fillers be selected for lineups? Comparing the match-to-description and match-to-suspect methods via a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Courtlyn Elkins; Myat Aung; Edwin James Burns; Ruth Horry
articles_hidden.abstract: Lineups should contain known-innocent individuals (fillers) who resemble the suspect. Two common filler selection methods are: the match-to-suspect method, where fillers are selected based on perceived similarity to the suspect; and the match-to-description method, where fillers are selected based on how closely they match the culprit description. This systematic review sought to examine how the match-to-description method has been implemented since it was first proposed and revealed the match-to-description method has been operationalised in various ways. Meta-analytic techniques were used to investigate how filler selection method impacts lineup outcomes. Results revealed the odds of making a suspect identification, both guilty and innocent suspect, are higher in lineups created using the match-to-description method than the match-to-suspect method. Results also revealed lineup construction method did not impact discriminability. However, the small number of studies directly comparing the methods limits our ability to draw conclusions. Thus, highlighting the need for high-powered, pre-registered research.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric validation of the Spanish-language version of the Power of Food Scale in adults: convergent, discriminative, and trait–state associations with eating behavior and hunger
articles_hidden.authors: Sofia Abrevaya; Delfina Sarciat; Sofia Stancanelli
articles_hidden.abstract: The Power of Food Scale (PFS) is a widely used measure of hedonic hunger — the psychological impact of food environments on motivation to eat. No validated Spanish version exists for South American populations. This study adapted and validated an Argentine Spanish version of the PFS in 810 adults. Item analyses showed adequate variability and acceptable corrected item–total correlations. Internal consistency was high (α = .91). Parallel analysis and exploratory factor analysis supported the original three-factor structure. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated acceptable fit; a bifactor model showed improved fit with an Explained Common Variance of .73, supporting use of the total score. Measurement invariance across biological sex was established. Item response theory analyses confirmed adequate discrimination for most items. Convergent validity was supported by strong associations with hedonic eating, binge eating, and eating disorder symptoms, and negative associations with intuitive eating. PFS scores differentiated binge-eating severity groups (AUC = .86) and showed incremental validity over established measures. Regression-based normative data are provided. The Argentine Spanish PFS is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing hedonic hunger in adults.

articles_hidden.title: Making Sense of Sensory Differences: Identifying Sensory Processing Phenotypes and Their Relationship to Social and Executive Functioning in Neurotypical Children.
articles_hidden.authors: Adrianna M Molenaar; Natalia Van Esch; Nichole Scheerer
articles_hidden.abstract: Sensory processing varies substantially across individuals, yet research on distinct sensory phenotypes has focused primarily on neurodivergent populations. We examined whether comparable sensory phenotypes could be identified in 200 children aged 4-12 years with no known neurodevelopmental or psychiatric diagnoses, and whether phenotype membership was associated with executive functioning, social competence, mental health, alexithymia, and neurodivergent traits. K-means clustering of parent-reported sensory processing identified four sensory phenotypes: Sensory Adaptive, Generalized Sensory Differences, Under-responsive/Filtering Differences, and Sensory Sensitive. Children in the Sensory Adaptive group showed fewer executive functioning difficulties than children in all other groups and higher social competence than those in the Generalized Sensory Differences and Sensory Sensitive groups. In contrast, phenotypes did not differ significantly in autistic or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder traits, alexithymia, anxiety, or depression. These findings demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in sensory processing among children without diagnosed conditions and suggest that sensory phenotypes may be meaningfully related to everyday cognitive and social functioning. Future transdiagnostic work should directly examine the extent to which these phenotypes are shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children.

articles_hidden.title: Why do preschoolers struggle with the 3-cups-task? Further evidence for cognitive asymmetries in representing what and where uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Marlene M. Meyer; Marina Proft; Hannes Rakoczy
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research on modal thought has yielded conflicting findings regarding children’s ability to represent mutually exclusive possibilities. While some studies suggest that even infants and non-human animals understand possibilities to some degree, older children struggle in experimental paradigms that require them to consider multiple alternatives. In the 3-cups-task, for instance, they fail to systematically prefer a certain reward (in A) over two uncertain options (in B or C). This has been taken as evidence for that children below age 4 lack genuinely modal representations of possibility. However, recent metacognitive research suggests that already three-year-old children can recognize epistemic uncertainty about possible, mutually exclusive object identities (X or Y). So, why do 3-year-olds metacognitively acknowledge their ignorance in some contexts, but obviously fail to do so in trying to solve the 3-cups task? We addressed this question in three preregistered experiments (N = 278 three-year-old children) in which we investigated whether details of the task pragmatics, question format or the contents of the uncertainty judgments pose specific performance factors in the 3-cups-task. There was no clear evidence that task pragmatics or question format per se explain these difficulties. But there was strong evidence that the content of the uncertainty judgments matters: Children found it much more difficult to represent uncertainty where an object is (in cups B or C) than to represent uncertainty which of two objects (X or Y) was in a given box. These results converge with other recent findings to suggest a fundamental where/what asymmetry in children’s early modal reasoning and raise crucial questions about the robustness of early modal competence.

articles_hidden.title: Comparing the efficacy of virtual reality and flat screen delivery of breath control training for anxiety management
articles_hidden.authors: Grace Yat Sum Leung; Naresh Subramaniam; Benjamin Cook; Lucie Daniel-Watanabe; Johanna Finnemann; Toby Woolley; Craig Powell; Sergey Sitnikov; Paul Fletcher
articles_hidden.abstract: Game-based biofeedback offers a promising approach for learning and practising breath control techniques to manage anxiety and stress. Traditionally known as a response-modulation emotion regulation strategy, biofeedback operates through a closed-loop system that measures and feeds back real-time physiological information for users to monitor and subsequently manage their bodily responses. Few studies, however, have directly compared breath control training integrated with game-based biofeedback across two-dimensional flat screen display and three-dimensional immersive environment. It remains unclear whether differences in realism and immersiveness might influence the efficacy of breath control training. The present study investigated training effectiveness and user evaluation of a novel biofeedback-based breath control game among forty-five healthy adolescents. The breath control training was delivered in both virtual reality (VR) and flat screen modalities in a randomised and counterbalanced order using a within-subject study design. Consistent with hypotheses, the biofeedback game significantly improved both subjective and physiological (standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) and heart rate) markers of anxiety. While the two modalities indicated comparable intervention efficacy, the VR biofeedback game contributed added benefits in increasing SDNN, a physiological indicator of stress that reflects overall autonomic nervous system activity, as well as facilitating greater levels of interest and enjoyment, as indicated by ratings of intrinsic motivation to engage in the self-regulation training. These findings suggest that VR-based breath control training may enhance engagement and specific physiological responses, with implications for the design, development and evaluation of VR games for improving anxiety and stress.

articles_hidden.title: Thinking About What Others Think of Me: Engagement and Negativity of Self-Referential Mentalizing in Adolescent Internalizing Affect
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Guazzelli Williamson; Gabriel León; Christopher James Machle; Ava Reck; Jennifer H Pfeifer
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is an important period for the development of mentalizing and self-referential processing, and a period of increased risk for internalizing disorders such as anxiety and depression. However, the relationships between these processes, particularly in adolescents’ daily lives, remain unclear. In this intensive longitudinal study, we investigate the relationship between two dimensions of self-referential mentalizing (SRM)—1) engagement in SRM, and 2) negativity of SRM—as well as their interaction, in relation to internalizing feelings and symptoms. 149 adolescent females (M = 16.26 years, Range = 13.83 to 20.38 years) completed one or more (M = 2.0 bursts completed per participant) 30-day diary bursts where they answered daily questions about 1) engagement in and 2) negativity of self-referential mentalizing (SRM) and daily feelings of anxiety and depression. They also completed questionnaires measuring severity of internalizing symptoms once at each burst. Using Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM), we find that, at the between-person level, while both SRM and negative SRM were associated with feelings of depression and anxiety, only negative SRM was significantly positively associated with feelings of depression and anxiety after controlling for SRM. Individual differences in SRM and negative SRM were also associated with psychiatric measures of generalized anxiety, overall anxiety, and depression. At the daily, within-person level, experiencing elevated SRM and negative SRM on a given day was associated with elevated feelings of anxiety and depression on that same day. Additionally, there was a significant interaction at the daily, within-person level such that daily SRM was more strongly associated with daily feelings of anxiety and depression when the content of that SRM was negative. Together, our findings suggest that negative SRM, in particular, may be key for understanding associations with overall feelings of depression/anxiety, as well as changes in daily affect at the within-person level. While SRM and feelings of depression and anxiety covary on a day-to-day basis, the strength of this daily coupling was largely unrelated to severity of internalizing symptoms, suggesting that these daily dynamics may represent normative, rather than clinical, processes—at least for female adolescents. Together, our findings highlight the importance of considering multiple dimensions of SRM jointly, with the negativity of SRM emerging as particularly important for understanding internalizing affect at both the between- and within-person level.

articles_hidden.title: Reporting of Race, Ethnicity, Sexual and Gender Minority Identity, and Youth Involvement in Evidence for Youth-Facing AI Mental Health Tools: Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Davis Austria; Farah Baklouti; Michael Arowolo; William T. Bryant; Charity Brown Griffin; Terri Collin Dilmore; Charlene Pope
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Youth-facing artificial intelligence (AI) mental health tools have moved from research prototypes to consumer products at scale, and nearly three in four (72%) US adolescents report having used an AI companion. Racial and ethnic minority and sexual and gender minority (SGM) youth carry a disproportionate mental health burden, yet how often the evidence for these tools reports who was studied has not, to our knowledge, been measured. The nearest prior review found race or ethnicity reported in 34 of 88 studies and examined gender-related indicators in none.
Objective: To measure what proportion of studies of youth-facing AI mental health tools report participants' race and ethnicity and SGM status; which groups are represented; whether outcomes are disaggregated by identity; the extent of minoritized youth involvement in design, development, or evaluation; and how reporting has changed from 2020 to 2026 and between rule-based and generative systems.
Methods: Scoping review under JBI methodology, reported against PRISMA-ScR, prospectively registered (OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/XUZAE). Five databases were searched (2020 to 2026) with no identity term in any search string, because absence of identity reporting cannot be measured in a corpus selected on its presence. Search recall was validated against a seed set (88.6% as prespecified, 62/70; 91.1% under the operative eligibility interpretation, 82/90; 100% on the highest-priority tier under both). Identity reporting was charted for every study—absence is data.
Results: 100 studies were included. 42 of 100 (42.0%) reported neither race/ethnicity nor SGM status; 27 (27.0%) reported both. Decomposed into sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) data elements, race/ethnicity was reported in 42 (42.0%), gender identity in 41 (41.0%), and sexual orientation in 14 (14.0%). Outcomes were disaggregated by identity in 19 (19.0%). Involvement of minoritized youth in design, development, or evaluation was documented in 10 (10.0%), and in 0 of 36 studies of generative systems, against 6 of 40 (15.0%) rule-based conversational agent studies.
Conclusions: The evidence base for youth AI mental health tools under-reports the identities of the youth it studies; gender-identity reporting was more common in studies published from 2023 to 2026 than in studies published from 2020 to 2022, whereas sexual-orientation reporting remained uncommon in both periods; and participatory involvement of minoritized youth is unreported in the generative literature (0 of 36 studies). Reporting completeness is an actionable target for journals, funders, and developers.

articles_hidden.title: Longitudinal, Reciprocal Associations Between Social Self-Evaluation and Depressive Symptoms Across the Second Decade of Life
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Guazzelli Williamson; Samantha Chavez; John Coleman Flournoy; Nicholas B. Allen; Jennifer H Pfeifer
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: A key developmental task in adolescence is social self-concept development. Adolescence is also a period of heightened risk for internalizing psychopathology, particularly depression. While prior research has found links between self-processing and depression, social self-concept remains understudied and the causal direction of these associations remains unclear. Methods: Data come from a longitudinal study of adolescent girls (N = 172, aged 10-13 at baseline, ~18-month inter-wave intervals). Results: We show that negative social self-evaluation and depressive symptoms display longitudinal, reciprocal associations across four waves of data spanning early to late adolescence. Additionally, while self-negativity increased over time, self-positivity did not change, and both aspects of self-perception were independently associated with depressive symptoms. Conclusions: These findings suggest that social self-evaluation and depressive symptoms mutually influence each other across adolescence, and that negative social self-evaluation may be a useful intervention target for preventing and treating depressive psychopathology among adolescents.

articles_hidden.title: Digital Mental Health Tools to Support Evidence-Based Treatments in Youth Psychotherapy: A Mixed Methods Study
articles_hidden.authors: Josephine Halporn; John Parkhurst; Galen D. McNeil; Ruben G. Martinez; Ren Mondesir; Tierney McMahon; Ashley A. Knapp; Guo Sisi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mental health clinicians in private practice represent approximately half of the outpatient workforce. Clinicians in this environment have more global negative attitudes toward implementing evidence-based treatments (EBTs), despite the proven efficacy of EBTs in treating children and adolescents. Digital mental health (DMH) tools may help streamline EBT implementation, thus reducing demands on clinicians. However, little is known about how clinicians in this group perceive and use DMH tools with youth. 

Objective: This mixed methods study examined how clinicians in private practice currently use and perceive DMH tools. 

Method: Explanatory sequential design included survey data collection from 79 master’s- and doctoral-level licensed clinicians in two large, diverse urban regions within the U.S. Qualitative interviews were completed subsequently with 15 clinicians for purposes of thematic analysis. 

Results: More than half of survey participants endorsed currently using DMH tools (60.9%, n = 39) or being open to doing so (34.4%, n = 22). Those already open to and experienced in EBTs viewed DMH tools most favorably. Qualitative findings provided key insights into how clinicians are using DMH tools, as well as facilitators and barriers to their use.

Conclusions: DMH tools are being used to support elements of EBTs, and could reduce time spent out of session on tracking, preparation, and documentation for private practice clinicians. Future research should address barriers identified here in user-centered design processes with this group.

articles_hidden.title: Processing Speed, Not Multitasking, Drives Expert Decision-Making Under Pressure
articles_hidden.authors: Eleanor Ruth Alice Hyde; Robert Schmidt; Daniel J. Carroll; Claudia Christina von Bastian
articles_hidden.abstract: The cognitive mechanism underlying high performance during decision-making under pressure – such as in first-person shooter (FPS) games – is still unclear: advantages in multitasking or general processing speed? To resolve this, we classified N = 230 players (16-34 years) of the video game Counter-Strike into four expertise clusters (Novice, Skilled, Emerging, Expert), assessing their processing speed and task-switching performance. To better understand the source of expertise effects, we used drift-diffusion modelling (DDM) to estimate non-decision and decision components of performance. Experts exhibited significantly faster reaction times than Novices, but no specific multitasking advantage was observed. The DDM revealed that this speed advantage was driven by higher drift rates and shorter non-decision times. No expertise-related differences were found in boundary separation, the strategic component of decision-making. Findings suggest that expert performance in decision-making under pressure is characterised by advantages in general processing speed rather than being associated with greater multitasking capabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Impact of Soundscapes on Mental Well-Being and Physiological Stress: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Harley Glassman; Brandon T. Paul; Frank Russo
articles_hidden.abstract: Soundscapes represent the acoustic environment perceived by humans, a phenomenon that holds significant implications for psychological and physiological health. While urban noise is a known stressor, natural soundscapes are theorized to provide restorative benefits through mechanisms which replenish cognitive resources subserving mental well-being. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence from peer-reviewed literature to examine how diverse acoustic environments impact mental well-being and physiological markers. A comprehensive search across scholarly databases identified ten studies spanning urban, natural, and virtual reality settings. The evidence was evaluated for certainty and risk of bias to ensure the current literature was synthesized rigorously. Qualitative findings indicated that natural soundscapes (e.g., birdsong, water sound) consistently facilitate faster stress recovery, lower heart rate, and reduced skin conductance compared to anthropogenic noise. Neuroimaging data further suggested that exposure to natural sounds correlates with decreased activity in brain regions associated with stress regulation. Quantitative findings confirmed a positive effect of pleasant soundscapes on health outcomes, though significant heterogeneity was observed across studies, likely reflecting diverse methodologies and environmental contexts. Individual differences, including noise sensitivity and personality traits, were found to moderate these effects. These results support Restorative Environment Theory and suggest that integration of natural acoustic environments into urban planning and healthcare design may mitigate the negative impacts of noise pollution. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs to evaluate the chronic health effects of sustained soundscape exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Noun memory advantage drives sentence internal primacy and recency at clause boundaries
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastián Mancha; Ellen Lau
articles_hidden.abstract: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks ‘chunk’ word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval. Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli. How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence’s component words in memory? In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause. Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall. Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results. We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

articles_hidden.title: What is it like for matter to matter?
articles_hidden.authors: David Vandenheever
articles_hidden.abstract: Consciousness research often asks where, when, or under what conditions neural processing becomes conscious. Here I introduce the Distributed Architecture of Valenced Evaluation (DAVE), which starts from a different premise. Nervous systems continuously represent states in terms of what those states imply for the organism, and these evaluations are physically instantiated in dispositions that bias bodily, attentional, predictive, and action systems. DAVE proposes that, where such organism-relative evaluation is embedded in the embodied dynamics through which a represented state can alter the organism, its evaluative character is already minimally phenomenal. Each such evaluative event constitutes a micro-quale: not a miniature conscious subject or an independently experienced percept, but a local phenomenal contribution to the experience of the organism. Recurrent interaction among many micro-qualia forms the richly differentiated, context-sensitive, and apparently unified phenomenal tapestry familiar in human experience. Attention, task demands, working memory, and self-representation selectively amplify, stabilize, and organize parts of this tapestry, producing increasingly integrated, accessible, and self-related forms of experience. Because introspection presents the integrated tapestry rather than its constituent evaluative events, phenomenal character may appear to be an additional property beyond the physical organization that constitutes it. This conception of phenomenal character makes the explanatory gap seem inevitable. DAVE does not solve the hard problem by discovering a mechanism that converts nonphenomenal processing into phenomenality; it attempts to dissolve the need for such a conversion by identifying minimal phenomenal character with organism-relative evaluative disposition itself.

articles_hidden.title: Oregon’s State-Regulated Psilocybin Services: Early Real-World Safety Signals
articles_hidden.authors: Jason B Luoma; Christina Chwyl; Dan Des Jarlais; Christopher Stauffer; Ximena Levander; Ryan Cook; Adie Wilson-Poe; Dennis McCarty; Philip Korthuis
articles_hidden.abstract: Interest in psilocybin has accelerated, with public access in the United States expanding through a rapidly evolving landscape of decriminalization, increased availability of psilocybin-containing products, and state-regulated facilitated service models (Hutchison et al., 2025). However, uptake may be advancing faster than the evidence base. Regulatory oversight is needed to inform population-level risk. Most supervised psilocybin safety data derive from clinical trials that enroll carefully screened participants and deliver interventions in tightly controlled settings. This limits the generalizability of safety data to the broader populations likely to seek services if psilocybin products are authorized for medical use in the United States (Tan et al., 2022).

articles_hidden.title: “The sun will still rise whether you’re an Olympian or not”: Exploring the changes in psychological state across four phases of injury rehabilitation among international figure skaters
articles_hidden.authors: Jamie Smokler; Isabelle Simm
articles_hidden.abstract: Injury is inherent within elite sport, often resulting in significant physical and psychological challenges. However, limited research has explored how elite figure skaters experience and interpret injury within the unique demands of their sport. This study aimed to examine the lived experiences of injury and rehabilitation among elite, international figure skaters. Eleven skaters (7 female, 4 male, M age = 24.09 years, SD = 4.36) with an average of 18.64 years of skating experience (SD = 4.15) participated in semi-structured interviews, derived from sport injury rehabilitation literature, conducted via Microsoft Teams. Interviews ranged from 31 to 102 minutes (M = 62.81, SD = 25.60). Data were analysed using a reflexive thematic analysis. Analysis revealed two overarching themes that progressed across injury recovery: psychological adaptation and reconstruction of athletic identity. Findings indicated that skaters initially experienced shock and catastrophic thinking, before progressing through sustained uncertainty, and active coping. Injury also challenged athletes’ sense of self, with skaters describing loss of purpose, and subsequent identity reconstruction though increased self-awareness and resilience. Evaluations, future research directions, and implications of findings are also discussed. Overall, findings highlight injury recovery as both psychological and physical, emphasising the importance of psychologically informed support throughout injury recovery.

articles_hidden.title: Neural Signatures of Impulsivity in Adolescence: A Multivariate Pattern Analysis of Reward and Loss Processing
articles_hidden.authors: Stefanie Fraga Gonçalves; Morgan Lindenmuth; Helmet Talib Karim; Rasim Diler; Cecile D. Ladouceur
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents experience mood disturbances and impulsivity that increase vulnerability to maladaptive risk-taking, yet the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of these phenotypes remain poorly understood. Thus, the current pre-registered study sought to optimize models predicting anhedonic, sad, and manic mood, as well as impulsivity, from multivariate frontostriatal neural responses during incentive (i.e., reward and loss) processing. Participants were adolescents (n=153, healthy 12–18-year-olds, 104 assigned female at birth) with moderate to severe depression, as well as some controls, to have a full range of symptoms. They underwent functional neuroimaging during a monetary incentive delay task and completed self-report questionnaires on mood and impulsivity. We optimized a pre-registered 3-fold nested cross-validation support vector regression model predicting impulsivity, which showed statistically significant but small predictive performance (R² = .02, MAE = .81). Feature importance analyses showed distributed signal across frontostriatal circuits, particularly cognitive and motor-related circuits. In addition, neural activity to loss anticipation followed by reward receipt and reward anticipation contributed most to model performance. As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the model with depression-residualized impulsivity to account for shared variance with depressive symptoms. This model showed modestly improved predictive performance (R² = .04, MAE = .80) with a similar pattern of feature contributions. No models successfully predicted anhedonic, sad, or manic mood. These findings suggest that multivariate neural activity within cognitive- and motor-related frontostriatal circuits during incentive processing is associated with impulsivity, and not mood disturbances, in adolescents, including those with mild to moderate depression. Public health efforts aimed at reducing impulsivity (and potentially risk-taking) should consider the role of incentive processing.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Factor Structure: Item-Level Functioning and Measurement Invariance of the ERQ-CA in Brazilian Children and Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Dannielle Melo Nunes; Pedro de Leon Brito; Leandro da Silva Sauer; André Luiz de Carvalho Braule Pinto
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined the structural and item-level psychometric properties of the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (ERQ-CA) in 525 Brazilian youth aged 8–17 years (M = 13.84; SD = 3.18), of both sexes (50.87% girls), enrolled in public schools.
