Participants completed the ERQ-CA and mental health and well-being measures. We evaluated the proposed two-factor structure, measurement invariance across sex and age, item discrimination and threshold parameters using Item Response Theory (IRT), Differential Item Functioning (DIF), and associations with external indicators. The results provided partial support for two-factor model, with heterogeneous global fit indices and evidence of localized residual dependence. Measurement invariance analyses supported equality of factor loadings and thresholds across sex and age. Sensitivity analyses indicated that age-related loading invariance was somewhat dependent on how the age groups were defined. DIF was detected in two Suppression items, but its score-level impact was minimal for sex and small but detectable for age. Associations with external variables were predominantly small to moderate in magnitude and showed distinct patterns for Reappraisal and Suppression. Overall, the findings support the interpretability of the ERQ-CA while also identifying localized model limitations and group-related item functioning that should be considered when interpreting scores.

articles_hidden.title: Lifetime Prevalence and Co-occurrence of Offensive Gun Use, Defensive Gun Use, and Nonfatal Firearm Victimization in a National Sample of US Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Brian M. Hicks; Dorothy Stearns; Amanda Price; Mark A. Ilgen
articles_hidden.abstract: Firearm-related encounters have the potential for high risk of injury, but few studies have estimated the prevalence and co-occurrence among offensive gun use (OGU), defensive gun use (DGU), and nonfatal firearm victimization (NFV) in a national sample. We did so with data from the National Firearms, Alcohol, Cannabis, and Suicide survey (N = 7034) of US adults that assessed broad definitions of gun use and victimization (e.g., gun displays to shootings). Lifetime prevalence was 5.2% (95% CI 4.5% to 6.0%) for OGU, 12.6% (95% CI 11.5% to 13.7%) for DGU, and 31.5% (95% CI 30.0% to 33.0%) for NFV. Using survey weights to extrapolate to the US adult population, we estimate nearly 13.9 million adults have used a gun offensively, 33.3 million have used a gun defensively, and 83.3 million have experienced NFV in their lifetime. Most respondents (~80%) only reported gun use and victimization that did not involve firing a gun. There was a high rate of co-occurrence between OGU and DGU (OR = 33.8, 95% CI 23.7 to 48.0), and between NFV and OGU (OR = 5.3, 95% CI 3.9 to 7.2) and DGU (OR = 4.5, 95% CI 3.7 to 5.6). Rates of OGU, DGU, and/or NFV were higher among respondents who were males, lower income, lived in more dangerous neighborhoods, current gun owners, and had a job that required carrying a firearm. Occupational firearm carriage was associated with especially high rates of OGU (20.5%, 95% CI 15.8% to 26.1%), DGU (49.6%, 95% CI 43.9% to 55.2%), and NFV (50.9%, 95% CI 45.2% to 56.5%). A large minority of Americans have had a firearm-related victimization experience, and a smaller but substantial proportion have used a gun for defense. OGU, DGU, and NFV frequently co-occur but event-level information is needed to delineate the mechanisms of overlap.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Average Changes: How the Distribution of Youth Mental Health Shifted Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic
articles_hidden.authors: Lianne P. de Vries; Elske Marra; Imme Rahmon; Tinca JC Polderman; Meike Bartels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Stress can affect not only average levels of mental health, but also how positive and negative aspects of mental health relate to one another. The COVID-19 pandemic provides a unique context to examine those population-level differences. We investigated youth mental health before, during, and after the pandemic by examining mean levels, association between wellbeing and depressive symptoms, and latent mental health profiles.
	Using large population-based samples from the Netherlands of youth aged 12–25 years, we compared mental health before (N = 14,146, 58% female), during (N = 14,308, 55% female), and after the pandemic (N = 37,797, 62% female) in a repeated cross-sectional design.
	Wellbeing and depressive symptoms were stronger correlated during (r = −.70) and after the pandemic (r = −.69) compared to pre-pandemic (r = −.49, ps < .001). Latent profile analyses further showed differences in the population distribution of mental health. Pre-pandemic, two profiles were identified, whereas during and after the pandemic three-profile solutions provided the best fit, including a large group with intermediate levels of wellbeing and depressive symptoms (38-40%). Across periods, most youth were classified in a high mental health profile (51-86%), whereas a smaller proportion were classified in a low mental health profile (8-14%). Loneliness, self-rated health, optimism, and stress exposure consistently differed between profiles. 
	Youth mental health differed across periods in average levels, the strength of the association, and distribution of wellbeing and depressive symptoms. These findings show the value of moving beyond average effects when studying population responses to large-scale stress.

articles_hidden.title: The Link between Warm Glow and Pro-Environmental Behaviors is Positive and Robust: A Scoping Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Linli Zhou; Cameron Brick; Disa Sauter
articles_hidden.abstract: When we engage in pro-environmental behaviors that align with our personal values, we can experience positive feelings, known as warm glow. Theories suggest a potential positive feedback loop such that people who anticipate feeling more warm glow are more likely to act pro-environmentally, and acting in line with their personal values may in turn elicit warm glow, thereby encouraging further pro-environmental behavior. There is considerable empirical work from psychology, marketing and economics investigating these relationships, but to date this work has not been systematically synthesized. A test of the strength and robustness of the theorized links is needed to answer the question of whether warm glow is in fact consistently related to pro-environmental behavior. We report a scoping review and meta-analysis probing the robustness of the associations between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Following the PRISMA guidance, we identified 94 papers with 251 effects based on 58,313 participants. A pre-registered three-level random-effects meta-analytic model was used to estimate overall effects and to examine moderation by behavioral domain and measurement approach. Sensitivity analyses were performed to test the robustness of the findings. Results indicate robust medium-to-large associations between both anticipated and experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors (rs: .43 – .53). Substantial heterogeneity persisted after accounting for moderators, suggesting meaningful variation in effect sizes across studies. Overall, these findings provide strong evidence of a clear link between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Future research using experimental and longitudinal designs will help clarify causal pathways in the positive feedback loop.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Inclusive Developmental Science: Translating Community Perspectives into Research Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Maheen Siddiqui; Rianne Haartsen; Anita Song; Roksana Seif Amirhosseini; Ana Maria Portugal; Chiara Bulgarelli; Anna Gui
articles_hidden.abstract: Developmental science continues to face challenges in engaging diverse families and ensuring diversity within the research workforce, limiting whose experiences and perspectives are represented in research. This study provides an empirically grounded, parent-informed account of the barriers and conditions that shape inclusive research practice. We conducted three participatory focus groups with parents from ethnic minority backgrounds in the UK (n = 17; two online, one hybrid). Transcripts were analysed using thematic analysis and integrated with insights accumulated across a year of Diversity in Developmental Science Network activities, including an online seminar series and conference panel. Findings were organised into four themes: barriers and enablers to research participation; building trust with communities; inclusive research design and transparency; and representation and cultural safety. Parents highlighted accessible and flexible practices, meaningful representation, culturally responsive materials, transparent communication, and stronger researcher-community relationships. Network activities further highlighted structural barriers and diversity within research teams.

articles_hidden.title: Parsing structured semantic knowledge from arbitrary text with GenAI
articles_hidden.authors: A.T. Lopes Rego; Joshua Snell; Martijn Meeter
articles_hidden.abstract: Frame Semantics offers a compelling framework for representing meaning as structured conceptual scenarios (frames). FrameNet operationalizes this theory as a lexical resource linking words to frames and their conceptual roles (frame elements, FEs). However, applying Frame Semantics to arbitrary text has historically required either laborious manual annotation or complex, task-specific classification pipelines that presuppose known targets and/or frames. Here we present an open-source method that leverages Generative AI (GenAI) to automatically parse semantic frames and their FEs from any input text, without requiring pre-specification of frames or target spans, or task-specific model training. The tool combines a retrieval step, in which candidate frames are identified via embedding-based semantic similarity, with a selection step, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) is prompted, using zero- or few-shot examples, to determine which frames are evoked, which spans trigger them, and which spans fill their FEs, returning a structured, machine-readable output. We detail installation, execution, and output interpretation, and provide a built-in evaluation module supporting exact, semantic, and graph-based matching against FrameNet's human-annotated data. This freely available tool lowers the barrier to frame-semantic analysis for researchers across linguistics, who wish to explore structured semantic content in naturalistic text, including in relation to behavioral and neural measures of language comprehension.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Average Effects: Childhood SES and the Shape of Adult Well-Being Distributions
articles_hidden.authors: Jinrui Liu; Shigehiro Oishi; Espen Røysamb
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on socioeconomic inequality and wellbeing focuses largely on mean-level analyses, leaving a distributional question underexamined: whether childhood financial circumstances (childSES) relate to not only where individuals land on average, but also who gains access to favorable outcomes and who remains at the lower end of the distribution. Using U.S. adult data from MIDUS 1 (N = 5570-5603), we applied generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS) to examine associations between childSES and life satisfaction (LS) and personal growth (PG) across mean, dispersion, and ceiling probability. Higher childSES was associated with higher mean LS and ~4% lower dispersion, reflecting a floor-buffering rather than ceiling-lifting effect. For PG, higher childSES was associated with greater odds of reaching the maximum score (OR = 1.15). These patterns largely replicated in MIDUS 2 (N = 3,541-3,556) and persisted after accounting for adultSES. Findings are limited to a U.S. sample from 1995-1996.

articles_hidden.title: Repurposing, redefining, and reimagining: A paradigm shift towards person-driven neuroscience in the digital age
articles_hidden.authors: Becky Inkster; Mark Sheppard
articles_hidden.abstract: The focus of neuroscience has traditionally hinged on collecting quantifiable physiological data that are often distanced from the lived experiences of people. In contrast, qualitative, subjective, and situational information provides rich context, but lacks the empirical precision needed to map to neural processes. To reconcile this gap, we established ‘The Lαβ’ as an interdisciplinary initiative that fuses person-driven experiences, personal reflection, and empirical neuroscience. People engage with their chosen experiences in their chosen settings while wearing a portable EEG headset. Timestamped information is then collected from a variety of sources. We introduce our novel neurotriangulation approach: A person‑driven synthesis of quantitative electrophysiological signals, qualitative observations, and subjective and situational information into a single analytic stream. Our aim is to provide people with opportunities for neuro-self-reflection. We use an ethics-first approach to preserve data sovereignty, privacy, autonomy, and agency for the individual. In this paper, we present real-world case studies to demonstrate our data collection, real-time field analysis, and co-interpretation methodologies. These case studies also underscore the neurotriangulation model as an approach to move beyond reductive, data-centric models toward a person‑driven paradigm. This shift allows neurodata to be more accessible, inclusive, and personally meaningful, while prioritising safety and subjectivity. This has the potential to reshape how we think about neuroscientific applications in fields such as education and training, anthropology, creative arts, wellbeing, and mental health. By repurposing and redefining the use of extant neurotechnology, we are reimagining a future in which our understanding of ourselves is person-driven, reality-based, and ethically sound.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging the Trust Gap: A Contractualist Framework for Trustworthy AI
articles_hidden.authors: Luis Marcos Vidal; Clara Pretus
articles_hidden.abstract: Trustworthy AI is defined by properties built into a system, but trust depends on how users perceive it, so a system can meet every requirement and still fail to be trusted. Human and artificial agents that justify decisions in contractualist terms, by appeal to what affected parties could reasonably accept, are trusted more than those that appeal to aggregate welfare or fixed rules, irrespective of the action selected, but why is unexplained. We propose that a contractualist justification discloses individualized regard, evidence that the affected party's standpoint entered the decision, which is what trust, as a judgment that an agent is willing to act well, is sensitive to. Perceived regard is the mediating inference and raises trust through two pathways: warmth, and the expectation that the agent's future decisions will take the perceiver's own stakes into account. The intentional stance is a gating condition rather than a mediator, deciding whether an agent can be the object of this inference at all, so the mechanism is shared by human and artificial agents and needs no genuine intentions. Such justification is the observable trace of virtual bargaining, a theory-of-mind process, and does not require agents with genuine mental states. We state five falsifiable hypotheses that discriminate the account from warmth, anthropomorphism, and mere-transparency alternatives, and identify moderators and a possible moral uncanny valley as further tests.

articles_hidden.title: Art Therapy for Recovery from Childhood Trauma in a Vietnamese Adolescent: A Case Study
articles_hidden.authors: THANH TU NGUYEN
articles_hidden.abstract: Childhood trauma is associated with self-injury and suicidal behaviour, yet traumatised young people often cannot put their experiences into words, particularly where family hierarchies limit emotional disclosure between children and parents, as in Vietnam. This case study describes a 17-year-old Vietnamese girl ("Lily") who presented with severe non-suicidal self-injury and previously undisclosed suicide attempts rooted in childhood adversity. She received a 12-session, three-phase intervention comprising House-Tree-Person (HTP) art therapy, prosocial community action and structured family sessions. Session records, journal entries, field notes and parent interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, and pre- and post-intervention drawings using compositional and iconographic visual analysis. Three themes were generated: art as a bridge to concealed trauma; consolidation of gains through prosocial agency; and relational repair within the family. The final drawing was interpreted as reflecting psychological integration and post-traumatic growth. Art therapy, supported by family engagement, the young person's active cooperation and a compassionate therapeutic relationship, may offer a culturally responsive pathway to recovery. Findings from a single, clinician-interpreted case without long-term follow-up are illustrative and require further study.

articles_hidden.title: Antenatal infant sleep information in Western Australia: A mixed-methods study of what parents received and what they wanted
articles_hidden.authors: Heather Liebregts; Alex Metse; Andrea R. Steele; Kelli Kathleen MacMillan; Rhonda Marriott; Renita Almeida
articles_hidden.abstract:
Problem. Pregnancy is a finite window wherein parents' expectations of infant care develop, yet parents’ experiences of and preferences for antenatal infant sleep preparation are uncharacterised. 

Background. Parents in Western settings commonly report infant sleep problems, and interventions are predominantly behavioural. Antenatal provision addresses sleep safety rather than developmental-relational preparation. 

Aim. To describe what antenatal infant sleep information Western Australian parents received, their satisfaction, preferences for its timing and provider, and what they wished they had received.

Methods. A mixed-methods online survey of 185 Western Australian parents and expectant parents (180 with a child aged 0–3 years; five pregnant). Closed items addressed information received, satisfaction, and preferences; an open-ended item was analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Findings. Just over half (53.5%; 99/185) received no antenatal information; where provided, midwives were the most frequent source (34.0%; 63/185) and satisfaction was modest. The antenatal period and first month were most endorsed (75.0%, 135/180; 66.1%, 119/180), with child health nurses (35.6%; 64/180) and midwives (30.6%; 55/180) preferred as providers. Four themes captured parents’ preferences: preparation for likely bedsharing; recalibrated expectations; validation of responsive caregiving; and non-prescriptive guidance.

Discussion. Provision was limited and only moderately satisfying. Parents sought guidance positioning them as decision-makers engaging with biologically typical infant behaviour. 

Conclusion. Relational, non-prescriptive preparation, including how to bedshare more safely, initiated antenatally by midwives and continued postnatally by child health nurses, would address an unmet need within existing perinatal care.

articles_hidden.title: Roles of conceptual development in the training and acquisition of compassion practices
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Condon; Lawrence Barsalou
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conceptual development is a fundamental feature of contemplative practice but has received little attention in contemplative science. In Buddhism, for example, the eightfold path begins with right view, which includes comprehension of interdependence, suffering, and so on. In Tibetan traditions, foundational practices introduce conceptual frames, including aphorisms and visualizations, that help access capacities for compassion and wisdom. In this article, we take a lifespan approach to examine how conceptual development supports compassion training. We focus on relational practices adapted from Tibetan Buddhism, which involve calling to mind sources of love, comfort, and safety to establish a secure base and an internal holding environment–an embodied stance of stillness, curiosity, and care for all physical and mental patterns. The theory of situated conceptualization (TSC) provides a nuanced cognitive neuroscience framework for understanding how situated and embodied experiences develop into conceptual knowledge across the lifespan, and it holds significant implications for how these practices can mature within a person over time.
	According to TSC, when meditations of compassion are engaged, the physical and affective qualities that occur within practice, such as warmth, care, and ease, can become part of the background conceptual knowledge for any mental pattern that arises within meditation. Over time, these qualities may increasingly emerge within the foreground of a given conceptualization. As patterns of mind are experienced and understood for what they are within an internal holding environment, the ruminative processes that fuel conceptualization can relax, and the constructed, empty nature of concepts and emotional states can more readily reveal itself–a process that supports advanced wisdom practices. Finally, because conceptualizations are situated in social and cultural contexts, the internal holding environment for patterns of mind can extend to all webs of connection that influence those patterns, becoming increasingly a capacity of compassion for the world at large.

articles_hidden.title: A Community-Based Implementation of The Family Check-up Is Associated with Lower Pediatric Emergency Room Utilization and Acute Care Services: A Health Service Utilization and Cost Analysis Study
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Schweer-Collins; Jonathan Woodward; Elizabeth Stormshak
articles_hidden.abstract: A large number of studies have shown that the brief three session Family Check-Up intervention is effective in promoting children’s social and behavioral development and in reducing problem behaviors. Research in this area has begun to examine the effectiveness of this program through real-world implementation studies. This brief report describes how a community-based implementation of the Family Check-Up is associated with reduced healthcare utilization, specifically acute care services including emergency department, inpatient, and urgent care utilization. Future implementation trials may benefit from including administrative data to examine the outcomes of the Family Check-Up in conjunction with cost and service utilization data.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond accuracy: extracting reaction-time biomarkers of sustained attention and cognitive flexibility from the UCancellation task
articles_hidden.authors: Boris Penaloza; Elnaz Vafaei; Anja Pahor; Susanne M. Jaeggi; Aaron R. Seitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding. Here, we derive two reaction-time (RT) biomarkers from our tablet-based UCancellation task in 388 young adults: intra-individual RT variability (RTV), a marker of sustained attention, and switch cost, an index of cognitive flexibility from transitions between two different task's target categories. Because consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of scanned distractors, both are confounded by search effort, which we remove with a scanning-load (p) correction framework. RTV behaved as a scored individual-difference measure: correction improved reliability and convergent validity against TOVA low-frequency RTV (n = 373), and a cross-target composite was the most reliable index. Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reversed with load—large and positive when targets were adjacent, reversing as scanning load increased—consistent with inhibition of return. Together, these metrics show that RT structure within a brief cancellation task carries attentional information that standard metrics alone does not capture.

articles_hidden.title: What this trial tells us about modified manualised psychodynamic psychotherapy for schizophrenia—and what it cannot
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Stefan Leucht; Björn Schlier
articles_hidden.abstract: Montag and colleagues report a randomised trial of modified psychodynamic psychotherapy for schizophrenia (MPP-S) plus treatment as usual (TAU) versus TAU alone. We welcome efforts to strengthen the evidence base for psychodynamic psychotherapy. Given the limited access to psychological treatment for people with psychosis and the, at best, moderate effects of existing pharmacological and psychological interventions this is a valuable effort to advance evidence-based treatment in psychosis. Several methodological decisions, however, complicate interpretation of its findings.

articles_hidden.title: Social comparison information is not always prioritized: Temporal performance feedback dominates self-assessment in dysphoria
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Englert; Thomas Meyer; Nexhmedin Morina
articles_hidden.abstract: Social and temporal comparisons inform self-evaluation. In educational and work settings, social comparison information seems to affect performance self-assessments more strongly than temporal comparison information. We investigated whether this “higher assigned priority of social comparison information” (HAPSCI) also occurs in people with symptoms of depression, a condition associated with aberrant feedback processing. In a false feedback experiment, we studied the effects of social and temporal comparison information on self-assessments in a sample of N=159 individuals with dysphoria. Participants received concurrent social and temporal comparison feedback on their cognitive performance in a visuospatial 2-back task, which was either favorable (improvement over time or outperforming other participants) or unfavorable (deterioration or being outperformed). Only temporal comparison feedback affected performance self-assessments, while only unfavorable social comparison feedback impacted objective performance. Our results suggest that HAPSCI may not generalize across populations. Individuals with depressive symptoms might be more receptive to temporal than social comparison feedback. We discuss how appraisal of the motivational significance of comparison outcomes, sample characteristics, and experimental procedures may shape effects on self-evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: From “Person = Me” to “Person = Man,” New Evidence from Eastern Matrilineal and Patriarchal Societies
articles_hidden.authors: Jialin Zhou; Xi Cheng; Yinyin Zang; April Hope Bailey; Yin Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: How do people imagine a generic “person”? Who comes to mind by default shapes downstream decisions, with harmful consequences when one gender stands in for everyone. Existing work finds that people often imagine a “person” as a man more than a woman. However, prior research is limited almost exclusively to Western adults, leaving the origins and development of these representations unknown. We examined two novel cultures with very different gender structures. In the unique and hard-to-reach matrilineal Mosuo society, both men and women showed a stable tendency to imagine a “person” as someone of their own gender. In a mainstream Chinese sample, boys and men imagined a “person” as a man, whereas for girls and women representations shifted across age groups and increasingly towards a male default. These results show that male defaults are not a given: Initial own-gender biases are reshaped to a male-generic model through culturally-specific factors.

articles_hidden.title: Improved inhibitory control following combined transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) and cognitive training in individuals with traumatic brain injury and impulsivity
articles_hidden.authors: Hamza Jamal; Jazmin Camchong; Kelvin O. Lim; Casey Gilmore
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Impaired inhibitory control and other impulsive behaviors are common after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but directly targeted treatments remain limited. Objective: To evaluate the preliminary effects and tolerability of prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) paired with executive function training in Veterans with a history of TBI and clinically relevant impulsive behavior. Methods: Twenty-five Veterans with mild (n=18), moderate (n=4), or severe (n=3) TBI were randomized in a double-blind design to active (n=13) or sham (n=12) tDCS. Participants completed five daily sessions of 2 mA tDCS for 20 minutes (anode AF7, cathode AF8) delivered during approximately 46 minutes of BrainHQ cognitive training. An untrained response inhibition task with simultaneous response and stop cues was administered before and immediately after the intervention and at 1-, 2-, and 3-month follow-ups. The primary outcome was the percentage of commission errors on stop trials. Results: The active group showed a greater pre- to post-intervention reduction in stop trial commission errors than the sham group (Group x Time: beta = -0.011, SE = 0.004, p = .004). No significant change was detected from post-intervention through the follow-up period, suggesting this level of reduced errors persisted for three months post-intervention. Self-reported impulsivity and performance on the cognitive training tasks did not show differential improvement after correction for multiple comparisons. Adverse effect ratings were low and did not differ between groups. Conclusions: Five sessions of prefrontal tDCS paired with cognitive training were well-tolerated and produced preliminary evidence of improved response inhibition on an untrained task. These results, while requiring confirmation in a fully powered trial, suggest that this neuroplasticity-based intervention may be a promising non-pharmacological approach for patients who suffer a TBI and are affected by impulsivity.

articles_hidden.title: Digital Twins in Mental Health Care: A Qualitative Study on Subjective Relevance, Acceptability and Implementation Considerations Co-Designed, Co-Produced and Co-Written with Experts by Experience and Academics
articles_hidden.authors: Lana Woelfl; Annika Stefanie Reinhold; Ulrich Reininghaus; Annette Zimpelmann; Sophia Thier; Lina Blank; Dusan Hirjak; Christian Rauschenberg; Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Digital Mental Twins (DMTs) - adaptive, data-driven models intended to represent individual’s mental health in real time - have been proposed as a basis for personalized mental health services and shared decision-making. However, empirical evidence on service users’ perspectives remains limited. This study aimed to investigate subjective relevance, acceptability, and implementation consideration of service users on the conceptual and methodological approach of DMTs. Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews with N=17 in-patient service users (mean age 35,8; 47% female) with differing mental health conditions (e.g., major depressive disorder, schizophrenia) according to ICD-10. Two experts with lived experiences contributed as co-researchers. The interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Results: Four overarching themes were identified: (1) Perceived role of DMTs in mental health care: Participants described DMTs as potentially beneficial, especially by providing “neutral” feedback to support reflection. (2) Perceived risks, barriers and potential adverse effects: Concerns about data privacy were common, alongside anticipated unintended consequences of continuous feedback and recommendations, including guilt, pressure, and self-fulfilling prophecies. (3) Balancing data utility and privacy: Participants emphasized the importance of integrating diverse data sources (e.g. self-reports, passive sensing, biomarkers), while highlighting the need for transparent data collection and user control. (4) Perceived clinical value and implementation preferences: Participants valued low-threshold support and preferred implementation of DMTs within blended-care models. Conclusions: This qualitative study delineates opportunities and challenges of DMTs from service users’ perspective. Overall, participants viewed DMTs as potentially valuable adjuncts to mental health care, while emphasizing that acceptability will depend on user-centered design, data transparency, and integration into clinical workflows.

articles_hidden.title: Human similarity judgments reveal fine-grained representations of relationships and actions in dynamic social scenes
articles_hidden.authors: Kathy Garcia; Leyla Isik
articles_hidden.abstract: How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes? Existing accounts typically rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations remains largely unknown. We collected 53,223 odd-one-out triplet similarity judgments from 232 participants on 250 naturalistic dyadic-interaction videos and trained a sparse-positive embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions. We show the learned dimensions explain twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, capture interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships with actions), and fractionate broad semantic content (e.g., parent-child interactions separate into caregiving versus affectionate play). The same dimensions predict fMRI responses in the visual cortex, including lateral visual pathway and superior temporal sulcus, better than pre-labeled annotations. Together, these results suggest that human representations of social scenes combine social relationships and actions in ways that pre-defined taxonomies miss, offering a behaviorally grounded target for future studies of social vision.

articles_hidden.title: Neural correlates of acute psychosocial stress: An activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis of ScanSTRESS studies
articles_hidden.authors: Lena Sophie Pfeifer; Christian J. Merz; Erhan Genç; Oliver T. Wolf; Sebastian Ocklenburg
articles_hidden.abstract: Acute psychosocial stress engages distributed neural systems involved in salience processing, cognitive control, and self-regulation. Although the ScanSTRESS paradigm provides a standardized approach to inducing psychoscocial stress during functional magnetic resonance imaging, findings across ScanSTRESS studies vary. Building on recent efforts toward greater harmonization, the present study aimed to synthesize the ScanSTRESS literature and identify consistent patterns of neural activation and deactivation. A systematic literature review was conducted (Web of Science, PubMed, citation screening of reviews/meta-analyses). Studies were eligible if they employed the ScanSTRESS/ScanSTRESS-C paradigm in healthy samples, used a within-subjects stress-versus-control contrast, and reported whole-brain coordinates. 13 datasets (N=833 participants) with low risk of bias (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale) were included. Activation likelihood estimation meta-analyses (ALE) were conducted separately for stress-related activations and deactivations. Stress-related activations converged in six clusters, including bilateral insula/claustrum, right middle frontal gyrus, left precentral/inferior frontal gyrus, right thalamus/lentiform nucleus, and left cuneus. Stress-related deactivations converged in ten clusters encompassing the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices, temporo-parietal regions, bilateral insula, and parahippocampal cortex. These findings identify a robust ScanSTRESS pattern, characterized by engagement of salience-related regions alongside widespread suppression of default mode and limbic structures. These results extend previous evidence and provide publicly available ALE maps to facilitate region-of-interest analyses in future ScanSTRESS studies. Although beyond the scope of the present study, future research should examine how neural stress responses relate to demographic variability as well as physiological and endocrine reactivity.

articles_hidden.title: From Exposure to Experience: Measuring Gaze-Based Visual Experience with Faces During Naturalistic Viewing
articles_hidden.authors: Nitzan Guy; Guy Malka; Galit Yovel
articles_hidden.abstract: Research across face recognition, social cognition, and clinical psychology treats visual experience as a primary mechanism for learning and successful categorization. As the field has shifted toward naturalistic, dynamic stimuli, there is a need to dissociate between exposure, which is the amount of time a target is presented, and experience, which is the amount of time an observer is looking at a certain target. Here, we present a pipeline that dissociates exposure from experience with faces during naturalistic viewing of a movie with multiple characters. This is achieved by combining screen-based eye tracking with deep neural network-based face detection and recognition to measure each participant's gaze-based visual experience with faces during naturalistic viewing, on a frame-by-frame basis. With a sample stimulus, we benchmarked our pipeline as an identity exposure extractor and achieved high face detection (~98%) and face recognition (85-88%) accuracies. In a proof-of-concept experiment, participants watched two episodes of a television series while their gaze was recorded. Our pipeline revealed participants looked at individual characters for less than 27% of their appearance time on average indicating that character appearance time overestimated participants' actual visual experience. Moreover, participants showed reliable individual differences in face-directed gaze, both in overall face-viewing tendencies and in character-specific preferences, with stable idiosyncratic preferences emerging when two characters competed for visual attention. Together, these findings demonstrate a meaningful gap between exposure and idiosyncratic gaze-based visual experience, highlighting the importance of dissociating experience from exposure when studying the role of visual experience in naturalistic viewing.

articles_hidden.title: Delusion-related aberrant prediction errors are bottom-up
articles_hidden.authors: Siyan Fan; Santiago Castiello; Martin Meyer; Praveen Suthaharan; Joshua Kenney; Daniel J. Hauke; Rick Adams; Sonia Bansal; James Waltz; Molly A. Erickson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Delusions are the fixed false beliefs that characterize serious mental illnesses like schizophrenia. Prediction errors are surprise signals that guide learning. They have been observed during causal learning in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC). They are registered inappropriately in people with delusions, driving learning towards irrelevant events. This learning correlates with delusion severity. We do not know, however, whether the rDLPFC is receiving the error signal, bottom-up, from other nodes, or, alternatively, whether rDLPFC prediction errors are communicated top-down from rDLPFC. It is also possible that the direction of processing differs between patients with delusions compared with otherwise healthy individuals who espouse delusion-like beliefs but are not delusional per se. 
Methods: Here, we attempt to distinguish these possibilities using cognitive computational neuroimaging, functional, and effective connectivity analyses of task-based fMRI data in people with schizophrenia (SZ, n=29), people with extreme esoteric beliefs (EEB, n=25), and controls with neither (CTR, n=24), focusing on prediction error processing. 
Results: During Kamin Blocking of causal learning people who endorse delusions evince aberrant prediction error signals in right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and anterior insula which correlate with delusion severity. Psychophysiological interaction analysis reveals errant coupling between these regions in people with delusions. Effective connectivity analysis locates the dysfunction in schizophrenia to bottom-up prediction error drive from insula to DLPFC. 
Conclusion: These data provide quantitative computational metrics for distinguishing delusions from other less problematic beliefs and establish that, in schizophrenia, aberrant prediction errors during causal learning arise from errant bottom-up drive from the insula to the rDLPFC. This may then serve as a marker for clinically relevant odd belief and a target for treatment.

articles_hidden.title: The Effect of Global and Local Attention Bias on Low Prevalence Search
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte M Kelly; Robin Celani; Juan Guevara Pinto
articles_hidden.abstract: Fields that require visual search for rare target items are particularly vulnerable to the low-prevalence effect (LPE). This means that TSA officers and radiologists can often miss the target they are looking for because of an induced bias that the target won’t be found. The LPE is notoriously difficult to mitigate. The current experiment attempted to implicitly improve performance in low-prevalence conditions by training participants to adopt a global or local attentional bias, via the Navon task. We hypothesized that the local processing bias would increase the number of items inspected and consequently increase search times and performance. In experiment 1 (N = 45), participants completed the Navon task and the search task in separate blocks. The manipulation did not yield an effect on the LPE; however, a trend emerged that encouraged us to investigate further.  In experiment 2 (N = 51), participants completed a randomized mixture of the Navon task and the search task. This experimental design was able to slightly increase the number of items inspected in the visual search when participants adopted the local processing bias compared to the global processing bias; however, the manipulation did not extend to search performance. Nonetheless, these findings suggest that implicit manipulations may be able to impact search behavior in low-prevalence conditions. Future studies should continue to investigate implicit forms of biasing and training to induce more robust effects on the LPE.

articles_hidden.title: Gender bias across LLMs is common and highly heterogeneous
articles_hidden.authors: Edoardo Bolzoni; Valerio Capraro
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding gender biases in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important as these systems become embedded in decision-support tools with real consequences. Prior research has focused only on a small set of models, leaving open the extent to which gender biases are common and heterogeneous across LLMs. We address this gap across ten models released between April 2025 and June 2026, spanning nine vendors, using two paradigms: gender attribution to stereotyped phrases (Study 1) and moral judgment of abuse or torture against a woman or a man to prevent a catastrophic outcome (Study 2). In Study 1, two of ten models attributed masculine-stereotyped phrases to female writers more often than the reverse, while three models showed the opposite pattern. In Study 2, several models converged on a male-disadvantaging asymmetry that was directionally consistent with a documented human tendency to protect female targets from harm, though the specific conditions under which this asymmetry emerged varied by model; three other models, by contrast, showed no variation across conditions. These results indicate that gender-related biases are common in LLMs. Their direction and magnitude, however, are highly heterogeneous, to the point that some models behave in diametrically opposite ways to others. Bias auditing should therefore be treated as an ongoing, multi-vendor process, rather than a one-time assessment.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive-Affective Factors Associated with Psychological Distress in Young Adults: A Cross-Sectional Structural Equation Modelling Study
articles_hidden.authors: Rose Seneviratne; Matt Garner; Emma Claire Palmer-Cooper
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: To examine concurrent associations among cognitive-affective factors associated with psychological distress in young adults. 
Methods: Cross-sectional structural equation modelling was conducted in a community sample of 841 young adults aged 18 to 30 years. Psychological distress was specified as a latent factor indicated by depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), anxious symptoms (GAD-7), and perceived stress (PSS-10). Mindfulness facets (FFMQ), metacognition (MSAS-18), resilience (ER89), and creativity (RDCA) were entered into two models with alternative structural orderings. Model fit was evaluated using the CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, AIC, and BIC.
Results: Model 1 showed acceptable-to-good fit (CFI = .98, TLI = .94, RMSEA = .07, SRMR = .03) and better comparative fit than Model 2 (CFI = .97, TLI = .90, RMSEA = .09, SRMR = .06). Model 1 statistically accounted for 53.9% of the variance in latent psychological distress. Acting with awareness (β = -.29), nonjudging (β = -.39), and nonreactivity (β = -.20) showed unique negative associations with distress, whereas observing showed a small positive association (β = .08). Resilience showed a direct negative association and negative indirect associations in configurations involving acting with awareness, nonjudging, and nonreactivity. Metacognition showed negative indirect associations involving acting with awareness and nonreactivity. Creativity showed a bivalent pattern: a positive indirect association involving observing and a negative indirect association involving nonreactivity.
Conclusions: Acting with awareness, nonjudging, and nonreactivity showed the clearest unique associations with lower psychological distress in young adults. These findings identify candidate self-regulatory capacities for prospective testing in preventive and therapeutic intervention research.

articles_hidden.title: Association between ADHD and multimorbidity in adulthood: a systematic review protocol
articles_hidden.authors: Steven Gilmore; Caroline Burke; Peter Barrett; Brian O'Donoghue; Frank Moriarty; emma wallace
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Multimorbidity is defined as the co-existence of two or more long-term health conditions within the same individual. While it is well established that Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is associated with both mental and physical health comorbidities, certain factors suggest ADHD could elevate the risk of accumulating multiple conditions over time. ADHD symptoms may impair self-management of long- term health conditions, while diagnostic overshadowing, whereby ADHD symptoms are misattributed to co-occurring conditions, may result in fragmented healthcare. Despite this, the impact of ADHD on the development of multimorbidity in adulthood remains underexplored. General Practitioners (GPs) are arguably well placed to take on a greater role in adult ADHD management, considering their integrative biopsychosocial approach to care and routine management of multimorbidity.

Aim:
The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to examine the association of ADHD with the development of multimorbidity in adulthood.

Methods:
This systematic review and meta-analysis, reported per PRISMA-P guidelines, will include observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, and sibling comparison designs) examining multimorbidity risk in adults with ADHD compared with adults without ADHD. Multimorbidity is defined as the coexistence of two or more long- term health conditions (in addition to ADHD). MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Web of Science Core Collection will be searched from inception, without language restriction, supplemented by citation searching and grey literature sources. Two reviewers will independently screen records and extract data, with disagreements resolved by discussion or third-reviewer arbitration. Risk of bias will be assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Tools. Where sufficient homogeneous data are available, random-effects meta-analyses will pool crude and adjusted effect estimates, with heterogeneity assessed using Chi2 and I2, and prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses will be conducted. Findings will be synthesised narratively where meta-analysis is not feasible.

Discussion:
This systematic review will provide a comprehensive synthesis of studies examining the association between ADHD and the development of multimorbidity in adults. With increasing recognition of the importance of a lifespan approach to ADHD management, this review will provide important information on the risk of multimorbidity and will support a holistic approach to clinical decision making for adults living with ADHD.

articles_hidden.title: The Language of Trauma: A Comparative Analysis Using Natural Language Processing and Traditional Text Analysis Methods
articles_hidden.authors: Giuliano Groer; Laurin Plank; Armin Zlomuzica
articles_hidden.abstract:
Post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with alterations in the recall of
autobiographical memories (AMs) regarding the traumatic event, but methodology of studies investigating traumatic and non-traumatic narratives in the context of PTSD vary. There is little consensus regarding the linguistic differences between different narrative 
valences and the influence of PTSD-symptomatology outside of clinical populations. We collected 450 narratives regarding traumatic, negative non-traumatic and neutral AMs of 150 healthy participants and their post-traumatic stress measured by the PTSD checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). For a comprehensive analysis of differences in linguistic patterns, we examined syntactic, lexical, semantic, and discourse-level features of the narratives. Compared to neutral narratives, traumatic narratives were linguistically richer, more PTSD-congruent in semantic content, less coherent, and were subjectively experienced as more emotionally intense and vivid. Trauma and negative narratives were largely similar in their linguistic and structural features, with differences confined to word count, death-related language, coherence, and semantic alignment with hyperarousal and intrusion symptom domains. Post-traumatic stress did not moderate any of the association between narrative categories and linguistic features, but higher PCL-5 scores predicted use of death-related words and how temporarily close participants felt to the traumatic event.
Although future research should replicate these findings in clinical comparison samples, the present study provides a comprehensive attempt to characterize the language of trauma narratives.

articles_hidden.title: Morphosyntax sans sight: Development of linguistic structure in blind toddlers
articles_hidden.authors: Lillianna Righter; Erin Elizabeth Campbell; Elika Bergelson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Part of language development necessarily involves connecting sensory input
with linguistic units. We asked whether visual input in particular was differ-
entially relevant for learning words and building grammar. While substan-
tial prior work (e.g. Bates & Goodman, 1997) confirms a tight link between
grammar and the lexicon, there could in principle be different degrees of
reliance on a visual referential world across them. To begin to tackle this
large question, we examined the productive morphosyntax skills of young
blind children (N=28, 14-55mo.), each matched to a sighted child of the
same productive vocabulary size, based on a parent-reported vocabulary and
early grammar checklist. We asked whether blind children’s morphosyntactic
skills were similar, advanced, or delayed relative to sighted vocabulary-size-
matched peers. We found no differences between blind and sighted children
across 6 morphosyntax measures. Blind children did show a delay in produc-
tive morphosyntax skills relative to sighted children, and this delay (roughly
9 months) was statistically longer than the delay reported for spoken vo-
cabulary in this same group (Campbell, Casillas, & Bergelson, 2024). We
also found that both age and vocabulary strongly predicted morphosyntax
scores for sighted children, but only vocabulary size (and not age) robustly
predicted morphosyntax for blind children. These results extend seminal
research in early language development in blind and sighted children (e.g.
Landau & Gleitman, 1985), highlighting close vocabulary to syntax links in
early childhood across groups, and supporting the idea that vision does not
contribute separably to either facet of language development.

articles_hidden.title: Quantifying context-dependent meaning representations: a novel procedure
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Mainetto; Hanneke den Ouden; Danny Merkx; Lisa I. Horstman; Naomi de Haas; Mona Garvert; Andrea E. Martin; Roshan Cools; Xiaochen Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: Our brains house representations of word meaning that are constrained by both the form and the sentence context of the word. For example, when hearing the sentence “They deposited cash at the bank”, we do not think about the bank of a river. These context-dependent meaning representations enable cognitive flexibility. Existing studies aimed at isolating such meaning representations have confounded them with operational processing requirements, due to reliance on inferential and surprisal effects during natural language comprehension. We introduce a novel symbol-based procedure for disentangling context-sensitive word meaning representations from the processing demands of word meaning inference. Participants were instructed to learn associations between sentence-constrained meanings of homonyms (“They deposited cash at the [bank]”) and symbols. Explicit word meaning representations were successfully captured by a task that required the spatial arrangement of these symbols based on their associated word meaning, with smaller distances between symbols representing the same meaning than between symbols representing different meanings. Contrary to the spatial arrangement task, in a priming task assessing implicit word meaning representations related to the same symbols, there was no evidence for semantic meaning priming of reaction times. This work provides a novel experimental procedure for measuring explicit word meaning representations in a manner that can be disentangled from changes in word meaning inference, but raises questions about the suitability of the priming task used for uncovering implicit meaning representations.

articles_hidden.title: Feedback helps children seek information to fill knowledge gap
articles_hidden.authors: Martina de Eccher; Nivedita Mani
articles_hidden.abstract: Effective self-regulated learning depends on metacognitive monitoring and control abilities, which allow learners to recognise what they do not know and adjust their learning behaviour to address knowledge gaps. However, children’s metacognitive abilities are still developing, which can hinder their ability to select relevant information effectively. This work examines whether providing feedback on children’s knowledge tests can assist their metacognitive monitoring and control processes, improving their ability to target information-seeking to fill knowledge gaps. In two experiments, 5-9-year-old children (N=203) completed a word-learning task on a tablet. They were then tested on their knowledge of the novel word-object associations and asked to report their (un)certainty in their answers. In the first experiment, children received feedback after each test trial. In both experiments, children received summary feedback at the end of the test. Afterwards, they could select some of the objects to hear their labels again and were tested on their recognition of the label-object associations once more. In both experiments, feedback boosted children’s ability to strategically seek information to fill their knowledge gaps. Moreover, when given feedback after each test trial, children based their uncertainty judgments on their previous performance. While this resulted in younger children’s uncertainty judgments to better reflect their performance, older children’s judgments were less accurate than without feedback. Importantly, children’s information-seeking was better guided by feedback than by their own subjective uncertainty, indicating that feedback provides a valuable external means for metacognitive control. Overall, the findings underscore the role of feedback in fostering the development of metacognition and self-regulated learning in childhood.

articles_hidden.title: English-learning infants’ perception of word stress patterns
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Katrin Skoruppa; Alejandrina Cristia; Sharon Peperkamp; Amanda Seidl
articles_hidden.abstract: Adult speakers of different free stress languages (e.g., English, Spanish) differ both in their sensitivity to lexical stress and in their processing of suprasegmental and vowel quality cues to stress. In a head-turn preference experiment with a familiarization phase, both 8-month-old and 12-month-old English-learning infants discriminated between initial stress and final stress among lists of Spanish-spoken disyllabic nonwords that were segmentally varied (e.g., [ˈnila, ˈtuli] vs. [luˈta, puˈki]). This is evidence that English-learning infants are sensitive to lexical stress patterns, instantiated primarily by suprasegmental cues, during the second half of the first year of life.

articles_hidden.title: Ecological Momentary Assessment of Mood: Reliability and Validity of a brief measure
articles_hidden.authors: Madeleine Jones; Nina H. Di Cara; Oliver Davis; Claire Haworth
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) is useful for capturing the time-sensitive variability in mood. However, there is no widely used, gold-standard momentary measure of mood, making it difficult to compare results across studies. Measures often vary in number of items, as an attempt to resolve the trade-off between reliability and missingness. 
Objective:
This study evaluated the performance of a brief EMA measure for mood in relation to reliability, missingness, and construct validity.
Methods:
We collected EMA data from a sample of young adults at a UK university (n=171). Participants received a notification from the PIEL Survey app on their mobile phones to respond to a short mood survey four times a day for two weeks. This survey was developed through co-production with a focus group and required participants to rate their mood (0–10) on five items: cheerful, frustrated, relaxed, sad, and worried. We assessed the within- and between-participant reliability using multilevel modelling methods. Construct validity was evaluated through comparison with scores on the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Principal Component Analysis was also used to explore the underlying dimensionality. We further considered compliance rates and the degree of ‘careless responding’ (defined by response times, standard deviations, and overall reliability).
Results:
Our data showed good internal consistency reliability and acceptable variance using both generalisability theory and multilevel modelling. There was high between-participant reliability (RkR≥0.98, RkRn≥0.98), and moderate within-participant reliability (Rc≥0.64, Rcn≥0.56) for both positive and negative items. High construct validity was also established: our measure showed moderate correlations with an existing, longer measure of mood. We found two Principal Components together explained 75.8% of the variance in our measure, which appear to represent distinct Positive and Negative Affect dimensions. We also found high compliance rates with only 23.3% of responses missing overall, showing some degree of variability across time window, weekday, and time in the study. Our sample contained no careless responders overall. 
Conclusions:
In summary, the five-item measure was brief enough to maintain high compliance in a non-clinical sample, without sacrificing reliability or construct validity. This shows promise for the use of shorter-item surveys in Ecological Momentary Assessment, which may enhance compliance rates and reduce the level of careless responding. Future studies should consider whether this measure also maintains reliability for different populations.

articles_hidden.title: The Perception and Metacognition of Time Within and Between Stimulus Modalities
articles_hidden.authors: Aris Yiu; Daniel R. Little; Simon James Cropper
articles_hidden.abstract: Time perception depends not only on judging duration but also on evaluating how accurate that judgement was. Our previous work compared visual, auditory, and audiovisual intervals separately and observed a modality asymmetry at short durations. The present study examined whether pairing them within a trial reproduces this pattern, and whether order matters. Eleven participants completed a modified temporal bisection task, bisecting two consecutive intervals then choosing the more accurate. Intervals were both audiovisual (AV), auditory followed by visual (A+V), or visual followed by auditory (V+A), tested at 1500 and 3000 msec. The AV condition ran twice, showing no reliable repetition difference. The modality asymmetry did not reappear once the two modalities were directly paired. Neither Modality nor Duration reliably affected the metacognitively-selected estimate. However, this stability did not extend to metacognitive accuracy, indexed by our Metacognitive Index (MCI), which was higher for V+A at the shorter duration, though only anecdotally (BF10 = 1.43). A hierarchical Bayesian model tracked the observed data closely, with individual consistency explaining much of the between-participant variability. In summary, perceiving a duration and judging one’s own performance may not be the same computation, with the latter more sensitive to modality-induced distortion.

articles_hidden.title: ­­­Neural markers of implicit metric processing in 6-to-10-year-old children
articles_hidden.authors: Katerina Drakoulaki; Mara Breen
articles_hidden.abstract: Introduction. Auditory processing is guided by exogenous and endogenous processes: neural responses adapt to hierarchically organized structures and task-specific conditions across development. Here, we investigated the endogenous selective attention mechanisms influencing subjective metric tracking of an isochronous sequence of identical tones in children 6-10-years-old. Methods. We adapted an adult imagined meter paradigm to map the developmental neural trajectories of implicit metric coding. High-density electroencephalography data were recorded from 112 children listening to undifferentiated tones grouped subjectively into quaternary or ternary meters in fast (450ms SOA) and slow (625 SOA) tempi. We predicted that mature metric encoding would manifest as adult-like N1 and late metric negativity (LMN) amplitudes to metrically strong beats. Results. Across four age cohorts, we replicated established findings on cortical auditory evoked potential morphological development. Behavioral accuracy on the task reflected more mature neural responses to imagined strong beats. High-scorers reliably showed negative responses in the N1 and LMN time windows for strong beats across hierarchies. Low scorers showed positive responses in the N1 and LMN time windows for strong beats, similar to other selective attention paradigms in this age range. Discussion. Metric tracking was modulated by tempo and meter: we suggest that fast tempo facilitated tracking by aligning with children's faster endogenous temporal preferences, while slower tracking was more difficult; similarly, tracking ternary meter was more challenging than quaternary, likely due to familiarity.

articles_hidden.title: Exploratory Item Response Matrix Factorization: Bridging Psychometrics and Machine Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Changsheng Chen; Wim Van Den Noortgate
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent evolution in psychological and educational assessments has challenged traditional exploratory psychometric methods regarding analyzing high-dimensional sparse data and making accurate predictions, while methods from machine learning present potential for addressing relevant issues. This study proposes Exploratory Item Response Matrix Factorization (EIRMF) based on matrix factorization and compares it with Exploratory Multidimensional Item Response Theory (EMIRT) by simulation data and real data. The results show that tuning the number of factors (as a hyperparameter) in EIRMF can be an effective tool for factor retention analyses compared to methods used in EMIRT. EIRMF slightly outperforms EMIRT in most cases regarding prediction accuracy. For parameter and multidimensionality recovery, we propose Select Pairwise Correlation (spCORR) as a new metric to evaluate methods with other existing metrics. The results show that EIRMF and EMIRT produce highly correlated item intercepts and moderately correlated item slopes and factor scores, and using rotation methods (such as Promax) can improve multidimensionality recovery. A higher number of items and samples improves methods’ performance, while higher levels of factors and missingness show adverse effects. Overall, EIRMF can be an alternative to EMIRT in tasks where EMIRT is less effective with bridging psychometrics and machine learning.

articles_hidden.title: Sex and gender differences in functional and participation experiences of students with developmental coordination disorder in higher education
articles_hidden.authors: Clare Copley; Kimberly Petersen; Madeleine Pownall; Lucy H Eddy
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent motor coordination difficulties that negatively impacts daily functioning and participation across the lifespan. Despite a high prevalence (5-6%), DCD remains under recognised in adulthood, creating particular challenges in contexts requiring high levels of independent participation, such as higher education. Sex and gender are also important to examine, given their potential to influence the recognition, presentation and lived experience of DCD. However, there is a notable lack of research exploring how sex and gender identity may impact these experiences. 
Aims: This exploratory study aimed to investigate whether functional challenges and participation experiences differed according to sex and gender identity among higher education students with DCD.
Methods: Data were collected via an online self-report questionnaire completed by 77 higher education students with DCD/dyspraxia across the UK and Ireland.
Results: Findings indicate high levels of functional difficulty and participation restriction across the sample, with fatigue often reported as a consequence. Females with DCD were significantly more likely than males to report challenges related to gross motor skills (p<.05, d=.60) and executive function skills (p<.05, d =.60). Participants who identified as a gender minority reported a higher incidence of difficulty with fine motor skills (p<.05, d=–.63) and executive function (p<.05, d =–.60) compared to cisgender participants. 
Conclusions: Findings indicate that students with DCD experience persistent functional challenges that restrict participation in higher education.  Experiences and support needs may also differ based on sex and gender identity.

articles_hidden.title: Effect of an online music program on behavioral co-regulation in mothers and children with cochlear implants and with normal hearing
articles_hidden.authors: Michela Santangelo; Chiara Barachetti; Miriam D Lense; Letizia Guerzoni; Domenico Cuda; Marinella Majorano
articles_hidden.abstract: Children with cochlear implants (CIs) could show disruptions of contingency in early interactions. Music and rhythmic activities could improve co-regulation in mother-child dyads with CIs. This study explores i) the impact of an online music program on behavioral co-regulation of dyads with children with CIs (CI-T; N = 15; M = 17.70 months, SD = 6.60) who participated in the program, a CI control group (CI-C; N = 16; M = 19.39 months, SD = 6.50), and dyads with normal hearing children (NH-T; N = 14; M = 16.14 months, SD = 3.55) who participated in the program; ii) the associations in the CI-groups between practices of music at home and behavioral co-regulation. The CI-groups were assessed at three (T1) and six (T2) months after CIs’ activation. The NH-T group was assessed before (T1) and after (T2) the program. Analyses of video-recordings revealed significant increases at T2 in the duration of mother-child contingent and affective behaviors in the CI-T group, compared to the CI-C group. In the CI-groups, correlational analyses show positive associations between maternal reports of music at home and mother-child contingent and affective responses. The potential of music activities for auditory rehabilitation after CIs activation is discussed.

articles_hidden.title: A Comparison of Mixed-Integer Linear Programming and Metaheuristics in Parallel Short-Form Construction
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Trautwein; Ulrich Schroeders
articles_hidden.abstract: Constructing parallel test forms requires balancing different construction goals, including content coverage, measurement precision, and equivalence across forms. We evaluated the accuracy and efficiency of two different psychometric approaches in parallel test constructions using two simulations: mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) uses fixed full-pool item-parameter estimates, whereas ant colony optimization (ACO) re-estimates item parameters for candidate subsets. In Simulation 1, we compared their parameter recovery across 1,000 randomly sampled item subsets per condition to quantify item-parameter uncertainty, varying (1) effective sample size per item (n = 100, 200, 500, 1,000), (2) model complexity (1PL, 2PL, 3PL), (3) latent trait distribution (normal, left-skewed), and (4) item-set proportion (10%, 20%, 30%). Full-pool calibration generally yielded more accurate and less variable parameter recovery, particularly for discrimination parameters in more complex models and smaller item sets. In Simulation 2, we assembled three parallel 40-item forms across 30 independently generated datasets in two exemplary conditions. MILP and ACO performed similarly in the 2PL condition, whereas in the 3PL condition ACO showed a slight advantage in parallelism and MILP achieved higher minimum test information. Across both conditions, MILP with full-pool calibration showed more consistent item-parameter and test-information recovery. Evaluating the same final ACO-selected items with full-pool rather than subset-specific re-estimates improved recovery on nearly all metrics. These findings indicate that repeated subset-specific re-estimation may not improve the psychometric properties of parallel short tests, but increase the risk of overfitting by allowing the search to capitalize on sample-specific estimation error.

articles_hidden.title: Affordance-Based Control in Driving Behavior: Integration of Perception and Action by Extending rho Coupling and Satisficing
articles_hidden.authors: Takayuki Kondoh; Hiroyuki Mishima; Nobuhiro Furuyama
articles_hidden.abstract: Action-control models in ecological psychology have evolved from pursuing a single optimal solution toward affordance-based control within safety regions. However, mathematically integrating these approaches with rho coupling theory remains insufficient. This study theoretically re-examines the "risk feeling formula (RFF)"—a linear sum of two optical variables derived from real-world driving data. Our analysis demonstrates that the RFF is structurally equivalent to rho coupling, yet its "intercept" distinctly functions as a "satisficing" threshold. Rather than representing an internal computational compromise, this threshold signifies direct perceptual attunement for initiating avoidance behavior while maintaining a safety margin. Furthermore, we propose an integrated mathematical representation of affordances as the linear sum of two action-scaled pi values, reflecting the extended body effectivities, corresponding to overt risk (rho_LF) and potential risk (rho_GF). By extending rho coupling to encompass satisficing, this framework elegantly models how actors dynamically balance contextual pressures without error-nulling. This integrated theoretical approach explains diverse human adaptive strategies and provides fundamental insights for future ecological human-centered design, including advanced driver assistance systems.

articles_hidden.title: PSYCHIATRY The Case for Starting Over
articles_hidden.authors: Abraham Peled
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Psychiatry is the only branch of medicine that still diagnoses without reference to the organ it treats. Psychiatry: The Case for Starting Over argues that this is a structural failure rather than a temporary gap. The descriptive nosology inherited from Kraepelin and formalized in the DSM achieved diagnostic reliability at the cost of validity. Its categories were assembled by committee consensus rather than grounded in mechanism, and so it cannot guide the circuit-targeted therapies now reshaping the field.
The book traces this problem historically and then builds an alternative from three converging lines of work. The first is computational neural-network modeling of psychopathology, from Hopfield and Hinton through Hoffman's simulations of schizophrenia and the author's own work. The second is systems neuroscience, including large-scale networks, global workspace and integrated information theories, attractor dynamics, and small-world connectivity. The third is Friston's Free Energy Principle and predictive processing.
From this synthesis the book introduces Neuroanalysis and its clinical instrument, Clinical Brain Profiling (CBP). CBP treats mental disorders as disturbances of dynamic brain-network organization and organizes them across four timescales of plasticity:
•	Cognizance plasticity (milliseconds) is centered on the central executive network and linked to psychosis and negative signs.
•	Reactive plasticity (minutes to hours) is centered on the salience network and linked to anxiety.
•	Adaptive plasticity (days to weeks) sits at the salience–default mode interface and is linked to depression and mania.
•	Developmental plasticity (lifetime) is centered on the default mode network and linked to personality disorder patterns.
The book reviews the neuromodulation toolkit: ECT, DBS, TMS, tDCS/tACS, psychedelic-assisted therapy, and focused ultrasound. It then proposes an entity-matched "grammar of plasticity" for selecting, combining, and sequencing these interventions. Guiding principles include strengthening prefrontal regulation before driving motivation, opening plasticity windows before directing them, and continuous biomarker monitoring.
Throughout, the author separates established science from theoretical proposal and untested hypothesis. He outlines what validation would require: prospective outcome trials, clinically feasible network measures, and a cultural shift from single-label diagnosis to multidimensional profiling. The result is a case for rebuilding psychiatry as a measurement-based, mechanism-guided clinical neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain
articles_hidden.authors: Benjy Barnett; Stephen M Fleming
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to perceptual absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding absence as a concept – in the form of the number zero – has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography (MEG) to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct to those evoked by perceptual absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

articles_hidden.title: Joint (versus individual) task representations are activated spontaneously and preferentially: evidence from switch cost asymmetry
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad; Kassandra Friebe; Günther Knoblich; Natalie Sebanz
articles_hidden.abstract: We routinely face the decision to act either alone or with another person. Research has found that humans exhibit a joint action preference, choosing to coordinate even when it is unnecessary and inefficient. Here, we tested one mechanism that might contribute to this preference: that joint task representations are activated spontaneously and preferentially to individual task representations. To this end, we conducted a secondary (meta)analysis of seven experiments (total N = 288) in which dyads completed a stimulus-response task requiring switching between individual and joint responses. Switch-cost asymmetry between the two trial types revealed that joint task representations were represented preferentially to individual task representations. This held even though participants did not coordinate intentionally, responding together only incidentally when a stimulus cued responses from both. In other words, the task was represented jointly and preferentially activated, spontaneously. Our results add to a body of joint action research indicating that a suite of spontaneous perceptual and cognitive processes automatically prepare us to coordinate with others.

articles_hidden.title: From what they hear to what they say: The distribution of word classes in the output of young English-speaking children and their caregivers
articles_hidden.authors: Antje Endesfelder Quick; Karsten Schmidtke-Bode
articles_hidden.abstract: Usage-based approaches propose that children assimilate the statistical regularities of their input. While prior studies have documented such input–output correlations for specific constructions, more systemic properties like word-class distributions have received less attention. The present study examines twelve English-speaking children aged two to three from the Manchester Corpus, comparing their part-of-speech (POS) distributions with their mothers' at three time points. Maternal distributions remain highly stable; children's speech is initially noun-heavy but approaches maternal patterns by age 2;9. These findings suggest that, even at more abstract levels of grammatical organization, children's developing grammars reflect the distributional properties of their input.

articles_hidden.title: Diffusion MRI Metrics as Markers of Neuroinflammation in Mental Illness
