articles_hidden.authors: Lena K L Oestreich
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroinflammatory mechanisms are increasingly implicated in mental illness, but their characterization in the living human brain remains challenging. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is sensitive to tissue microstructure and offers a scalable approach for studying immune-related brain changes, yet it does not measure inflammation directly. Inflammatory processes alter the cellular and extracellular geometry that constrains water diffusion, and glial activation, edema, demyelination, and axonal injury may produce overlapping or opposing diffusion signatures. This review evaluates the extent to which commonly used and emerging dMRI metrics can support an inflammatory interpretation. It distinguishes signal representations, including diffusion tensor and kurtosis imaging, from biophysical models such as free-water imaging, neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging, diffusion basis spectrum imaging, and newer compartment models, and examines their mechanistic sensitivity and limitations. A review of studies combining dMRI with immune-related measures in psychiatric populations identified a heterogeneous literature dominated by small samples, peripheral biomarkers, and within-group associations. Free-water measures showed the most consistent associations with inflammatory markers, whereas tensor-derived findings were variable and large population studies indicated very small effect sizes. Evidence from compartment models, molecular imaging, and intervention studies remains sparse. Validation studies in experimental, histological, ex vivo, and cellular systems demonstrate that diffusion signals can reflect immune-related microstructural change but are not specific to inflammation. Future work should prioritize multimodal validation, mechanistically informed acquisition and modeling, and explicit testing of competing explanations. Once validated, dMRI could provide a scalable means of mapping immune-related microstructural change across the brain in mental illness.

articles_hidden.title: TO MONETIZE OR NOT: INFLUENCE OF INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES AND GENDER IN MONETARY VALUATION OF MEANINGFUL EXPERIENCES
articles_hidden.authors: Jude A. Beale; Anne Z. Murphy
articles_hidden.abstract: Money is a universal measure of value that influences most decisions. For centuries, humans have used it to exchange goods and experiences. Research in psychology and behavioral economics, however, shows that there may be limits to what individuals are willing to exchange for money. This study examined the monetary values people assign to personal experiences, and whether willingness to engage in monetary valuation differs between males and females. Five hundred and twenty-nine participants completed an online survey in which they provided the minimum amount of monetary compensation it would require to complete ten separate hypothetical scenarios, with the option to refuse any task. The hypothetical tasks ranged from temporary restrictions and social isolation to public disclosure, loss of memories and permanent identity changes. Based on the results from previous economic decision-making studies, we hypothesized that females would refuse to price tasks more than males and that males would request higher compensation for priced tasks. We also hypothesized that permanent or identity-altering tasks would result in higher refusal rates than temporary ones in both genders. Whether resistance to monetary valuation is a consistent individual tendency was also examined. Our results showed that participants who refused to price one hypothetical task were more likely to refuse other tasks. While no gender differences were observed for any task regarding the monetary value requested, females refused significantly more tasks than males (4.43 vs. 3.17, p < .001). Refusal rates were highest for permanent or identity-altering tasks and lowest for temporary tasks. Lastly, refusal rates for loss of digital pictures/videos were nearly identical to losing contact with friends and family. Together, these findings suggest that monetary valuation involves two separate decisions: whether or not to assign a monetary value and, if so, how much to request. Individuals differ consistently in their willingness to engage in monetary valuation, and gender influences the decision to engage rather than with the amount requested.

articles_hidden.title: Multivariate Resting-State EEG Organization in Autism: Shared Age-Related Structure and Diagnostic Context Dependent IQ Associations
articles_hidden.authors: Yang WANG; Yingying Wang; Sandra Chan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) studies of autism have often sought categorical
differentiation between autistic and typical neurodevelopmental groups, with limited stability
across features or classifiers. A neurodiversity-informed perspective views autism as part of
human neurodevelopmental variation, while recognizing associated disability and support needs.
In this view, overlap between autistic and non-autistic EEG distributions is not merely
classification noise, but may reflect shared dimensions of neural organization. A complementary
question arise is whether position along these dimensions has different functional meaning across
diagnostic contexts. We conducted an exploratory secondary analysis of 726 eyes-open resting-
state EEG features previously extracted in a published multi-site autism EEG study, with a final
analytic sample of 767 children and adolescents: 344 controls (CON), 347 participants classified
by the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule as Autistic Disorder (ADOS-A), and 76
classified as Autism Spectrum (ADOS-S). Principal component analysis was applied once to the
pooled sample without including age, sex, IQ, or diagnostic group. The dominant component
(PC1) was interpreted post hoc by examining its EEG feature loading pattern, its association with
chronological age, the consistency of this age association across diagnostic groups, and the
concentration of age-related variance across components. We then tested whether age-adjusted
position on this component was differentially associated with general cognitive performance
(i.e., IQ) across groups. PC1 explained 15.94% of feature variance and was characterized by the
strongest positive loadings on delta-band power and the strongest negative loadings on sample
entropy. PC1 showed a significant negative association with chronological age (𝑟 = −0.846,
𝑝 < .001), indicating that older age was associated with relatively lower delta power and higher
sample entropy along this component, consistent with previously reported developmental EEG
changes. Age-related EEG variance was concentrated primarily on PC1 rather than on
subsequent components, supporting its interpretation as a shared age-related EEG dimension.
After removing PC1’s linear association with age, residual PC1 scores (PC1r) were negatively
associated with IQ within the ADOS-A group (𝑏 = −0.612, 𝑝 < .001), but not within the
control or ADOS-S groups. Pairwise slope contrasts indicated that this association was
significantly more negative in ADOS-A than in CON, whereas ADOS-A vs. ADOS-S and
ADOS-S vs. CON contrasts were not significant. These findings shift emphasis from categorical
EEG abnormality toward individual variation within a broadly shared age-related EEG
organization, in which brain–cognition coupling depends on diagnostic context.

articles_hidden.title: Metacognitive Ownership in Human–AI Regulation: Construct Definition, Boundaries, and a Research Agenda
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin; Daniel H. Chang
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can suggest criteria, evaluate learners’ work, and recommend or carry out revisions, yet it is often unclear how learners direct these decisions when they study with AI. In this conceptual paper, we introduce metacognitive ownership: learners’ governance of standards, evaluative judgments, and actions within a learning episode in which AI or another external source contributes to at least one of these functions. Here, governance refers to how learners direct the use of that contribution. Drawing on self-regulated learning, human–AI regulation, agency, and evaluative judgment, we define three components: standards appropriation, monitoring-judgment governance, and control authorization. These components address the criterion a learner uses, how the learner reaches an evaluation, and what guides the next action. Control authorization also requires a realistic opportunity to act differently. A hypothetical example illustrates how a learner can evaluate AI advice and reach an incorrect conclusion, or accept correct advice without examining it. After distinguishing metacognitive ownership from related constructs, we set out four principles for interpreting evidence about each component. We then offer two tentative propositions about later advice decisions and continued learner regulation when support is reduced. The research agenda asks whether these interpretations are reproducible, add to existing explanations, and withstand evidence that challenges them. The framework provides a basis for examining learner-governed assistance; its relationships with learning require empirical evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: Estimating the Hyperlocal Patterning of Environmental Quality and Health and Wellbeing
articles_hidden.authors: Arianna M Gard; Mengyu Liao; Deena Ahmad Shariq; Joelle Fuchs; Sriparna Sen; Taylor Leigh Wilds; Hyung Cho Kim; Brian Kim; Taylor M. Oshan
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite a robust literature linking environmental conditions to health and wellbeing, much of our understanding of the spatial patterning of human behavior is at coarse geographies and without attention to the psychological components of wellbeing (e.g., identity resolution, coping).This investigation queries the hyperlocal spatial patterning of psychological constructs related to environmental quality and health and wellbeing, in a sample of 367 adult residents (63% female, 43% Black or African American) in Washington, DC. Residents were recruited via address-based population-based sampling. Administrative measures of environmental quality were more strongly spatially organized than perception-based measures, but measures of health and wellbeing did not show any hyperlocal spatial patterning in this dataset. Findings elevate the relevance of Geographical Psychology, and the need for interdisciplinary research to better operationalize resident’s space and time allocation as a precondition for understanding environmental effects on health and wellbeing.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Psychotherapy: Understanding How Therapy Supports Brain-Based Change
articles_hidden.authors: Marc L. Copersino; Jamie Berry
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychotherapy can be conceptualized as a structured, experience-dependent process of learning supported by neuroplasticity. Although psychotherapies differ in theory, technique, and therapeutic entry points, they may engage overlapping functional domains of therapeutic learning and change. This chapter presents a transdiagnostic, domain-based framework in which neuroplasticity provides the biological capacity for change and learning serves as the overarching therapeutic process. Five interacting domains organize the framework: emotion regulation and threat learning; cognitive control and belief updating; memory updating and integration; motivation, reinforcement, and habit learning; and social and relational learning and co-regulation. These domains are conceptual organizers rather than discrete mechanisms common to all psychotherapies. Repeated and emotionally meaningful experiences may support changes in expectations, emotional responses, memories, behavior, self-understanding, and interpersonal functioning. The framework also provides a practical structure for neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE). Connecting therapeutic activities with accessible explanations of relevant neuroscience may clarify the treatment rationale, reduce self-blame, support engagement, and foster realistic expectations about change. Consistent with a biopsychosocial perspective, the framework integrates neurobiological processes with meaning, agency, relationships, and environmental context rather than treating them as competing explanations. Domain-based NIPE may help bridge neuroscience and psychotherapy, although its effects on treatment engagement, therapeutic alliance, persistence, and clinical outcomes require empirical evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: Motivational and Consummatory Anhedonia Represent Distinct Affective and Behavioral Responses to Effortful and Rewarding Activities in Daily Life
articles_hidden.authors: Tatiana Pillsbury; Samantha A. Betters; Marta Migo; Shiyin Liu; Aje Oluwagbohunmi; Sarah Etuk; Wenwu Sun; Caroline Conway; Michael Tilghman Treadway; Jessica Cooper
articles_hidden.abstract: Anhedonia is a common psychiatric symptom defined as a loss of interest in or ability to enjoy previously rewarding activities. Although early definitions of anhedonia conceptualized it as a unitary construct, more recent formulations have emphasized the potential importance of distinguishing changes in motivation (motivational anhedonia; “MA”) from changes in hedonic capacity (consummatory anhedonia; “CA”). Evidence for these two domains has been derived from animal models highlighting distinct neurobiological pathways supporting motivational and hedonic responses, as well as human behavioral and pharmacological work highlighting distinct effects of these pathways on motivated and consummatory behavior. While this foundational work has been broadly supportive of the distinction between MA and CA, it remains unknown whether these two domains produce clinically meaningful differences in lived experience of daily activities. In the current work, we used an experience sampling approach in 162 adults (48.7% with current anhedonia as determined by clinical interview) to determine whether self-reported differences in MA and CA severity would be differentially associated with effort and reward levels of activities planned and completed in daily life. Consistent with the hypothesis that MA and CA are meaningful constructs, we observed markedly different associations with behavior in daily life. While elevated MA was associated with effort aversion, higher CA was associated with selective deficits in selecting rewarding activities. Moreover, symptoms of MA and CA were associated with distinct patterns of affective responses to levels of effort and reward in experienced activities. These data provide evidence for distinct manifestations of MA and CA in daily life and further support the hypothesis that they reflect distinct etiopathophysiologies that may benefit from different treatment strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Neural representations of emotional working memory in athletes
articles_hidden.authors: Leiting Li; Shuning Tang; SunMeirong; Yiwen Li; QiMengdi; Jimei Xie; Dongwei Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on athletic expertise often emphasizes performance differences, leaving less clear how athletes and non-athletes represent emotional information during working memory. We examined whether group differences involve the timing and content of neural representations as memory demands change. Two experiments used a sequential emotional working memory task with loads of two or four images. Experiment 1 compared 25 athletes (16 female, mean age: 20.16 years) and 25 non-athletes (16 female, mean age: 21.04 years) using positive and negative images; Experiment 2 used negative images and included 36 athletes (19 female, mean age: 19.92 years) and 37 non-athletes (19 female, mean age: 20.41 years) in the final electroencephalography (EEG) sample. EEG time–frequency analysis exhibited that athletes showed lower theta power during encoding and maintaining comparing to non-athletes. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) further revealed that athletes showed greater arousal representations, while non-athletes showed greater semantic representations. When memory demand increased, visual-model similarity suggested that athletes can keep the visual information precisely, but non-athletes showed a load-dependent decline of visual representations. These findings provide novel neural evidence that athlete-related differences in emotional working memory involve the timing and content of neural representations, rather than a uniform behavioral advantage.

articles_hidden.title: When and Why are Social Categories Overused Relative to Individuating Information? A Bayesian Approach to Identifying Biases in Impression Formation Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Thalia Vrantsidis; Wil Cunningham
articles_hidden.abstract: When making inferences about others, people often need to integrate multiple types of information, including the person’s social categories (e.g., occupation) as well as other “individuating” information (e.g., their behaviors). The current work re-examines this integration process, to understand when and why it produces biases involving over-reliance on category information. We identify two key challenges in identifying such biases, and develop a novel Bayesian modelling approach to overcome them. As a first step in applying this approach, the current work examined a set of novel predictions based on viewing the Continuum Model of impression formation in light of this Bayesian approach. Specifically, a series of six studies tested whether occupation categories might be overused in general, or especially in conditions thought to reduce effortful processing (i.e., greater cognitive load or information consistency). Results showed no evidence of category overuse, nor of shifts in this direction, in any of these conditions (though some ambiguity remained about the load manipulation’s effectiveness). This provides initial evidence against the idea that intrinsic differences in how these categories are processed or represented will lead to their overuse. A seventh study provided the first direct evidence of a case where categories were overused: when contextual factors (i.e., background goals) made them the category especially relevant, while processing resources were limited. More broadly, the current work developed the theoretical and methodological foundations for identifying category overuse that stems from biased inference processes, and demonstrated the power of this approach for understanding when and why such biases occur.

articles_hidden.title: Development and characterization of a standardized stimuli set of 240 famous faces in Quebec
articles_hidden.authors: Nastasia Maria Mitrikeski; Mélodie Leclerc; Zihao Geng; Maxime Montembeault
articles_hidden.abstract:
Famous faces are especially well suited to studying the semantic component of face processing because they carry a sense of familiarity shared across individuals. Recognizing famous faces is not only relevant to research, but it is also clinically informative. Famous-face recognition deficits are observed in prosopagnosia and neurodegenerative disease. They are differentially affected across dementia syndromes, making their assessment useful for differential diagnosis. Testing familiar face processing requires stimuli suited to a specific geographic and sociocultural context, which has led to the development of standardized famous-face databases in France, Great Britain, Spain, and Portugal. However, no such standardized set currently exists for the Quebec population. We therefore created a stimuli set of 240 locally and internationally known famous
people across four categories (politicians, singers, actors, and athletes), spanning different time periods and including famous people of different races, ethnicities, ages, and genders. Through an online survey on Qualtrics, adults aged 40 to 79 from Quebec are rating the famous faces on distinctiveness, familiarity, valence, and name frequency, alongside measures of famous face recognition, naming, knowledge, and agreement. Descriptive statistics were obtained for each famous face, and the standardized stimuli set will be available in open access once data collection is complete. Future directions include the development of new cognitive tests for face processing impairments, notably in neurodegenerative disorders.

articles_hidden.title: What Works, What Doesn't, and Why We Can't Tell the Difference: Contextualizing Evidence-Based Practice in Public Education and School Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan L. Farmer; Emily Nicole Srisarajivakul; Samuel Y. Kim; Imad Zaheer
articles_hidden.abstract: Public schools are charged with educating every child who enters them under a legal and ethical mandate that practice be grounded in evidence, yet the gap between that mandate and routine practice remains substantial across public education. Using school psychology as a case study, we argue that evidence-based practice's (EBP) persistent failure to close this gap reflects a mismatch between the inherited framework and the structural and institutional conditions of public education, rather than practitioner values alone. Six interrelated failures are documented: conflation of EBP as a decision-making model with specific intervention adoption; inconsistent evidentiary standards; demographic mismatch between research samples and served populations; commercial capture of the evidence infrastructure; failures of contextual fit and transportability; and the absence of mechanisms for discontinuing ineffective practices. These failures persist through professional ossification and school psychology's location within education bureaucracies. In response, we propose an epistemological architecture adapted from evidence-based public health, operationalized here as the evidence-based school psychology (EBSP) model, with a three-level evidentiary sequence that provides the de-implementation mechanism the current framework structurally lacks. We offer recommendations for practitioners, trainers, and researchers to operationalize this model in practice.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroinflammation as a shared mechanism linking epilepsy and psychiatric  comorbidities
articles_hidden.authors: Beatriz Eiris; Tamiris Prizon; Ana Carolina Medeiros; Thais Forner Batelli; José Eduardo Peixoto-Santos; Joao Pereira Leite; Rafael Naime Ruggiero
articles_hidden.abstract:
Although epilepsy arises from diverse etiologies, neuroinflammatory processes have emerged as a key factor in epileptogenesis. Neuroinflammation activates a complex network of cellular and molecular mechanisms involving microglia and astrocytes, as
well as the production of pro-inflammatory mediators such as interleukin IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, with inflammasome signaling representing a major upstream driver of these responses. These inflammatory processes contribute to increased seizure susceptibility and facilitate seizure propagation. Beyond their role in seizure generation, inflammatory mechanisms have also been implicated in the development of psychiatric disorders commonly associated with epilepsy. Depression, anxiety, and psychotic disorders occur at disproportionately high rates in people with epilepsy, particularly in those with temporal lobe epilepsy. Notably, many of these psychiatric conditions are associated with inflammatory alterations. This convergence suggests that neuroinflammatory signaling may represent a shared pathophysiological mechanism linking epileptic network dysfunction and psychiatric symptomatology. In this review, we synthesize clinical and experimental evidence supporting the involvement of inflammatory pathways in both epilepsy and its major psychiatric comorbidities. We discuss the molecular mediators, cellular mechanisms, and neural circuit alterations that may underlie this association and evaluate their potential utility as biomarkers and
therapeutic targets for improving neuropsychiatric outcomes in epilepsy.
Keywords: Neuroinflammation; Seizure; Epilepsy; Depression; Anxiety; Psychosis.

articles_hidden.title: Implementation Outcomes and Effectiveness of a Personalized Single Session Cognitive Behavioral Intervention for Depression and Anxiety
articles_hidden.authors: Yui Ting Chloe Au; Yousheng Lester LAI; Jolie LOH; Mary Eileen McNamara; Jasper A. J. Smits; Kean J. Hsu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Single-session interventions (SSIs) have become increasingly popular
psychotherapeutic interventions in recent years due to their potential in providing a therapeutic
and problem-focused experience in one encounter. However, less focus has been given to
dissemination and implementation outcomes for SSIs within existing healthcare settings. This
study evaluated the effectiveness and suitability for broad implementation of a personalized
Single Session Cognitive Behavioral Intervention (SSCBI) for depression and anxiety,
delivered in a university-based training clinic in Singapore. Using a mixed-methods design,
adult therapy clients (N = 24) completed pre-treatment and follow-up measures assessing
depression, anxiety, and cognitive and affective subjective well-being. Quantitative analyses
showed reductions in both symptoms of depression (d = 0.94, p < .001) and anxiety (d = 0.45,
p = .038). Semi-structured interviews were conducted with clients (n = 9) and clinicians (n =
9), and thematic analysis identified twelve key themes mapped to five implementation
outcomes: acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, fidelity, and adoption. Both clients and
clinicians reported high acceptability of the intervention, highlighting its structure, relevance,
and utility in supporting coping skill development. Clinicians felt the protocol was feasible and
appropriate for clients with relatively less complex presentations, with full protocol adherence
achieved across all therapeutic sessions. Recruitment (63.5%) and completion (78.1%) rates
exceeded the pre-registered feasibility benchmarks. These findings provide preliminary
evidence supporting our personalized SSCBI as an effective and scalable brief psychological
intervention, particularly suited for resource-limited settings. Future research should
investigate its longer-term impact, cost-effectiveness, and broader applicability in community
and primary care contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing Parent and Youth Perceptions of Attachment:  Validation of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI)
articles_hidden.authors: Jason W. Payne; Sebastian Dys; Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Attachment is a robust protective factor for youth mental health. This study examined the factor structure and validity of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI), a 16-item measure of youth (8–18 years) attachment in parent and other caregiving relationships. Structural validity was assessed using parallel youth and parent report formats among over 2,000 respondents from both clinical and community samples.
Method: Participants were caregivers in three independent clinical samples and one community sample (N = 571, 407, 220, and 551) and youth self-reporting in the first clinical sample (N = 571). Youth were 7.5 to 18 years old (sample means 13.4 to 14.6), 51% to 61% female, and 61% to 78% White. Caregivers were predominantly mothers (80% to 96%). Confirmatory factor analyses were followed by multi- informant models and tests of associations with caregiver-reported internalizing and externalizing problems.
Results: A two-factor structure replicated across all samples under a single specification, whereas a one- factor model fit poorly. Differential associations with youth internalizing and externalizing problems supported the discriminant validity of each subscale. Multi-method analyses confirmed that anxiety and avoidance were distinguishable across informants, while moderate parent-youth convergence suggested complementary rather than interchangeable perspectives.
Conclusions: The findings support the AAAAI as a measure of attachment anxiety and avoidance in both parent and youth report. For research and clinical practice, the two subscales capture distinct attachment patterns, and parent and youth forms together show where caregivers and youth see the relationship similarly and where they differ.

articles_hidden.title: Individual differences in eye movements dynamics of free viewing conscious and unconscious naturalistic scenes
articles_hidden.authors: Shaked Lublinsky; Yoni Pertzov lab; Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg; Liad Mudrik
articles_hidden.abstract: Different individuals produce different gaze patterns while exploring the world. Here we examined whether these differences occur also when viewing a scene unconsciously. We reanalyzed the data collected in Lublinsky et al., 2025, looking for two types of individual differences; content-based individual differences, which depend on the visual stimulus presented, and content-free individual differences, which do not relate to the observed stimuli. In two experiments, 52 participants viewed scenes consciously and unconsciously, rendered invisible via Continuous Flash Suppression (CFS). We found reliable content-based individual differences in the conscious condition only, suggesting that unconscious processing of scenes does not evoke consistent patterns within individuals. On the other hand, we found consistent content-free individual differences in both visibility conditions. In the unconscious condition, these most likely reflect consistent gazing patterns on the CFS stimulation (i.e., the changing color patches). Yet these content-free measures showed differential strength for seen vs. unseen trials, thereby validating participants' subjective reports. These findings provides novel means to support a dissociation between conscious and unconscious processing under CFS, which is notoriously difficult due to methodological challenges.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding Stigmatization of Organic and Conventional Farmers: Occupational Taint, Dehumanization, and Perceived Burden
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas David; Gaétan Marinho; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Farmers face substantial physical and mental health risks, yet the role of public stigma toward agricultural groups remains insufficiently understood. This study examined stigmatization of organic and conventional farmers in France, using social distance as the main indicator of social rejection, and investigated whether it was associated with perceived vital forces and burdens, occupational taint, dehumanizing perceptions, and infra-humanization. A sample of 250 French participants completed an online questionnaire assessing perceptions of both organic and conventional farmers. Conventional farmers were evaluated less favourably than organic farmers across all stigma-related dimensions. However, partial correlation analyses showed that the same two dimensions remained robustly associated with social distance toward both groups: perceived burden and biologization. Item-level analyses of the perceived burden dimension further suggested that social distance was especially related to the perception that farmers benefit from collective wealth without sufficient contribution. Overall, the findings suggest mainly quantitative rather than qualitative differences between stigmatization of organic and conventional farmers: conventional farmers appear more strongly stigmatized, but social rejection toward both groups relies on similar social-perceptual pathways.

articles_hidden.title: Orthography Shapes L2 Stress PerceptionAcross Development: Evidence from L1 Mandarin Learners of Portuguese
articles_hidden.authors: Chao Zhou; Guilherme D. Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite growing evidence that written input shapes second-language speech learning, its role in suprasegmental acquisition remains underexplored. This study examines whether orthography facilitates lexical stress identification through syllable weight. Portuguese is well suited for this question because stress placement is strongly conditioned by syllable weight, which is transparently encoded in the writing system. A total of 186 L1 Mandarin speakers identified stress location in Portuguese pseudowords presented either auditorily or with accompanying written forms. Naïve listeners used syllable weight as a stress cue only when orthographic information was available, whereas experienced learners showed weight sensitivity from auditory input alone. For experienced learners, however, orthography did not further enhance weight sensitivity; instead, it biased responses toward the default penultimate- stress pattern. These findings suggest that orthographic effects change over L2 development, interacting with auditory cue weighting and distributional regularities in L2 stress perception.

articles_hidden.title: Selflessness, Self-Centeredness, and Mental Health in Dyads: Indirect Associations Through Affective and Functional Pathways
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas David; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health is embedded in interpersonal contexts, yet little is known about whether psychological modes of functioning can affect the mental health of close others through dyadic processes. Drawing on the Self-centeredness/Selflessness Happiness Model (SSHM), this article examined whether selflessness and self-centeredness were indirectly associated with another person’s mental health through two interpersonal pathways: emotional contagion and functional convergence. Two dyadic studies were conducted among French pairs who knew each other and interacted regularly: a student-close other sample in Study 1 and a general population sample in Study 2. Across both studies, no direct partner effects were found. However, indirect effects emerged via the proposed affective and functional mediators: selflessness was associated with higher partner positive mental health, whereas self-centeredness was associated with lower partner positive mental health and higher partner negative mental health. Additional invariance analyses supported the robustness of these structural paths across samples and relationship types. These findings suggest that selflessness and self-centeredness may have interpersonal implications for mental health through affective and functional mediating pathways.

articles_hidden.title: Executive Function and Perceived School Well-Being Across Child- and Adult-Centered Educational Contexts: An Exploratory Study
articles_hidden.authors: Laura González; Marina Oliva Lozano; María Jesús Pardo-Guijarro; Silvia Guerrero
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s socioemotional and cognitive development is shaped by the contexts in which they grow, with school playing a key role in well-being and executive function (EF). This study examined whether the association between EF and perceived school well-being differed across school contexts aligned with Child–Environment Interplay (CEI) and Teacher–Text–Centered (TTC) models. 105 preschool and primary school children participated (NCEI = 70; NTTC = 35). EF was assessed through inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility tasks. Perceived school well-being was explored through a structured interview addressing engagement, environment and support, and aggression-related experiences. No overall differences emerged in EF or interview-based well-being. However, higher well-being was associated with lower EF in TTC, but not CEI, schools, while higher perceived aggression was associated with lower EF across both approaches. A qualitative subsample provided insight into how young children interpreted school experiences. These findings suggest that the association between cognitive skills and perceived school well-being may vary across educational contexts and highlight the value of young children’s perspectives into research on school life.

articles_hidden.title: Near-random behavior in strategic games
articles_hidden.authors: Tal Boger; Dorsa Amir; Sami Ryan Yousif
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans struggle to produce random behavior when asked to do so, leading some to suggest that our ability to randomize is attenuated (or even absent). Here, we demonstrate that the capacity for random behavior is much greater than previously acknowledged: Humans can behave in (near) optimally random ways when the context demands it. We created a custom, online version of the game Battleship in which participants competed against one another. On each turn, one player chose a tile on a 3x3 grid to place a ship, while the other player tried to guess the ship’s location. Across six preregistered studies, this strategic context led to dramatic increases in random behavior relative to closely matched non-strategic tasks. Such random behavior was also remarkably flexible and optimal depending on context; both players readily incorporated varying information about the game (e.g., that tiles can differ in value) while simultaneously accounting for their opponents’ knowledge of that information. A computational model validated these findings and revealed nuanced differences across contexts. Contrary to decades of work finding that humans fail to randomize, we find that strategic games promote highly flexible, near-random behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Difficult to be a People Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing—meaning the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others—has gained a lot of interest in lay psychology. Only recently have scientific endeavors been devoted to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. To address this gap, we subjected the People Pleasing Scale to item response-theoretical examinations as per the polytomous graded response model (N = 2,538). Its three subscales (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) provided favorable item discrimination, widely dispersed item thresholds (even though the thresholds to obtain high scores were located at best at moderate levels), and ample levels of item information and reliability across the three latent trait spectra. These findings underscore that people-pleasing, as measured with the People Pleasing Scale, refers to an everyday rather than a clinical construct. As such, it is apt to be used to assess people-pleasing in studies across diverse areas of academic psychology and for applied contexts alike.

articles_hidden.title: Development and characterization of a standardized stimuli set of 240 famous faces in Quebec
articles_hidden.authors: Nastasia Maria Mitrikeski; Mélodie Leclerc; Zihao Geng; Maxime Montembeault
articles_hidden.abstract:
Famous faces are especially well suited to studying the semantic component of face processing because they carry a sense of familiarity shared across individuals. Recognizing famous faces is not only relevant to research, but it is also clinically informative. Famous-face recognition deficits are observed in prosopagnosia and neurodegenerative disease. They are differentially affected across dementia syndromes, making their assessment useful for differential diagnosis. Testing familiar face processing requires stimuli suited to a specific geographic and sociocultural context, which has led to the development of standardized famous-face databases in France, Great Britain, Spain, and Portugal. However, no such standardized set currently exists for the Quebec population. We therefore created a stimuli set of 240 locally and internationally known famous
people across four categories (politicians, singers, actors, and athletes), spanning different time periods and including famous people of different races, ethnicities, ages, and genders. Through an online survey on Qualtrics, adults aged 40 to 79 from Quebec are rating the famous faces on distinctiveness, familiarity, valence, and name frequency, alongside measures of famous face recognition, naming, knowledge, and agreement. Descriptive statistics were obtained for each famous face, and the standardized stimuli set will be available in open access once data collection is complete. Future directions include the development of new cognitive tests for face processing impairments, notably in neurodegenerative disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Meta-Analytic Evidence for an Ecological Account of the Relationship between Acculturative Stressors and Adaptation
articles_hidden.authors: Dinh-Hung Vu; Kinga Bierwiaczonek; Mike W.-L. Cheung; Rongtian Tong; Jonas R. Kunst; Nora C. G. Benningstad; Evita Willemiek van Duin; Karine Lindholm; Colleen Ward
articles_hidden.abstract: Acculturative stressors, reliably associated with poor migrant adaptation to receiving societies, are highly context-dependent. Yet, how context shapes the stressor-adaptation relationship remains poorly understood. In two pre-registered meta-analyses, we tested the moderating role of structural, cultural, and temporal factors in cross-sectional data (Study 1) and examined the temporal dynamics in longitudinal data (Study 2). Study 1 (k = 229, N = 66,409) modelled origin and receiving country contexts simultaneously to test specific migration routes. Structural factors, such as the receiving country’s poverty, inequality, and unemployment, intensified stressor-adaptation associations. Effects of cultural factors mostly concerned socio-cultural adaptation, most notably stronger stressor-adaptation associations when migrants moved from collectivistic to individualistic societies. For temporal context, longer residence in the receiving country was linked to weaker stressor-adaptation associations. Study 2 (k = 22, N = 8,555) validated the cross-sectional finding that stressor-adaptation associations attenuate over time: effects were stronger and reciprocal at earlier timepoints.

articles_hidden.title: Theorytopia: Psychological Science in 2050
articles_hidden.authors: Luiza Yuan; Denny Borsboom; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Jason Nak; Anne M. Scheel; Noah N'Djaye Nikolai van Dongen; Laura Francina Bringmann; Kyra Evers; Pritam Laskar; Willem Frankenhuis
articles_hidden.abstract: The year is 2050, and psychology has transformed into a theory-driven science—a Theorytopia. Drawing on initiatives and frameworks developed over the past decades since the Theory Crisis, three main advancements have made this transformation possible. First, specialization in theory construction within psychology ensures that theories are tested independently of those who propose them. Methodologies and training in theorizing have been strengthened, while new repositories, such as the “Garden of Living Theories,” promote cumulative record-keeping. Second, worldwide efforts consolidate robust psychological phenomena, reduce reliance on WEIRD samples, and systematize theoretical concepts. Measurement validation and studies probing context-dependency and auxiliary assumptions are now valued research directions in psychology, providing improved empirical bases for rigorous conceptual work. Third, stronger theories better serve the public. Computational modeling, tighter collaboration with stakeholders, better intervention design, new interfaces between science and the public, and the active inclusion of diverse perspectives are improving not just psychology’s societal impact, but also its epistemic value. In this paper, we describe what discussions, actions, and structural changes have led to these drastic improvements, and invite readers to participate in co-shaping the future of a psychological Theorytopia.

articles_hidden.title: Generative AI Use in Selection Testing: Applicant Perceptions, Behaviors, and Test Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Matt Brown; Michelle Martin-Raugh; Emily Gallegos; Michael Grossenbacher; Jessica Haig
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is potentially an effective tool for cheating unproctored internet tests (UIT). However, the practical threat posed by GenAI depends not only on its capabilities, but also whether applicants choose to use it and can do so effectively under real, high-stakes testing conditions. We conducted a series of large-scale surveys of US job applicants who completed selection test batteries in 2026 (n = 141,766) to observe the availability of GenAI assistance, decisions to use that assistance, and the extent to which its use yields higher test scores. Nearly half of applicants reported using GenAI during their job search (49%) but were more likely to use GenAI to help write resumes or to learn about jobs than to help during selection testing. Applicants who used GenAI during testing (9% of all applicants) scored lower on GMA (d = -0.28) and most personality traits (ds between -0.51 and -0.29). Effect sizes were consistent in magnitude and direction across job families, job zones, or AI adoption for work. Our findings suggest that the threat of GenAI on UIT depends not only on the capability of GenAI tools, but also on whether applicants choose to use them and can do so effectively under real testing conditions.

articles_hidden.title: The Effects of Group-Based Community Interventions on Social Reintegration of Marginalized Adults with Mental Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Thorup Dalgaard; jakob Kaarup Jensen; Jasmin Sami Adada; Maya Christiane Flensborg Jensen; Elizabeth Bengtsen; Mikkel Helding Vembye; Elizabeth Tipton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background 
Adults with mental illness who also experience social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, yet scalable interventions addressing both dimensions of recovery remain limited.

Aims 
To evaluate the effects of group-based community interventions on social reintegration and mental health among socially marginalized adults with mental illness.

Methods 
We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions delivered in OECD countries. Searches identified 28,980 records; 62 studies met the inclusion criteria and 49 studies, contributing 349 effect sizes, were included in the meta-analysis. Outcomes were classified as social reintegration or mental health. Meta-analytic models accounted for dependent effect sizes within studies.

Results 
Group-based community interventions improved social reintegration (g = 0.195, 95% CI [0.122, 0.268]) and mental health (g = 0.215, 95% CI [0.090, 0.340]) relative to control conditions, corresponding to effects approximately 2.3 and 1.4 times larger, respectively, than the typical improvements under treatment as usual. Effects varied substantially across studies and outcomes, while measured moderators explained little of this heterogeneity. Effects on social reintegration and mental health were positively associated. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses and showed little indication of publication bias. Nearly half of studies were preregistered and contributed approximately two-thirds of all effect sizes. Preregistered studies yielded smaller social reintegration effects than non-preregistered studies, although the average effect remained statistically significant and substantively meaningful.

Conclusions 
Group-based community interventions can improve both social reintegration and mental health among marginalized adults with mental illness, suggesting that they may support multidimensional recovery. Their potential value therefore extends beyond scalability and lower delivery costs to substantively meaningful improvements in outcomes. However, substantial unexplained heterogeneity indicates that benefits are unlikely to be uniform across populations, interventions, and settings.

What is already known on this topic
Adults experiencing both mental illness and social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, while existing systematic reviews on group-based interventions have largely focused on specific diagnoses, intervention types, or psychiatric symptoms.

What this study adds
Across 49 studies contributing 349 effect sizes, group-based community interventions produced positive average effects on both social reintegration and mental health. Effects in the two domains were positively associated, but substantial heterogeneity remained largely unexplained.

articles_hidden.title: From Probabilistic to Deterministic Missingness: When Predictive Mean Matching Breaks Down Under MAR
articles_hidden.authors: Kristian Kleinke; Henrik Gaisbauer
articles_hidden.abstract: Predictive mean matching (PMM) is usually considered a good alround imputation method that yields unbiased statistical inferences in many scenarios. A known drawback of PMM is that it imputes observed values and thus, by design, cannot make extrapolations beyond the range of the observed data. Nor can it make interpolations in regions, where the data are sparse. The purpose of the present paper is to further explore the breaking points of PMM and to provide applied researchers with a practical tool to diagnose if there are sufficient observed donor cases in all regions of the data space for PMM to work. In a Monte Carlo study with 752 conditions, we systematically varied the missingness mechanism from missing completely at random via probabilistic mechanisms of increasing selection sharpness up to a deterministic threshold. Under probabilistic selection, PMM was nearly unbiased even under relatively high missingness rates. When the outcome, however, was missing beyond a threshold (e.g., when a follow-up is administered only to those above a certain screening score), the slope in a bivariate regression model was attenuated by almost exactly the proportion of missing values, irrespective of the true effect, the sample size, and the number of donors. One noteworthy finding of our simulation was that confidence intervals tended to fail before point estimates did. A diagnostic computed from the observed data—the mean distance from each case to be imputed to its nearest potential donor—predicted coverage closely (ρ = −0.92). We provide an R function for this check and recommend running it before selecting PMM as imputation method in a given scenario. In situations where no suitable donors can be found, applied researchers should select other imputation methods (that can extrapolate).

articles_hidden.title: The Modulation of Mood Through Absorption in Music Listening
articles_hidden.authors: Bradley Austin-Keiller; Frank Russo; Karina J Linnell
articles_hidden.abstract: Music listening is widely used to regulate emotion, yet the listener-level processes underlying affective change remain under-specified. This longitudinal study examined musical absorption as one such process, testing a novel Musical Absorption Training (MAT) protocol designed to scaffold absorptive engagement. Adults aged 55 and older (analytic N = 49) completed 16 listening sessions over four weeks. Participants were randomly assigned either to eight sessions of guided MAT followed by eight unguided sessions, or to unguided listening throughout. Valence and arousal were rated before and after each session, state absorption after each session, and trait absorption (AIMS) at baseline, Session 8, and Session 16. Mixed-effects models showed that greater state absorption predicted larger within-session increases in valence and arousal, driven mainly by within-person fluctuations. MAT did not raise state absorption during the guided phase, but after guidance ended, absorption was preserved in the MAT group. Trait absorption increased over time without a significant Group × Time interaction; however, higher state absorption during the maintenance phase predicted higher trait absorption at study end. These findings identify absorption as a promising listener-level correlate of music-related mood change and offer preliminary evidence that structured attentional guidance may help sustain absorptive engagement across repeated listening.

articles_hidden.title: Low-certainty modals not future tenses cause increased psychological discounting
articles_hidden.authors: Cole Robertson; Sean Roberts; Asifa Majid; Tammy Lu; Phillip Wolff; R. I. M. Dunbar
articles_hidden.abstract: Speaking a language that obliges the future tense for linguistic Future Time Reference (FTR) has been hypothesised to cause speakers to perceive delayed outcomes as temporally distal and therefore less valuable (“temporal discounting”). Conversely, we hypothesise that the obligation to use low-certainty modal verbs, e.g. may, causes speakers to construe risky and delayed outcomes as riskier and therefore less valuable (“combined discounting”). We experimentally elicited free-text FTR responses and measured construals of future temporal distance and discounting of (risky) delayed rewards in speakers of Dutch (which does not oblige FTR marking) and English (which does). We used statistical mediation models, which parse out an indirect effect of a predictor on an outcome via a mediating variable, a direct effect of a predictor on an outcome, and a total effect—the other two combined. English speakers construed future events as temporally proximal, which in turn caused less (rather than more) temporal discounting (indirect effect). The direct effect went in the opposite direction, meaning there was no population-level difference in temporal discounting (no total effect, Study 1). When we measured combined discounting, English speakers discounted more (a total effect, Study 2). Further, English speakers used more low-certainty language and this caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). Future tense use did not impact construals of temporal distance, meaning future tense use did not mediate an effect on combined discounting (Study 2). We addressed possible cultural confounds by testing Dutch-English bilinguals (Study 3). When bilinguals were tested in English, they used more low-certainty modal verbs, which in turn caused increased combined discounting (an indirect effect). This was moderated by self-reported English proficiency, indicating language, not culture, is responsible for effects. Results suggest effects of FTR grammar are not driven by obligatory future tenses affecting temporal discounting, but by obligatory low-certainty modals affecting combined discounting.

articles_hidden.title: A Revolution in Search of an Estimand: On the Idionomic Proposal of Hayes et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Magnus Johansson; Matti Vuorre; Nils Olof Wilhelm Hentati Isacsson; Kristoffer Magnusson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Hayes et al. (2026) argue that clinical psychology is stalled by an “ergodic error”, the application
of group-level statistics to individuals, and propose idionomic analysis as the remedy. We agree
that pooled associations do not need to describe individuals and that treatment effects vary
between people, but the proposed remedy does not answer the clinical question. Personalizing
treatment is a causal problem, yet Hayes et al. never state which causal quantity, or estimand,
they target. Their evidence consists of observational within-person associations, which cannot
separate effects from confounding that varies over time. Applied to observational data, none of
the recommended methods can identify a causal effect. Non-ergodicity shows only that pooled
and individual associations may differ, not that causal effects do. The reported heterogeneity is
also questionable, in part because person-level estimates from short series are imprecise. The
reliability Hayes et al. cite against this concern describes person means rather than within-
person variation, and the statistics summarizing heterogeneity have not been adequately
checked against simulated data in which there is no heterogeneity. Designs that randomize
treatment within or between persons can target person-level and conditional effects, within
limits set by carryover and irreversible change. Rather than the proposed idionomic revolution,
clinical psychology needs to join the causal revolution, in which the estimand is stated before
the data are analyzed.

articles_hidden.title: Five More Items Matter: Comparing Structural Validity, Response Bias, and Nomological Networks in 10- and 15-Item Big Five Measures Across Nations
articles_hidden.authors: Zhangchu Xu; Yuke Yang; Zhihao Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Ultra-short Big Five measures are widely used to reduce respondent burden while retaining acceptable measurement quality. Yet when personality domains are represented by only two or three items, it remains unclear whether modestly greater item coverage translates into better measurement performance across cultural contexts. The present study compared the Ten-Item Personality Inventory (TIPI), the 10-item Big Five Inventory (BFI-10), and the 15-item Big Five Inventory-SOEP (BFI-S) across four sources of validity evidence: factor structure, measurement invariance, response bias, and nomological networks, using three large-scale cross-national datasets. Conventional confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) models showed inadequate fit across all three measures and were frequently affected by Heywood cases. Exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM) analyses indicated that BFI-S showed better recovery of the expected five-factor structure than TIPI and BFI-10, although cross-cultural variability remained. TIPI and BFI-10 were not subjected to measurement invariance testing because their baseline structures did not support meaningful comparisons, while BFI-S demonstrated relatively robust demographic invariance but weaker cross-national invariance. All measures showed directional response bias, with the largest contribution observed in BFI-10 and the smallest in BFI-S. Moreover, greater response bias was associated with larger deviations in personality–criterion associations across countries. Despite limited item coverage, all three measures reproduced theoretically expected nomological associations, with BFI-S showing greater cross-national consistency. Overall, expanding from two to three indicators per Big Five domain was associated with improved structural recovery, reduced response bias, and more consistent external associations. However, this modest increase in item coverage did not eliminate the inherent limitations of ultra-short personality assessment, highlighting the continued importance of considering measurement purpose, context, and cultural applicability.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Difficult to be a People Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing—meaning the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others—has gained a lot of interest in lay psychology. Only recently have scientific endeavors been devoted to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. To address this gap, we subjected the People Pleasing Scale to item response-theoretical examinations as per the polytomous graded response model (N = 2,538). Its three subscales (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) provided favorable item discrimination, widely dispersed item thresholds (even though the thresholds to obtain high scores were located at best at moderate levels), and ample levels of item information and reliability across the three latent trait spectra. These findings underscore that people-pleasing, as measured with the People Pleasing Scale, refers to an everyday rather than a clinical construct. As such, it is apt to be used to assess people-pleasing in studies across diverse areas of academic psychology and for applied contexts alike.

articles_hidden.title: A puzzling situation: How cooperation and social observation influence visuospatial problem-solving
articles_hidden.authors: Federico Cassioli; Nellia Bellaert; Mandy Rossignol; Clay B. Holroyd; Rudi De Raedt
articles_hidden.abstract: Human problem-solving rarely occurs in social isolation. Yet how cognitive performance and subjective experiences vary across social situations, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in social anxiety (SA), remains underexplored. In this preregistered, within-subject experiment, 101 healthy young adults completed a visuospatial problem-solving task, involving tangram puzzles of different difficulty levels (1,818 trials total) across three social conditions: alone or joined by an experimental confederate acting as either a scrutinizing observer or an active cooperator. Using hierarchical Bayesian modeling, we modeled task performance and post-trial self-reported experiences, and tested whether SA, measured with the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, moderated the effects of social condition. Both performance and self-report ratings were modulated by task difficulty and social condition. Relative to performing alone, being observed was associated with a decrease in the probability of success and higher post-trial anxiety. Cooperation facilitated performance and reduced perceived difficulty. Crucially, SA moderated the effect of cooperation on post-trial anxiety: cooperation produced the largest reduction in post-trial anxiety among participants with greater fear of being observed. This buffering effect was specific to social-evaluative fear rather than general trait anxiety or task performance. Our findings reinforce the view that cognitive performance and participants’ experiences are jointly shaped by the social context in which they occur.

articles_hidden.title: Bounded rational world modelling
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel David Jones; Antonia Reul; Paul Rauwolf
articles_hidden.abstract: The effective navigation of complex environments requires forming and acting on memories of actions, states, and values; features collectively referred to as a 'mental model'. But what are the decision rules that shape world model acquisition? Dominant normative responses to this question characterise the decision about what information to engage with, and the fidelity in which to encode that information, in terms of cost-value optimisation. However, this is untenable in natural environments of any complexity. The current report presents new empirical support for a complementary characterisation of world model acquisition based on realistic assumptions about human decision-making. Across two pre-registered experiments, N=108 people explored a virtual machine in which combinations of action switches map to symbolic information with associated values. In experiment one, participants were incentivised to maximise value acquisition under costs, while in experiment two participants were incentivised to explore the machine without costs. Each experiment involved a test battery assessing participants' understanding of the machine. We show that varying value structure dramatically shapes world model acquisition - in particular, knowledge of low-value options is sparse under search costs. Search is affected by lapses in memory, and metacognitive awareness of learning progress is poorly calibrated with accuracy. Most importantly, comparison to optimal benchmarks suggests that shortfalls in human performance are attributable to satisficing against a subjective aspiration threshold and updating world models locally in light of the feedback elicited. These results demonstrate that noisy myopic satisficing is a core decision rule shaping world model acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: An Integrative Theory of the Noradrenaline System: Meta-Control through Expected Information Gain
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Living organisms constantly balance exploration and exploitation to adapt to changing environments.
While the neuromodulator noradrenaline (NA) is known to regulate arousal, attention, and information
seeking, its precise computational function remains elusive. Here, we propose an integrative theory of
the noradrenergic system, suggesting that it encodes expected information gain (EIG), a measure of how
informative the environment is over time, and that it uses this quantity for the meta-control of adaptive
behavior. We illustrate this theory using a hierarchical active inference model in which the NA system
acts as a higher-level meta-controller that dynamically adjusts a set of parameters (η) of a lower-level
behavioral controller, modulating exploration rate, the balance between deliberative and habitual control,
perceptual precision, learning rate, and cognitive flexibility. Simulations demonstrate that NA-based
EIG estimation and meta-control enhance performance in volatile environments by promoting directed
exploration, facilitating rapid shifts away from maladaptive habits, sharpening sensory evidence, and
accelerating learning following context changes. These results unify multiple facets of noradrenergic
function under a single computational objective, providing a novel perspective to explain tonic and
phasic NA activity in estimating EIG and meta-controlling behavior. Summing up, this framework
provides a principled link between neuromodulation, exploration, and adaptive behavior, suggesting
that the noradrenergic system implements a fundamental mechanism for inferring and exploiting the
informational richness of the environment.

articles_hidden.title: Nausea and disgust as aversive interoceptive signals in psychopathology.
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Bagley; Camilla Nord
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Disruptions in reinforcement learning are reliably seen across
psychiatric disorders. Yet the origins of reinforcement learning are in interoceptive
signals: we learn to pursue primary interoceptive rewards, such as calories, or avoid
primary interoceptive punishments, such as nausea. Interoceptive punishments may
drive diverse aspects of psychopathology, from enhanced disgust processing in
obsessive compulsive disorder to restricted eating behaviour in anorexia nervosa.

Aims: To determine the role of interoceptive punishments in psychopathology, we
tested a) whether the experience of the interoceptive punishment of nausea covaried
with psychiatric symptoms and b) whether learning about a close proxy of
interoceptive punishment—disgust—predicted psychopathology.

Method: In a large representative sample (n=308), recruited online, participants
completed a battery of questionnaires, on which we conducted a factor analysis, and
a learning task, to which we fit computational reinforcement learning models. This
enabled us to quantify both disgust-related and unrelated psychopathology as well
as reinforcement learning measures from disgust-based, fear-based and points-
based outcomes.

Results: Self-report measures of nausea were strongly and generally predictive of
psychopathology, unexpectedly spanning nearly all symptoms and syndromes. A
similar pattern emerged for self-reported disgust. This suggests that enhanced
experience of interoceptive punishment is a general feature of psychiatric
symptomatology. Additionally, a subset of questionnaires (contamination OCD,
blood-injury phobia and spider phobia) related to computationally-derived measures
of behaviour on a disgust-learning task, indicating a potential mechanism of
interoceptive punishment learning.

Conclusions: These findings provide insight into a previously-unexplored symptom
of mental health problems, nausea, and demonstrate a potential mechanism by
which aversive interoceptive learning may contribute to psychopathology, revealing a
new potential interoceptive treatment target.

articles_hidden.title: Affordance-Based Control in Driving Behavior: Integration of Perception and Action by Extending rho Coupling and Satisficing
articles_hidden.authors: Takayuki Kondoh; Hiroyuki Mishima; Nobuhiro Furuyama
articles_hidden.abstract: Action-control models in ecological psychology have evolved from pursuing a single optimal solution toward affordance-based control within safety regions. However, mathematically integrating these approaches with rho coupling theory remains insufficient. This study theoretically re-examines the "risk feeling formula (RFF)"—a linear sum of two optical variables derived from real-world driving data. Our analysis demonstrates that the RFF is structurally equivalent to rho coupling, yet its "intercept" distinctly functions as a "satisficing" threshold. Rather than representing an internal computational compromise, this threshold signifies direct perceptual attunement for initiating avoidance behavior while maintaining a safety margin. Furthermore, we propose an integrated mathematical representation of affordances as the linear sum of two action-scaled pi values, reflecting the extended body effectivities, corresponding to overt risk (rho_LF) and potential risk (rho_GF). By extending rho coupling to encompass satisficing, this framework elegantly models how actors dynamically balance contextual pressures without error-nulling. This integrated theoretical approach explains diverse human adaptive strategies and provides fundamental insights for future ecological human-centered design, including advanced driver assistance systems.

articles_hidden.title: Sex and gender differences in functional and participation experiences of students with developmental coordination disorder in higher education
articles_hidden.authors: Clare Copley; Kimberly Petersen; Madeleine Pownall; Lucy H Eddy
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterised by persistent motor coordination difficulties that negatively impacts daily functioning and participation across the lifespan. Despite a high prevalence (5-6%), DCD remains under recognised in adulthood, creating particular challenges in contexts requiring high levels of independent participation, such as higher education. Sex and gender are also important to examine, given their potential to influence the recognition, presentation and lived experience of DCD. However, there is a notable lack of research exploring how sex and gender identity may impact these experiences. 
Aims: This exploratory study aimed to investigate whether functional challenges and participation experiences differed according to sex and gender identity among higher education students with DCD.
Methods: Data were collected via an online self-report questionnaire completed by 77 higher education students with DCD/dyspraxia across the UK and Ireland.
Results: Findings indicate high levels of functional difficulty and participation restriction across the sample, with fatigue often reported as a consequence. Females with DCD were significantly more likely than males to report challenges related to gross motor skills (p<.05, d=.60) and executive function skills (p<.05, d =.60). Participants who identified as a gender minority reported a higher incidence of difficulty with fine motor skills (p<.05, d=–.63) and executive function (p<.05, d =–.60) compared to cisgender participants. 
Conclusions: Findings indicate that students with DCD experience persistent functional challenges that restrict participation in higher education.  Experiences and support needs may also differ based on sex and gender identity.

articles_hidden.title: Detecting Response Styles in Visual Analogue Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik Vollbracht; Tanja Lischetzke; Mirka Henninger
articles_hidden.abstract: Response styles are prevalent in self-report data and may bias parameter estimates. While there are various approaches for detecting response styles in Likert-type data, models for visual analogue scales remain scarce. We propose a novel modeling framework that extends the beta item response model by Noel and Dauvier (2007) to jointly detect extreme response style, midpoint response style, and acquiescent response style. Estimated in a Bayesian framework using Stan, the model performed well in a comprehensive simulation study. Parameter recovery was primarily influenced by the number of (reverse-scored) items and the variance of response styles, whereas sample size had a negligible effect. The model’s practical utility is illustrated using empirical data (Kuhlmann et al., 2017), for which it demonstrated superior model fit compared to the original beta item response model. Overall, the proposed framework provides researchers with a principled approach to account for response styles in visual analogue scale data.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Distance Is Domain-Relative: Comparing Value-Based and Norm-Based Distances Using the Cultural Fixation Index
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Eriksson; Pontus Strimling
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers enter cultural distance, a single number, as a general-purpose control for cultural difference and use it to select study sites they hope are culturally distant. Both practices assume that the number is a stable property of a society pair, independent of the cultural content the items represent. We test that assumption using the cultural fixation index (CFst) of Muthukrishna et al. (2020), holding the estimator and societies fixed while varying content. Within the World Values Survey, distance matrices constructed from political and moral-religious value items share only about a quarter of their variance. Across domains, distance matrices built from value items and Global Study of Everyday Norms ratings share between about a tenth and a fifth of their variance, depending on the minimum sample per society. The low cross-domain agreement persists under controls for survey era, coding resolution, reliability, distance formula, and sample composition. Cultural distance is only defined relative to the content domain from which its items are drawn and does not reliably transfer to another domain. Researchers should name the domain from which a cultural-distance measure is constructed and match it to the research question.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
articles_hidden.authors: Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; Patricia Opondo; Juan David Leongómez; Yuto Ozaki; Zixuan Jia; Suzanne Purdy; Patrick E. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. Critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on new data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators (“Many Voices”), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles_hidden.authors: Leili Rouhi; Zuleykha Gasimova; Valerie A Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: Monitoring processes, such as confidence, are assumed to guide control processes, such as whether to change or persist with a response. Yet whether this monitoring–control link depends on the same working memory (WM) resources implicated in reasoning itself remains unclear. Fuzzy-trace theory (FTT) holds that reasoning relies primarily on low-effort gist representations and that errors arise when a salient but inappropriate gist interferes with the appropriate one. Drawing on FTT and the meta-reasoning framework the role of WM in reasoning, monitoring and control. Participants (N = 998) solved belief-bias syllogisms with and without conflict between validity and believability in a two-response paradigm. They gave an initial answer under a concurrent WM load, a response deadline, or both, followed by a confidence rating and a final answer. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined, and this decline was similar for conflict and non-conflict problems. Confidence was reliably lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems across all conditions, and confidence reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time regardless of WM constraints. Monitoring resolution, however, was low even without constraints. These results suggest that WM constraints impair reasoning generally but leave conflict detection and control sensitivity largely intact. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate their own correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a more general limitation of monitoring rather than a consequence of constrained resources.

articles_hidden.title: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D): A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing the Therapeutic Alliance
articles_hidden.authors: KHAIRUL KORAI
articles_hidden.abstract:
Individual with dyslexia frequently experience persistent reading difficulties that extend far beyond academic environments, contributing to heightened anxiety, low self-esteem, and chronic psychological distress. In traditional mental health counseling, literacy-heavy tools such as written intake questionnaires, thought journals, and dense psychoeducational handouts impose a heavy extraneous cognitive load. This load exhausts working memory and triggers reading anxiety, effectively diverting mental bandwidth away from core therapeutic processing. To address this barrier, this paper introduces a conceptual framework: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D). Grounded in a narrative synthesis of existing literature, this model positions artificial intelligence not as a replacement for human clinicians, but as an accessible cognitive scaffold managed under ethical oversight. The framework synthesizes Cognitive Load Theory, the Triadic Therapeutic Alliance model (Client, Therapist, and AI), and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles. By leveraging Generative AI summaries, speech-to-text journaling, and multimodal text-to-speech presentation, AAIC-D offloads reading and writing effort, restoring the client's emotional capacity for therapeutic engagement. Finally, we address critical counseling practice governance concerns including algorithmic bias, data privacy under HIPAA/GDPR, and client over-reliance offering actionable guidelines to humanize and democratize psychological care. 

Keywords: Dyslexia, Assistive AI, Therapeutic Alliance, Cognitive Load Theory, Universal Design for Learning, Counseling Psychology, Cyberpsychology
