Drawing on novel survey experiments, we compare the information-seeking behavior of independents and partisans by examining the importance they attach to different candidate attributes and the quantity of information they seek before choosing between candidates. We find that independents and partisans rank candidate attributes in similar ways, with both groups prioritizing issue positions over socio-demographic characteristics. Yet, independents rely less on candidate partisanship and acquire more information than partisans across a variety of hypothetical electoral conditions. These differences persist across levels of political knowledge, suggesting that independents and partisans use distinct decision rules when evaluating political candidates.

articles.title: Beyond Good and Bad Controls: Endogenous Legal Factors in Sentencing Research
articles.authors: Jose Pina-Sánchez; Andrzej Uhl
articles.abstract: Observational studies of institutional decision-making often rely on explanatory variables that are themselves partly constructed through the process under investigation. In sentencing research, many legal factors are defined by the judge and may therefore act simultaneously as confounders and mediators. Controlling for them may introduce post-treatment bias, whereas omitting them may reintroduce confounding bias. We propose overcoming this impasse by conceptualising judicially-defined legal factors as variables affected by measurement error. Using a typical regression model of racial disparities in the U.S. Federal Courts, we demonstrate how sensitivity analyses based on SIMEX and Monte Carlo simulations can be used to assess the bias arising from judicial disagreement and judicial prejudice. We show that even modest levels of uncertainty in discretionary legal factors can generate substantial and unpredictable bias, affecting estimates of racial disparities even when measurement error is entirely random and therefore unrelated to race.

articles.title: Distributional Validity of a Korean Synthetic Persona Panel: Evidence From the Korea Media Panel Survey
articles.authors: Howard Kim; Keun Tae Cho
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) personas are proposed as survey respondents, yet validation outside English-speaking contexts is scarce. We evaluate how well a Korean synthetic persona panel used to condition Gemini 3.5 Flash and EXAONE reproduces digital and artificial intelligence (AI) service-use distributions of the Korea Media Panel Survey. About 8,000 personas per model answered eight service-use items and eight attitudinal constructs; responses were compared with weighted survey estimates. The overall mean absolute error (MAE) was 14-19 percentage points (pp), with binary item-mean correlations of 0.70-0.91 across waves. Segment error across five axes was 14-18 pp, with between-group signed-error ranges of 49.6/34.7 pp (Gemini/EXAONE; 39.5/31.2 without the non-comparable teen cells). Errors were model-specific: an age stereotype (Gemini) versus an acquiescence-consistent level bias (EXAONE). Generative-AI overestimation was consistent with temporal misalignment; short-form underestimation was framing-sensitive and persisted under randomized order (both shown for Gemini). Post-hoc holdout calibration on 30% of the real data, with the correction form selected inside the calibration set, cut cell MAE from 18.3/15.1 to 4.9/4.4 pp, yet direct estimation from that subsample was more accurate than the calibrated panel (3.6 pp), a synthetic-informed shrinkage estimator beat its real-only counterpart by at most 0.7 pp, and the correction did not transfer competitively across waves. The calibrated panel kept an advantage only below roughly 250-860 real responses (at most 2.3 pp over a real-only shrinkage estimator) or, for one model, on unobserved segments. In this setting, synthetic panels are not survey substitutes; their value is diagnostic.

articles.title: Language Replacement and Individualism: Linguicide as a Measurable Cultural Variable
articles.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles.abstract: Cross-cultural research has linked grammatical features, especially the obligatory use of subject pronouns, to national individualism, but such links are hard to separate from language family, wealth and history. This study treats colonial language replacement as a measurable variable and asks whether colonized countries whose majority home language became a European colonizer's language are more individualist than colonized countries that kept their own. Using a 55-country dataset and a validated individualism index (Akaliyski et al., 2025), I compare 10 replaced-language and 9 retained-language countries, controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure. Replacement was associated with 12.1 points higher individualism (95% CI [8.0, 16.2]). The association was larger where English, which requires overt subject pronouns, did the replacing (17.5 points) than where Spanish or Portuguese, which allow pronoun drop, did so (11.4 points), though the difference between the two was not statistically significant (p = .10). The replacement association persisted when census-based settler population share was controlled, and settler share showed no independent association. This test rests largely on a single case: Ireland, where the population remained and the language shifted, scored with the English-speaking settler states. Within Ireland (N = 3,057), residents of areas where more Irish was spoken in 1911 placed less weight on self-direction values today, while present-day daily use of Irish showed no association. Within Latin America, Indigenous language retention was inversely associated with individualism, but this could not be separated from national wealth. Replacement was not associated with autism prevalence once diagnostic capacity was controlled. I argue that language replacement offers a direct, measurable proxy for linguicide and a route for testing claims about language and selfhood.

articles.title: From volume to care: an ethic of aver cura for tourism and host-community well-being
articles.authors: Christian Josef Wiedermann; Patrick Rina; Harald Pechlaner; Fulvio Longato
articles.abstract:
Purpose. This paper proposes an ethic of care — aver cura — as an integrative concept for destination development that connects two disconnected uses of "care" in tourism scholarship and specifies how the concept can be observed and measured.
Design/methodology/approach. The paper is conceptual. It synthesizes tourism studies, public health and the ethics of care, and illustrates the argument through the single case of Meran, South Tyrol, a historic alpine health resort.
Findings. Tourism research invokes care as an ethos, while public health and health tourism treat care as provision; the two seldom meet. An ethic of aver cura, built on caring for self, others and place, integrates them and reframes success from volume to sustaining visitor, resident, worker and landscape together. Civic trust, distinct from commercial destination trust, is the operational core through which care becomes measurable.
Research limitations/implications. The six propositions are conceptual and untested; they set a future agenda for comparative and longitudinal research.
Practical implications. Destinations would shift from volume metrics to civic-trust and community indicators and to recurring deliberative governance.
Social implications. The approach foregrounds the well-being of residents and tourism workers alongside that of visitors.
Originality/value. The paper offers an integrative concept of care that bridges ethical and public-health registers, distinguishes civic from commercial trust as its measurable core, and grounds care in a destination's own formative logic rather than importing it from outside.

Preprint of a manuscript currently under review at the Journal of Tourism Futures (Emerald). This is the submitted version and has not been peer-reviewed.

articles.title: Making Place for Health and Good Life: Tourism at the Intersection of Philosophy and Public Health
articles.authors: Fulvio Longato; Patrick Rina; Christian Josef Wiedermann
articles.abstract: Tourism is increasingly promoted as a resource for health, and destinations market the well-being their landscapes are said to afford; yet the notion of well-being invoked where tourism and public health meet requires further specification, as the fields that converge there do not necessarily use the term in the same sense. The conceptual analysis clarifies well-being by distinguishing its psychological dimensions from its philosophical characterisation in terms of human flourishing, and frames health from a salutogenic perspective. Human flourishing and salutogenesis intersect particularly through meaningfulness and the ways persons engage with what places make possible. Drawing on the phenomenology of the tourist experience and on the literatures of therapeutic landscapes and restorative environments, the paper argues that places contribute to health through multiple and potentially interacting pathways involving characteristics of settings, activities and experiences, and their social and environmental contexts. Embodied pathways further show the interconnection of experiential and bodily dimensions of health. The paper draws out implications for public health and participatory destination design. Alpine tourism destinations provide a suitable context in which these relationships can be examined empirically.

articles.title: "How do I survive the next 12 hours?": Disability and lived experiences of extreme heat in the UK
articles.authors: Hollye Kirkcaldy; Annayah Miranda Beatrice Prosser; Keren MacLennan; Christina Demski
articles.abstract: As extreme heat becomes a more frequent consequence of climate change, understanding how marginalised populations experience it is critical for adaptation. Disabled people are routinely categorised as ‘at-risk’, yet research largely quantifies heat risk at population level, leaving lived dimensions of heat experience for Disabled people under-explored, particularly in the UK. Drawing on theories of ableism and psycho-emotional disablism, this qualitative study asks how Disabled people in the UK experience extreme heat and what shapes their capacity to adapt. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 27 self-identified Disabled adults across the UK between July and September 2025 and analysed data using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Across three main themes, participants depict heat as an actively disabling environmental condition which erodes capacity, diminishes identity, exposes ableist assumptions in adaptation and is mediated by material and structural conditions across housing, care and urban infrastructure. Current adaptation frameworks contain significant blind spots, including the temporal and psycho-emotional dimensions of heat harm, and are, in some respects, actively harmful for Disabled people. Addressing this requires a fundamental interrogation of whose knowledge informs the design of heat adaptation policy in the UK.

articles.title: A Reader’s Guide to the Rubin Report
articles.authors: John Levi Martin
articles.abstract: This was written for those readers of the Rubin report who are outsiders to the discipline of sociology, and look to this report as a guide to the state of this field.  Given the publicity this report has received, it would be reasonable for them to imagine that there is warrant for its claims.  There have been many responses to this report, but (as far as I know) none that have simply focused on whether she actually marshaled evidence to support her arguments, and whether she correctly represents her sources.

articles.title: Efficiency, Elasticity, and Disruption: A Mechanistic Framework for Socio-Technical System Transitions
articles.authors: Vitor Miranda de Souza; Diogo Figueirinhas; Brian D. Fath; Fredrik Nilsson
articles.abstract: Efficiency improvements are persistently accompanied by demand expansion and increased resource throughput, systematically undermining sustainability strategies in operations and supply chain management. While existing explanations rely on behavioural assumptions or empirical correction factors rather than structural accounts, this paper develops a first-order mechanistic formulation of efficiency-induced demand expansion, introducing system elasticity εsys as a structural property of socio-technical configuration. Building on and generalising Ayres and Warr’s framework, we derive the service relationship S ∝ η^(ε_sys−1) and its resource corollary R ∝ η^(ε_sys−2), establishing two sustainability thresholds: ε_sys > 1 for service expansion and ε_sys > 2 for absolute resource growth. Two independent empirical cases – the 19th-century steam engine and contemporary computing – yield ε_sys ≈ 3.5, consistent with the backfire condition. The formulation reframes the operational challenge from governing resource efficiency to governing service elasticity.

articles.title: When Red Is - and Is Not - Blood: A Corpus-Assisted Cognitive-Semantic Analysis of Five Settler Australian Texts (1874-1907)
articles.authors: Nguyen Huynh Si Tan
articles.abstract: This study investigates when the colour term RED is conceptually connected with BLOOD and when the two domains remain independent in settler Australian literary discourse. The data comprise five complete public-domain texts published between 1874 and 1907 by Marcus Clarke, Henry Lawson, Miles Franklin, Joseph Furphy, and Jeannie Gunn. The study adopts a corpus-assisted qualitative design combining full-text lexical retrieval, paragraph-level concordance reading, cognitive-semantic annotation, and counterexample analysis. A verified analytical set of 30 concordance contexts was assembled across the five texts to test explicit BLOOD-RED bridges against competing RED and BLOOD pathways; the set is deliberately criterion-based and is not treated as a frequency sample. Three direct bridge types are attested: blood-red compounding, blood as a colour comparator, and bodily circulation as a causal basis for visible redness. The same texts also provide systematic counterevidence to any general RED IS BLOOD equation. RED occurs independently in landscape, fire, flora, atmospheric description, and conventional idioms, while BLOOD extends independently to violence, personhood, descent, temperament, inheritance, vitality, and exploitation. The findings support an asymmetrical partial-overlap model: BLOOD can motivate RED, but RED does not entail BLOOD, and many figurative BLOOD constructions have no chromatic component. The analysis further shows that red soil, red gum, and comparable Australian landscape expressions cannot be classified as blood imagery without local lexical or causal co-activation. Methodologically, the study demonstrates the value of separating lexical semantics, metonymic motivation, metaphorical extension, and literary symbolism before cross-linguistic comparison.

articles.title: The Darkside of Collegiality: From Audit Culture to Participatory Taylorism
articles.authors: Abe Walker
articles.abstract: Cultures of shared governance in academia may appear as a noble tradition to be upheld and defended against the steady encroachment of audit culture. However, building upon recent interest in the ‘dark side’ of collegiality, this theoretically-motivated article proposes that the collegial ideal of collective and participatory decision-making now co-exist alongside performance metrics in an uneasy alliance that softens their surface-level opposition. Invoking the paradoxical concept of ‘participatory Taylorism,’ this study demonstrates that faculty engagement is essential to audit culture’s apparent staying power. Performance metrics survive by opening themselves to the demos, inviting robust debates about their composition and legitimacy – provided these dialogues stop short of contesting audit culture itself. In this sense, permissible modes of shared governance perform a type of ‘collegiality-washing,’ substituting a simulacra of participation for the real thing.  Moreover, because ‘participation’ is precisely the lever through which performance measures exert their influence, conventional oppositional strategies risk co-optation. In a university setting that demands constant engagement and actively recuperates dissent, resistance may take the form of withdrawal, silence, or even a more recent trend, ‘quiet quitting.’

articles.title: Informing Instruction During Educational Disruptions: A UTAUT-Informed Mixed-Methods Study of Grade 11 Students' Evaluations of YouTube for Oral Communication Learning
articles.authors: Jo Michael Llamelo
articles.abstract: Educational disruptions can require students to rely on supplementary digital resources when ordinary classroom interaction is restricted. This study examined how 26 Grade 11 students enrolled in Oral Communication at a private senior high school in Legazpi City, Philippines, evaluated YouTube during emergency remote teaching in Academic Year 2020-2021. A convergent, cross-sectional mixed-methods survey used 17 six-point Likert-type items organized through UTAUT-informed domains, each paired with an open-ended prompt. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, while 442 written explanations were analyzed through deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis and integrated with their corresponding ratings. Domain means were generally favorable, ranging from 4.48 for behavioral intention to 5.08 for facilitating conditions. Internal consistency was strong for performance expectancy (α = .82) but weaker for the other domains (α = .37-.65), so domain-level results were interpreted cautiously and alongside item-level and qualitative evidence. The qualitative analysis produced 28 substantive codes synthesized into five cross-domain patterns: controllable multimodal explanation supported comprehension; YouTube expanded explanatory options but required active selection; educational value depended on content and presenter quality; access was flexible but infrastructure-dependent; and acceptance was pragmatic and supplementary rather than substitutive. Across 442 rating-explanation pairs, 75.3% were congruent positive and 15.4% were qualified or mixed. The findings suggest that students valued YouTube primarily as a flexible supplementary resource for clarification, review, and continuity rather than as a replacement for teacher-led instruction. Notably, connectivity and infrastructure concerns remained visible even among participants selected for online readiness, underscoring the distinction between nominal readiness and reliable access.

articles.title: Adolescent Online Leisure, Media Literacy, and Emotional Distress from Online Victimization: Evidence Across Fifty Countries and Economies
articles.authors: Yunqi Wang; Yan Ruth Xia; James A. Bovaird; Maria Rosario T. de Guzman; Paul Springer; Xiaoran Sun
articles.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has accelerated adolescents’ engagement in online activities. However, research on adolescents’ technology use and mental health often overlooks the complexity of online behaviors and the role of media literacy without examining specific mechanisms. This study addresses the gap by analyzing survey data from 295,843 adolescents aged 15-16 years across 50 countries and economies from Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) collected in 2022, examining the relations among adolescent online leisure, media literacy, and emotional distress from online victimization. Structural equation modeling results revealed that both adolescents’ online leisure and media literacy are positively associated with their emotional distress from online victimization experiences, such as exposure to unwanted content. Findings provide important implications for research, theories, and practices, highlighting an urgent need for parenting practices and interventions to promote adolescents’ media literacy and digital skills to navigate the online environment and mitigate online risks.

articles.title: Captured by the Ballot: Non-Partisan Judicial Elections and Democratic Erosion in Mexico
articles.authors: Brett Ryan Bessen
articles.abstract: Public tolerance for democratic erosion is often attributed to voter partisanship. Voters are thought to overlook undemocratic maneuvers to support the partisan in-group. Yet, backsliders  often disavow traditional parties and frame their reforms as non-partisan. I examine the role of voter partisanship in non-partisan elections, showing how elite manipulation of the information environment can generate partisan outcomes that facilitate backsliding—even when citizens prefer non-partisan outcomes on average. I examine Mexico’s 2025 judicial elections, pairing a conjoint experiment with an analysis of the electoral results. While the conjoint indicates that voters preferred independent judges, the electoral results indicate that government-aligned candidates on illicitly circulated voter guides (acordeones) received the most support, contributing to the partisan capture of the Supreme Court. Elite manipulation of the information environment and electoral incentives—rather than partisan preferences among the eligible electorate—were primary contributors to the court’s partisan capture.

articles.title: Digitalización de la información política y Democracia: Paradojas, contradicciones y desafíos. Una propuesta inter-transdisciplinar de análisis conceptual
articles.authors: Ángel Gutiérrez Escobedo
articles.abstract: Resumen: Tomando un punto de partida interdisciplinario (Thompson, 1996), presentamos una propuesta de análisis para la información política en las democracias para la época de lo virtual; que trabaja con los principios de la teoría general de sistemas sociales (Luhmann, 2022; 1981) y la teoría de la información (Shannon, 1948). Algunos intentos contemporáneos para entender dicho escenario de información y democracia (Huang, 2026) ponen especial énfasis en la paradoja que surge entre libertad de expresión e información para la democracia. Partiendo de la teoría general de sistemas sociales, entendemos que la comunicación política no produce información para sus observantes sino que se relaciona con la continuidad, adaptación o reproducción de la misma comunicación; es decir, mediante la comunicación digital, los actores políticos han acoplado sus comunicaciones en la exageración o el escándalo, desarticulando la racionalidad tradicional en la política donde la calidad y alternativas de información suele ser necesaria (Dahl, 2009) desplazándola por una inmaterialidad que va un poco más allá del espectáculo (Debord, 1995), pero que reincide en la misma realidad política. Esto es importante para entornos como México porque atraviesa el derecho a la libertad de expresión en tanto que la comunicación de opiniones extremistas puede ser utilizado por diversos actores para deslegitimar otras formas de comunicación (Russo, 2025) como también un mecanismo para limitar derechos. Finalmente, sus efectos ocultos, la información política virtual/digital permite facilitar el entendimiento o aceptación de decisiones materiales que de otra forma podrían parecer aberrantes mediante estiramientos de la verdad, es decir, discusiones o debates en torno a tópicos que se podrían considerar fundamentales (Vössing, 2024). Termina con una serie de consideraciones para el análisis político contemporáneo puesto que la situación global de las democracias mantiene tendencias de erosión (Stokes, 2025) y se emplea la ironía por lideres políticos para consolidar el poder o des-presupuestar instituciones. Se necesitan estudios que visibilicen y permitan combatir esta contradicción.

articles.title: Adverse Outcomes Among Youths Admitted to Compulsory Institutional Care: A Swedish Matched Cohort Study
articles.authors: Amber L. Beckley; Fredrik Sivertsson; Sofi Oskarsson; Catherine Tuvblad; Peter Larm
articles.abstract: Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care represent a particularly vulnerable population with substantial behavioral, social, and health-related needs. However, evidence on their long-term outcomes relative to other high-risk youths, and on when adverse outcomes emerge following discharge, remains limited. We examined the characteristics of youths admitted to compulsory institutional care in Sweden, compared their overall and adulthood outcomes with matched youths from the general population and compulsory social care, and examined the timing of adverse outcomes following discharge. The Swedish Longitudinal Compulsory Care Study (SLCCS) includes all youths admitted to compulsory institutional care (CIC) in Sweden between 2000 and 2020 (n = 14,677), matched to youths from the general population (14,349 pairs) and compulsory social care (8,879 pairs). Analyses were stratified by sex and included descriptive statistics, fixed-effects regression, Cox proportional hazards models, and Kaplan–Meier analyses. Criminal behavior and substance use were the most common reasons for placement. The CIC group experienced poorer outcomes than both comparison groups overall and in adulthood. Compared with matched women from the general population, adjusted hazards of substance use disorder (HR = 7.83, 95% CI 6.07–10.10) and all-cause mortality (HR = 8.42, 95% CI 3.01–23.54) were nearly eightfold higher among women admitted to compulsory institutional care. Corresponding hazards among men were fivefold higher for substance use disorder (HR = 5.11, 95% CI 4.26–6.12) and threefold higher for all-cause mortality (HR = 3.11, 95% CI 2.02–4.77). Kaplan–Meier analyses indicated that mental health and substance use diagnoses were concentrated within the first five years following discharge. Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care face an elevated risk of adverse outcomes extending into adulthood, and the first five years following discharge may represent an important period for aftercare and support.

articles.title: Empirical Reasoning About FOI Request Delays in the European Union
articles.authors: Jukka Ruohonen
articles.abstract: Freedom of information (FOI) is a human right and an important concept for the transparency and accountability of governments and public administrations. It is also essential for democracy. Despite a long research lineage on FOI laws and their use by citizens, existing empirical knowledge is still limited regarding the inner workings of FOI requests. This limitation applies particularly to the European Union (EU) and the documents possessed by its various institutions. To help at addressing this limitation, the paper presents a few empirical observations about FOI requests in the EU context. By using a dataset containing 500 requests made between 2022 and early 2023, the insight presented cover the EU institutions targeted, the requesters making FOI requests, and particularly the bureaucratic delays in handling of FOI requests. According to results based on a regression analysis, the bureaucratic delays vary according to both the EU institutions and the individual requesters.

articles.title: Maternal Solidarity: Unconditional Cash Prescriptions and a Moral Economy of Motherhood in Flint, Michigan
articles.authors: Caroline Doenmez; Jenny LaChance; Mallory Goldsworthy; Mona Hanna
articles.abstract: How do mothers make meaning out of the experience of being “prescribed” no-strings-attached cash to improve their family’s health and life chances? This paper explores the impact of Rx Kids, the first community-wide cash transfer program for mothers and newborns in the United States. Launched in Flint, Michigan, in January 2024, the program seeks to “prescribe away” child poverty by providing cash transfers to mothers during and after their pregnancies. The program design stands apart from other cash transfer programs due to its universal and unconditional features: it ensures that all pregnant mothers in a participating community can receive the cash and does not impose any spending restrictions or reporting requirements on them. This paper is interested in Rx Kids’ cultural impact as ascertained through mothers’ narratives of their involvement with the program. Drawing on 46 interviews conducted with mothers in Flint, we ask: What did the unconditionality and universality of the program mean to them? Through their narratives, we identify how the transfer of monetary resources to the mothers elicited profound moral considerations. As mothers moved through the process of encountering, applying to, participating in, and advocating for the program, they narrated grappling continuously with the question of maternal worth and worthiness. Through their affective experiences of disbelief, astonishment, mistrust, anxiety, gratitude, and compassion for other mothers, we argue that the participants give voice to a moral economy of motherhood in Flint, circulating and contesting cultural values regarding reproductive labor and maternal worth. Ultimately, we show how through participating in the program, the mothers were actualized as both the recipients and providers of what we term “maternal solidarity,” an unconditional mode of care premised on a shared understanding of the pronounced and ubiquitous challenges of contemporary motherhood.

articles.title: Responsibility to Prepare: From Individual Security to Collective Resilience
articles.authors: Paulus Damgaard; Jonas Toubøl; Lærke Høgenhaven
articles.abstract: In the context of heightened geopolitical tensions, European societies increasingly frame private crisis preparedness as integral to societal resilience. Once viewed as antisocial survivalists, preppers now offer insight into civil society’s role in prepar-edness. Drawing on a netnographic study of one of Denmark’s largest Facebook prepper groups (2015-2024), this article examines how the group members per-ceive responsibility for crisis preparedness across four periods: before COVID-19, during the pandemic, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and following the Danish government’s 2024 appeal for household preparedness. Findings reveal a dominant individualistic framing in stable times, but a shift towards collective understandings of responsibility following official communication during crises. The article con-tributes to sociological research on crisis preparedness by demonstrating how per-ceptions of crisis contexts and state communication shape preppers’ responsibility frames, challenging static portrayals of preppers as antisocial and highlighting how individualised practices of preparedness can evolve into collective orientations that complement state capacity.

articles.title: Localized Multimodal Interfaces in English-Default Mobile Apps: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis of Non-Native Users' Perception
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
The purpose of this research project is to examine how English-default and localized multimodal mobile interfaces affect user perception across six constructs: comprehension, cognitive load, motivation, inclusivity, tonal reception, and credibility. Onboarding and upgrade screens from three globally used applications (Duolingo, Spotify, and Notion) were analyzed as experienced by Italian-locale users whose devices were set to Italian, but whose interfaces remained predominantly in English. 
A mixed-methods design was used, combining qualitative multimodal discourse analysis of 24 application screenshots with quantitative descriptive statistics from a Likert-scale perception survey (n = 56). The multimodal analysis utilized a visual grammar framework, whereas the survey constructs were based on cognitive load theory, Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and digital credibility research. 
Results show moderately positive comprehension and tonal reception across all three applications, largely supported by visual elements such as mascots, icons, and color-coded calls to action. Inclusivity scored lowest overall. Italian L1 participants reported higher perceived effort and lower credibility than non-Italian participants, with the sharpest differences observed in upgrade flows.
The findings are examined in the context of linguistic justice, English as a lingua franca, and discursive legitimation. The findings support biphasic localization strategies and suggest avenues for future research employing behavioural metrics and expanded participant samples.
Keywords: multimodal discourse analysis, localization, English-default interfaces, cognitive load, linguistic justice, user experience, mobile applications

articles.title: What the Balkan Barometer Can and Cannot Rank: A Measurement Audit of the Western Balkans' Flagship Survey
articles.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles.abstract: The Balkan Barometer, annual since 2015 with roughly 1,000 face-to-face interviews in each of six Western Balkan economies, is cited across the region as what its citizens think. We evaluate it as a measuring instrument from the Regional Cooperation Council's own released microdata for 2023 to 2025, within a total survey error frame. The published percentages reproduce from the microdata (440 of 444 cells within one point). Of the fifteen pairwise economy differences on each of thirty 2025 headline items, 71 percent are resolvable at a design effect of 2.0, but only 40 percent of adjacent-rank pairs are: six points is the least difference at which two economies of 1,000 can be told apart. The WB6 figure is an unweighted mean of six economies whose populations differ tenfold; under population weights it moves by 6 to 12 points on the most-quoted items, including EU membership (64 versus 58 percent in 2025). Of twenty-three headline series present in all three editions, four are comparable throughout; between 2024 and 2025 the changed series moved by 14 points on average against 6 for the stable ones. The 2025 institutional battery is scalar invariant once two cells are freed, police in Kosovo* and courts in North Macedonia; with them freed, Kosovo*'s raw-score lead disappears and the top three economies cannot be separated. The two published editions score 16 of 32 on a documentation checklist built from what the ESS, the Eurobarometer and the AAPOR Transparency Initiative publish routinely; precision, comparability and limitations score zero. We report two database errors and a file anomaly for correction, and close with the four things a technical report would need to contain.

articles.title: Blaming Across the Aisle: Political Contrasting and Blame Attribution in the Danish Parliament
articles.authors: Markus Lundsfryd Jensen; Rune Egeskov Trust; Kenneth C. Enevoldsen; Sara Kolding
articles.abstract: Political discourse is widely perceived to be growing more hostile, yet robust evidence remains scarce. This study examines blame attribution in the Danish Parliament from 1997 to 2026, combining a purpose-built classifier, BlameBERT (F1: 0.80), with multilevel statistical modeling. The classifier is constructed using an annotation-efficient pipeline for blame attribution in low-to-mid resource languages. The results reveal a banana-shaped trajectory, with blame declining until around 2016 before entering a significant and sustained increase in recent years (2019-2026). Government status consistently influenced blame attribution - an effect we term political contrasting - with opposition parties blaming substantially more than governing parties. This effect was moderated by ideology: The blame-dampening effect of governing was less pronounced among right-wing parties, and ideological extremity amplified blame more strongly on the right. In recent years, the interaction between political wing and ideological extremity intensified, suggesting an ideological hardening of the blame rhetoric concentrated on the right of the political spectrum. Taken together, these patterns suggest that the perceived rise in harsh political language reflects not merely a general rhetorical drift, but an ideologically asymmetric hardening of political discourse. A sensitivity analysis showed that the conclusions were robust to varying classification thresholds.

articles.title: Organising the Social Layer: How Organisational Paradoxes Shape Engagement in Cryptocurrency Communities
articles.authors: Annika Aebli; Fabienne Silberstein-Bamford; Joshua Silberstein Bamford
articles.abstract: Cryptocurrencies (crypto) and their underlying blockchain technologies are designed around the promise of collective organising without reliance on centralised authority, intermediaries, and hierarchical coordination. Yet sustaining collective participation in decentralised networks without conventional forms of coordination remains an organisational challenge. This study demonstrates that keeping participants engaged in crypto communities depends on continuous work within crypto’s social layer. Drawing on the organisational paradox lens and 26 semi-structured interviews with developers, team members, and regular users across four crypto communities, we show that sustained engagement depends on balancing organisational paradoxes rooted in communication, decision-making, and community development: technical discourse versus social-media-style interaction, decentralised participation versus centralised guidance, and scaling versus a sense of authentic community. Our findings suggest that continually balancing, rather than resolving these tensions is essential for engagement and community cohesion. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of decentralised organising by showing how collective participation can be maintained in organisational arrangements that seek to reduce reliance on conventional centralised structures. More broadly, we show that decentralisation does not eliminate the need for organising but relocates much of this work to the social layer of interaction, coordination, and community building, where contradictory demands must be continually negotiated to keep participation workable and sustainable.

articles.title: Still Secularizing: Cohort Replacement, Rebound, Overreporting, and Gender Convergence in a Pooled Analysis of Eight National Surveys
articles.authors: David Eagle; Joshua Gaghan
articles.abstract: Recent reports claim young men in the United States are becoming more religious. This would signal an end to the longstanding pattern of cohort-driven declines in religiosity. Pooling young-adult trends within eight national surveys measuring affiliation, attendance, salience, prayer, and biblical literalism, we find no measure shows a credible increase among young men, and the youngest cohort is no more religious than its predecessor was at the same age. The gender gap is narrowing because women are secularizing faster, not because men are returning, which likely reflects gender-based ideological realignment. Religiosity has rebounded from its pandemic trough, but not credibly past pre-pandemic levels, and the gap between self-reported attendance and time-use diaries has widened. Intense religious identity is also declining across cohorts. Variability between surveys, a post-pandemic rebound, and growing measurement drift are all confounding patterns of religious change. Cutting through the noise, cohort replacement continues to organize American religion.

articles.title: Agreeing in Principle, Disagreeing on Policy: How Beliefs About the Gender Pay Gap Shape Fairness Concerns and Policy Preferences
articles.authors: Fabian Kalleitner; Jule Adriaans; Ole Brüggemann; Cristóbal Moya; Sandra Bohmann
articles.abstract: Willingness to reduce gender inequalities partly depends on whether people are aware of them and consider them unfair. Extending scholarship centered on inequality misperceptions, we focus on beliefs about the sources of the gender pay gap (GPG), experimentally varying people's ability to attribute pay disparities to women's choices. Preregistered survey experiments in the U.S. and Germany show that information about larger (vs. smaller) and within-job (vs. overall) GPGs independently increases awareness, raises perceived unfairness, and translates into general support for government action. Initially less-supportive groups (conservatives, men) showed some of the largest increases in general support. Yet, updated beliefs did not increase support for specific policies, such as pay transparency laws or gender quotas. These findings suggest that information campaigns can affect beliefs about GPG's size and sources, but even perceiving GPGs as unfair does not bridge the gap between abstract commitment to gender equality and concrete policy support.

articles.title: Algorithms of Fabrication: Generative AI and the Reshaping of Democratic Resilience and Regime Stability
articles.authors: Guy Schleffer
articles.abstract:
The 2024 election cycle marked a strategic turning point in digital influence. While previous interference relied on algorithmic distribution, Generative AI (GenAI) has introduced a paradigm of automated fabrication, fundamentally reshaping the mechanics of political stability. This article examines GenAI as a strategic amplifier whose impact is filtered through the institutional structures of four distinct regime types.
In Strong Democracies, synthetic content accelerates epistemic erosion, dissolving the shared factual reality necessary for deliberation. In Weak Democracies, it fuels precision radicalization, enabling populist actors to bypass institutional gatekeepers and dismantle oversight from within. Conversely, Strong Autocracies co-opt GenAI for digital fortification and automated narrative control, while Weak Autocracies face synthetic volatility, where low-cost deepfakes bypass porous censorship, triggering rapid destabilization. The article concludes by proposing a four-pillar policy framework including standardized content provenance, liability reform, strategic hardware controls, and transnational enforcement to restore information integrity in an increasingly deregulated global environment.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: Heed the warning: how NATO can find and fill the gaps in its warning systems
articles.authors: Nikki Ikani
articles.abstract: Intelligence warning failures are too often viewed in binary: Either intelligence succeeded or it failed. In reality, often only segments of the warning chain collapse while others operate well. This Outlook paper treats warning success as a spectrum rather than as a pass/fail test in a new framework for warning performance. It illustrates the use through three recent case studies: the fall of Kabul (2021), Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (2022) and the Niger coup (2023). The decisive shortfall across all three cases was the failure to reconcile divergent NATO member state views into an operational consensus within NATO. There are practical solutions for integrating NATO capabilities to institutionalize rapid after-action reviews, conduct periodic divergence drill exercises, prepare contingency packages and further embed red team analyses.

articles.title: Detecting Inequality in Noisy Communication: Promises and Pitfalls of Large Language Models
articles.authors: Susanne Reinhardt; Jonathan J.B. Mijs; David Schieferdecker; Michael Vaughan
articles.abstract: How inequality is communicated shapes how it is explained, understood, and legitimated or contested. Yet studying these communicative processes at scale is challenging because inequality is multidimensional, often expressed implicitly and relationally, and context dependent. We argue that large language models (LLMs) shift, but do not eliminate, these methodological challenges. We trace the development from manual content analysis to rule-based computational approaches and machine learning to LLMs and assess how these methods combine conceptual alignment, semantic sensitivity, contextual sensitivity, and scalability. LLMs help relax some longstanding trade-offs between semantic sensitivity to meaning and scalability, thus promising more comprehensive analyses of established research questions and opening possibilities for comparative research across contexts. Yet untapping their full potential for research on inequality communication depends on addressing problems concerning conceptual validity, representation, comparative measurement, and substantive inference. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for rigorous LLM-based inequality communication research.

articles.title: L’IA dans les élections municipales 2026 : Des usages qui appellent un regard nuancé
articles.authors: Antoine Marie
articles.abstract:
The municipal elections of March 15 and 22, 2026 constitute the first
French local election in which generative artificial intelligence has
massively entered campaign practices. This research brief offers a
balanced analysis of documented uses, distinguishing legitimate
applications (poster generation, programmatic chatbots, content
synthesis) from confirmed abuses (defamatory deepfakes, misleading
images, astroturfing). While these new technological capabilities raise
legitimate concerns for the integrity of democratic debate, we argue that
their impact must be put in perspective in light of the literature on the
limited effects of mass political communication and the actual
determinants of disinformation consumption. Rather than a
catastrophism that risks fueling generalized distrust, we advocate for an
approach grounded in media literacy and the strengthening of
professional journalism.

articles.title: A New Era of Political Socialization? The Interplay Between Political Social Media Exposure, Conspiracy Thinking, and Political Distrust Among Dutch Younger vs. Older Generations
articles.authors: Tamar Montagne; Anouk Smeekes
articles.abstract: In recent years, populist radical-right parties (PRRP) have gained substantial electoral support in European countries, especially among younger voters. However, few studies have focused on the generational divide in PRRP voting behavior and the factors that explain why current younger generations are more likely to vote for PRRP. The current study addresses this research gap by examining whether generational differences in PRRP voting can be explained by variations in political social media exposure (PSME) and its indirect pathways through conspiracy thinking and political distrust, while accounting for the moderating role of anti-immigrant attitudes. Drawing on insights from developmental psychology, political psychology, and political science, we developed an interdisciplinary framework. We tested our expectations in the context of the Netherlands using data from the Dutch Parliamentary Election Study 2023, drawing on a sample of Dutch eligible voters. Results showed that current younger generations (Generations Y and Z) were more likely to vote for PRRP compared to older generations, partly explained by their higher PSME and subsequently, stronger conspiracy thinking and political distrust. Results further showed that the effect of conspiracy thinking on PRRP voting was particularly pronounced for respondents with low levels of anti-immigrant attitudes.

articles.title: Health-Related AI Information Seeking, Anxiety, and Professional Mental Health Service Use Among U.S. College Students
articles.authors: Tania Akter
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are becoming more widely used in students’ daily lives, yet little is known about how anxiety relates to college students’ use of generative AI for health-related information seeking. This exploratory study examined associations between anxiety, health-related generative AI information seeking, and professional mental health service use among U.S. college students. Survey-weighted logistic regression models were used to assess these associations. Results showed that higher anxiety scores were associated with greater odds of reporting health-related AI use. Among students who reported health-related AI use, higher anxiety was also associated with greater odds of professional mental health service use. Findings suggest that health-related generative AI use is an emerging behavior modestly associated with anxiety and may coexist with professional mental health help-seeking among college students.

articles.title: What is edtech for? A cross-national popularity index of educational apps
articles.authors: Lulu Shi; Basak Bozkurt
articles.abstract: Digitalisation in education is so far described through broad indicators such as market growth, venture capital investment, infrastructure provision, or device availability in schools and homes. While useful, these measures reveal little about for what purposes digital technologies are used in education, and how these purposes vary across national contexts and time. This article addresses these gaps by developing an education app popularity index based on daily top-200 education app rankings across twelve countries between 2017 and 2023: Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Norway, Poland, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Drawing on app metadata, education apps are categorised according to the services and functions they offer to understand for what purpose they serve. The ranking is then aggregated to analyse category prominence over time and across countries to understand popularity of education apps by category. The study makes three contributions. First, it provides a granular account of what educational apps offer, showing that the educational app landscape is not dominated by a single type of service but consists of a heterogeneous mixture of tutoring tools, management platforms, parent-facing communication apps and a range of apps supporting infomal learning. Second, it shows the popularity of different types of digital education services and how and their popularity shift over time. Third, it shows that these patterns vary across country contexts. Differences across countries point to that edtech usage is not only driven by individual preferences but by distinct institutional arrangements and cultures. Lastly, this study also advances a methodological approach for understanding the realities of edtech deployment by using Google Play Store data, the world’s largest app market in terms of content volume.

articles.title: The Vanishing Mutual Citation
articles.authors: Maayan Matsliah
articles.abstract: Mutual citation – a pair of publications that cite each other – provides a simple measure of reciprocation linkage within scientific literature. Such pairs arise because papers are not published in strict sequence: authors often cite each other's preprints and working papers, add citations during revision, and sometimes publish related papers together. Using OpenAlex citation data from 1975 to 2023, we ask two questions: how has the rate at which papers reciprocate citations changed over five decades, and are interdisciplinary papers reciprocated less often than non-interdisciplinary papers? Contrary to both expectations, reciprocation declined sharply rather than rising with improved discoverability of scholarly work, and interdisciplinary papers did not reciprocate less than non-interdisciplinary papers. Mean mutual citations per paper fell by ~88% and the pooled mutual-citation rate fell by ~95% between 1975 and 2023. Papers citing three or more fields (interdisciplinary) exceeded the reciprocation rates of papers citing one or two fields (non-interdisciplinary) across a central band of six reference-count deciles (10-46 references, accounting for approximately 58% of the corpus), reciprocating up to 17% more. The two groups converged at 47-64 references (a 0.6% gap, non-interdisciplinary papers slightly ahead), and non-interdisciplinary papers reciprocated up to 28% more at the shortest and longest reference lists (3-9 and 65-5,000 references).

articles.title: Press freedom shapes the link between mainstream and social media use for news and climate change understanding: evidence from 30 countries
articles.authors: Laurent Cordonier; Didier Witkowski; Florian Cafiero
articles.abstract: A recent meta-analysis examining the relationship between individuals’ information behaviour and their views about climate change found that, on average, using social media and other user-generated online sources was more strongly associated with science-consistent climate beliefs than using mainstream media. The present study, however, investigates whether these associations vary across countries depending on the level of press freedom, as mainstream journalism is better able to foreground scientific expertise and challenge misleading climate claims when operating freely, whereas social media may provide a partial alternative to constrained domestic mainstream coverage. Accordingly, mainstream media use was hypothesised to be more positively associated with science-consistent climate beliefs and knowledge in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, while the opposite pattern was expected for social media use for news. The analysis draws on a survey of 23,500 respondents in 30 countries. Within each country, survey-weighted models estimated associations between mainstream and social media use for news and four outcomes: belief in the existence of climate change, belief in its anthropogenic nature, belief in its negative consequences, and climate change knowledge, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Overall, mainstream media use was more often positively associated with science-consistent beliefs and knowledge than social media use. Cross-national analyses then tested whether these country-specific associations varied with press freedom, controlling for socioeconomic development. For each outcome, the association with mainstream media use was more positive in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, whereas the association with social media use for news showed the opposite cross-national pattern. These findings suggest that mainstream media generally contribute more to public understanding of climate change than social media, especially where press freedom is greater, while social media may play a partial compensatory role where domestic journalism is constrained.

articles.title: Researcher well-being as a leading indicator in research-funding governance: A system dynamics exploration of top-down versus bottom-up allocation
articles.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Satoshi Sano
articles.abstract: Governments face a recurring dilemma in dividing public research funding between top-down, competitive, mission-oriented programmes and bottom-up, investigator-led institutional grants. This research note presents an exploratory system dynamics model that endogenizes researcher motivation, conceived following self-determination theory as a slow-moving stock of psychological capital, within the feedback structure linking funding allocation, research outputs, and societal returns. Simulation experiments across three policy scenarios reveal a consistent time-asymmetric pattern. First, accelerating the shift toward competitive funding produces an earlier but lower peak in societal returns, followed by sustained decline. Second, shifting toward bottom-up funding restores motivation but opens a transition valley in returns whose depth grows with transition speed. Third, delayed corrective reallocation exhibits hysteresis: once motivation is depleted, even aggressive reallocation requires roughly two decades before returns recover. One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis indicates that these qualitative patterns persist across the tested parameter ranges, while the level of long-run returns proves highly sensitive to the weight placed on discretionary research time, around which the baseline system undergoes a regime shift. The model implies that researcher well-being functions as a leading indicator of research-system health, preceding declines in publication-based lagging indicators. We derive three testable propositions and outline an agenda for empirical calibration, beginning with a national baseline survey of researchers being launched in Japan. For funding governance, the results imply that monitoring leading indicators and pacing allocation transitions matter as much as choosing the allocation ratio itself.

articles.title: ‘Intersectionality in the Mind’: Applying an Intersectional Lens to the Study of Lay Perceptions of Inequality
articles.authors: Margherita Cusmano
articles.abstract: Research on lay perceptions of inequality has typically examined economic, gender, and racial inequalities separately and treated social positions additively. Using migrants as a case study, this study employs an intersectional lens to investigate perceptions of inequality. Drawing on interviews and group discussions with 47 participants, the analysis shows, first, that individuals framed different inequalities as interdependent, showcasing what I term ‘intersectionality in the mind’. Second, their intersectional social positions informed how they understood broader patterns of inequality. These findings demonstrate the value of intersectional approaches in analysing the complexity of lay perceptions of inequality. This study points toward methodological and conceptual developments that can better capture both how people cognitively link inequalities and how intersecting social positions inform these perceptions.

articles.title: Systematic Evaluation of Nation-State Propaganda in LLM Outputs
articles.authors: Kevin T. Greene; Jacob N Shapiro
articles.abstract: The rapid growth and usability of AI is creating new risks to information quality, including the possibility that chatbot responses spread propaganda from state-backed influence campaigns. There is little systematic evidence regarding how frequently LLMs spread such narratives when responding to user queries. Previous attempts to assess these risks rely on small numbers of evaluation questions, use opaque query construction procedures, and fail to account for key sources of uncertainty in model responses. We address these gaps with an automated, reproducible pipeline that samples documented state-backed propaganda and news items, programmatically generates evaluation questions, and audits LLM-generated responses. We evaluate whether five prominent models: (1) reproduce arguments aligned with documented Kremlin propaganda narratives; (2) present the Kremlin perspective on events without providing corrective context; and (3) cite known propaganda outlets. We find substantially lower rates of propaganda-aligned responses and propaganda-source citation than prior small-sample work would suggest. These risks are particularly rare for questions resembling ordinary information searches about Ukraine. Our approach enables systematic comparisons across models and issue areas, supports ongoing monitoring, and could be extended to many other hotly-debated topics.

articles.title: Reassessing the Role of Offline Teachers in the Era of Online Learning: In the context of India’s National Education Policy 2020
articles.authors: Rakesh Kumar Pandey; Soniya
articles.abstract: India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisages a substantial expansion of higher education and identifies online education as an important instrument for increasing access. The assumption that online learning can simultaneously expand educational access and reduce instructional costs, however, requires closer examination, particularly when online courses are incorporated into regular undergraduate and postgraduate programmes. This paper examines whether such integration can sustain the completion rates and learning outcomes normally expected from regular classroom-based education. Drawing on reported completion-to-registration data from selected online education providers, a critical review of the literature on learner engagement and learning outcomes, and a conceptual analysis of different pedagogical approaches, the study examines the relationship between learner maturity, self-directed learning, teacher interaction, and instructional requirements. The analysis suggests that large-scale access to online content does not necessarily translate into comparable levels of course completion. It further argues that pedagogical approaches designed to enhance engagement—including blended learning, active learning, problem-based learning, and personalised instruction—require sustained interaction with teachers, mentors, or facilitators. The paper therefore questions the assumption that online education will necessarily reduce instructional requirements. It proposes a hybrid pedagogical model in which online learning complements rather than replaces classroom teaching for young learners, supported by structured facilitation and mentorship to sustain completion rates and learning outcomes. Despite their low completion rates, fully online courses may be particularly appropriate for mature, self-directed lifelong learners seeking flexible opportunities for continuous skill and knowledge development.

articles.title: Delisting and dispersal: author communities before and after removal from Scopus
articles.authors: Marek Deja
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Delisting removes a journal from an index but not its authors. This study asks whether cohorts disperse or share destinations and whether concentrated inflow is associated with receiving journals' subsequent delisting.

Design/methodology/approach: The analysis reconstructs interval-valued delisting dates from successive Scopus lists, assigns delisted event clocks to matched cohorts, and compares destination overlap with margin-preserving, opportunity-structured, and matched-observed benchmarks. A six-month-landmark discrete-time hazard model handles right censoring and competing exits.

Findings: Delisted-journal output averaged 66.7% below the post-event reference path. For 121 cohorts, median observed-to-expected overlap was 2.40 under the opportunity-structured benchmark. Across 55 matched sets, delisted cohorts overlapped 10.6 percentage points less than references (95% CI [-0.14, -0.07]), a gap that predated delisting and was smaller but present on venues new to the author. An exploratory hazard analysis showed a positive in-sample association between concentrated inflow and receiving journals' subsequent delisting, but extensive censoring and short follow-up preclude a stable magnitude claim.

Research limitations: Delisting is non-random; estimates are descriptive contrasts, benchmark deviations, and conditional in-sample associations.

Practical implications: Synthetic benchmarks establish residual cohort structure; matched observed cohorts test whether it is event-specific.

Originality/value: The study provides a two-stage design for event-specific concentration claims. Pairing a constrained randomisation with matched observed cohorts reversed the substantive conclusion.

articles_hidden.title: MAGA Republicans as  “Particularistic Authoritarians” on the Welfare State:  Parallels with the European Populist Right
articles_hidden.authors: Jake Haselswerdt; Hang Qi; Suhyun Cho
articles_hidden.abstract: Has MAGA remade the Republican politics of the welfare state? While Republican voters have traditionally favored retrenchment, the so-called “populism” of the MAGA movement suggests that the social policy preferences of right-leaning Americans are due for reexamination. Drawing from the “particularistic authoritarian model” of European populist radical-right voters, we expect MAGA Republicans to favor benefits for deserving groups, stronger “workfare” policies, less social investment, and more restrictive deservingness criteria. We test these expectations using a 1,000-respondent module of the 2025 Cooperative Election Study. Factor analysis and regressions show that MAGA Republicans are substantially more supportive than non-MAGA Republicans of policies benefiting seniors and express levels of support comparable to those of Democrats and other respondents. MAGA Republicans also show somewhat stronger endorsement of restrictive deservingness criteria than other Republicans, while differences between the two Republican groups are less pronounced for social investment. Overall, the results indicate that MAGA Republicans do not simply favor either welfare state expansion or retrenchment. Instead, they distinguish among forms of social protection according to their beneficiaries and perceived deservingness.

articles_hidden.title: Are the children of homeowners increasingly advantaged? Trends in relative and absolute mobility of homeownership in Europe
articles_hidden.authors: Selçuk Bedük; Enrico Benassi; Philipp M. Lersch
articles_hidden.abstract: Homeownership is declining among younger generations across Europe. A common assumption is that this decline has been increasingly stratified by parental homeownership, due to rising house prices and the growing importance of parental financial support. We show that this assumption does not hold for the average European (and for most countries). Using data from EU-SILC 2011 and 2019 covering 24 European countries, we examine trends in relative and absolute mobility of homeownership for birth cohorts 1951 to 1984. On average, relative mobility remained largely stable across cohorts, while absolute mobility increased. The apparent stability of relative mobility masks a deeper structural cohort shift: downward mobility increased from 14 per cent to 38 per cent, while upward mobility declined from 23 per cent to 8 per cent between cohorts born in the early 1950s and early 1980s. Therefore, homeownership has declined significantly for both children of homeowners and renters. We also compare absolute and relative mobility trends across countries and show that they often diverge for two reasons. First, a mechanical effect of the origin distribution: in countries with widespread parental homeownership, relative mobility largely reflects changes in upward mobility. Second, the source of mobility: using two novel counterfactual simulations, we show that observed absolute mobility changes mainly stem from structural shifts in homeownership chances, rather than strengthening parent-child associations.

articles_hidden.title: The Relationship between China's One-Child Policy and Female Empowerment
articles_hidden.authors: Wendi Wang; Qing Guan; Natalie Nitsche
articles_hidden.abstract: Vanessa Fong (2002) theorised that China's One-Child Policy (OCP; 1979–2016) enhanced female empowerment by removing competition from sons and allowing daughters to obtain resources traditionally reserved for sons. However, no systematic review has comprehensively assessed the available evidence on this issue. Drawing on Fong’s framework, we examined the relationship between the OCP and female empowerment across seven subfields: family investment and parental support, education, employment and career development, gender attitudes and norms, intergenerational relationships, reproductive rights and autonomy, and other social dynamics. We searched six scientific databases, yielding 1265 sources and, after applying exclusion criteria, analyzed 32 studies published between 2002 and 2024. The majority (21 of 32) report a positive relationship between the OCP and female empowerment. Resource concentration driven by reduced sibling size emerges as a central mechanism, benefiting only-daughters in family investment, education, and career development. In contrast, impacts on mothers are more mixed; while the OCP reduced childbirth burdens and enhanced life autonomy, it also violated reproductive rights and imposed disproportionate contraceptive burdens on women. Moreover, it emerges the OCP's empowering effects were contingent on external conditions, such as local educational and economic resources or place of residence. We point out various research gaps in the existing literature, amongst other the consistent failure to distinguish the OCP’s effects from concurrent socio-economic transformations. Nonetheless, the evidence suggests that the OCP, together with broader social changes, has shaped women's lives and promoted female empowerment, although its impacts were neither uniform nor inherent, but rather shaped by contextual factors.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Students’ Attention Boundaries in GAI-Assisted Learning: Development and Validation of the GAI-Mediated Learning Boundary Scale and Latent Profile Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: XI ZHAN; Yuxiang Shi; Peiyun He
articles_hidden.abstract: The Generative AI (GAI) is reshaping the temporal and spatial organization of college learning and the perceived boundary crossing between teacher-assigned tasks and self-directed learning. This study developed and validated a scale to assess college students’ attention boundary management in GAI-mediated learning. Analyzing data from 1904 students at 3 colleges in China, the study established a five-dimensional structure: Flexibility, Fragmentation, Immersion, Positive Spillover, and Negative Spillover. Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis confirmed the scale’s psychometric properties. A Latent Profile Analysis identified four distinct student profiles, Protective, Strained, Overextended, and Engaged Permeability Management. Supplementary heterogeneity analyses examined differences across the four profiles by gender, grade level, university, purposes and duration of AI use, and other learning-related characteristics. Based on these, this study proposed profile-specific recommendations. The study provides a validated instrument for assessing students’ attention boundaries in GAI-mediated learning, identifies heterogeneous student profiles, and offers differentiated practical implications.

articles_hidden.title: Recordable participation and the construction of student engagement in UK higher education
articles_hidden.authors: Xinqi Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Student engagement is widely invoked as evidence of educational quality, yet its meanings are contested. This article examines how the concept is constructed and mobilised in UK higher education research, policy and institutional documentation. Drawing on Bacchi’s problematisation approach and Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis, it analyses a purposive corpus of 36 texts: 23 conceptual and research texts, two policy documents and 11 institutional documents from three West Midlands universities. Iterative close reading identifies three connected patterns. Multidimensional accounts of engagement are narrowed into visible proxies; evaluative infrastructures privilege meanings that can be documented and compared; and these constructions redistribute responsibility in ways that obscure unequal conditions of participation. Worked coding examples show how support, attendance, digital traces and regular logging become linked in institutional procedures. The article argues that recordable participation acquires authority because it can serve as evidence of both student conduct and institutional quality. This does not eliminate relational or participatory meanings, but places them at a disadvantage within systems organised around demonstrable performance. The contribution is to explain how the demand for evidence connects conceptual narrowing to unequal recognition, and why institutions should distinguish the visibility of participation from the conditions that make participation possible.

articles_hidden.title: From Governance to Government? The European Commission and the three faces of politicisation
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Nicoli; Lorenzo Lombardi
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on the politicisation of the European Union has concentrated on reactive, bottom-up contestation of existing EU action. This article argues that such an understanding is incomplete because it conflates politicisation of issues with politicisation of institutions. We distinguish three faces of politicisation. Reactive politicisation refers to the public contestation of existing EU competences. Proactive politicisation occurs when supranational actors claim a political mandate in order to justify wider discretion. Induced politicisation emerges when intergovernmental conflict over already politicized state functions creates a vacuum that the Commission can try to fill, thereby inheriting the political character of the function itself. The empirical sections focus on induced politicisation. They reconstruct three episodes: Jean-Claude Juncker's attempt to use EMU deadlock to place the Commission at the centre of euro-area reform; the failed institutionalisation of an EU Finance Minister, a euro-area fiscal capacity, and a more political treasury function; and Ursula von der Leyen's attempts to centralise foreign-policy initiative during successive geopolitical crises. The argument is that politicisation does not only constrain supranational action. Under specific institutional conditions it can also widen supranational authority by transforming the Commission from guardian of the Treaties into a proto-governmental executive.

articles_hidden.title: Sectoral Credit Reallocation and Consumer Credit Expansion: A Difference-in-Differences and Decomposition Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Gudzenko Vladislav
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines sectoral bank-credit reallocation in Kyrgyzstan by combining a difference in differences (DiD) comparison around 2015 with a detailed accounting analysis for 2019–2025. The research question is how conclusions about reallocation depend on the comparison period, portfolio denominator and distinction between shares and real balances. Four focal lending categories are compared with a residual category in a historical series extended through 2025. The full-portfolio DiD contrast is +1.28 percentage points for 2010–2025, but −0.17 points when the window begins in 2012; the group gap already changes substantially before 2015. In the recent period, consumer loans rise from 11.8% to 33.6% of bank credit and account for 42.5% of the nominal increase in the outstanding portfolio. CPI-deflated non-consumer credit grows by 49.3%. Agriculture loses portfolio share while its real balance grows by 12.3%; industry and construction experience real declines of 34.7% and 17.5%. A symmetric decomposition separates the changing consumer-credit mix from redistribution within non-consumer lending. The integrated findings show why positive period-average sectoral contrasts can coexist with recent share losses and uneven real growth. DiD remains descriptive, and the decomposition is an accounting identity. Neither identifies the effect of accession or consumer-credit crowding out. Independent verification of the historical inputs remains incomplete.

articles_hidden.title: Analisis Value Chain Upgrading Komoditas Kakao melalui Strategi Branding dan Diferensiasi Produk di Sabang
articles_hidden.authors: Daudy Sukma; Sofia Keumalasari; Azlina; Zahriatul Aini; Aulia Hafizah Nazwa
articles_hidden.abstract:
Kakao Sabang memiliki potensi terroir — rasa dan aroma khas — namun
produksi dan luas lahan menurun dalam lima tahun terakhir, dengan mayoritas
biji masih dijual non-fermentasi bernilai rendah. Penelitian kualitatif ini
memetakan rantai nilai (value chain analysis atau VCA) dan mengidentifikasi peluang peningkatan nilai (value chain upgrading atau VCU) kakao Sabang
melalui wawancara mendalam terhadap petani, pengumpul, UMKM pengolah,
dan Dinas Pertanian Kota Sabang, dilengkapi triangulasi sumber. Hasil
menunjukkan premi harga fermentasi mencapai 200 persen, namun hanya
terealisasi pada jalur petani–UMKM, belum pada jalur pengumpul umum.
Ditemukan pola functional upgrading organik berupa UMKM yang berperan
sebagai pengumpul mutu. Penelitian ini merumuskan strategi branding berbasis
marketing mix 7-P dengan perspektif consumer agency, merekomendasikan
perluasan insentif fermentasi dan formalisasi Indikasi Geografis sebagai
instrumen branding jangka panjang.

articles_hidden.title: Youth physical activity in transitioning subsistence societies varies by biological maturity and market integration
articles_hidden.authors: Lee Gettler; Vidrige Kandza; Jessica K. Hlay; Haneul Jang; Rahul C. Oka; Francy Kiabiya Ntamboudila; Derlan Brenez Bihoundou Mouketou; Chelvin Destin Siassia Vindou; Evrahd Ngalekandza; Brel Koubemba
