articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Physical activity patterns across childhood and adolescence help shape long-term health and contribute to the allocation of limited resources among growth, maintenance, and reproduction during maturation. The vast majority of data on youth physical activity comes from post/industrial societies. We know relatively little about youth physical activity in smaller-scale subsistence contexts where youth routinely contribute to production and household tasks under energetically demanding conditions. Methods: Using wearable technology, we measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and sedentary behavior among BaYaka forager and Bantu fisher-farmer youth (N=206; obs. days=798) in the Congo Basin. These communities live under energetically-demanding conditions and varying degrees of early market integration. Results: Youth were highly physically active, averaging 4.07 hours of daily MVPA. Forager females had the highest routine MVPA, although foragers were more sedentary than farmers. Developmentally, youth who were more pubertally advanced engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA, and older youth were more sedentary. Youth residing in the most market-integrated village engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA compared to the least-integrated village. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that youth facultatively adjust their activity levels as they biologically mature and that physical activity is lower with incipient market integration. The routinely high levels of youth physical activity in these communities underscore the gap between subsistence lifestyles in energetically-demanding environments and physical activity in post/industrialized societies. From a global public health perspective, our findings highlight a crucial window during early economic transitions for public health interventions aimed at preventing physical inactivity and the chronic disease burden associated with lifestyle shifts.

articles_hidden.title: Insights into the scale, organisation, implementation and motivations behind dog culling in a rabies-endemic setting
articles_hidden.authors: tasmin alexander; Kennedy Lushasi; Lwitiko Sikana; Anna Czupryna; Elaine Ferguson; Mirava Yuson; Deborah Nadal; Nicholas Hanley; Nai Rui Chng; Sarah Cleaveland
articles_hidden.abstract: Culling is recognised as ineffective and potentially counterproductive for sustainable dog population management and rabies control, yet the practice persists in many countries. Empirical data on the scale, organisation, implementation and motivations behind culling remain sparse, limiting understanding of its persistence, and implications. Focusing on Tanzania, a rabies-endemic country where culling has been documented, this study uses a mixed-methods approach, combining two structured surveys (survey of occurrence, n = 51; survey of practice in districts reporting culling, n = 16) and in-depth interviews with district and field-based veterinary and livestock officers (n = 8). Culling was reported in 45% of surveyed districts (23/51). Culling events were reportedly led by veterinary departments, often with involvement of other sectors and communities, with officers also describing communities as carrying out some culling independently. Culling was motivated by complaints, requests and orders about the number of and harms attributed to free-roaming dogs. Roaming dogs were culled regardless of ownership, sterilisation and vaccination status, using methods inconsistent with humane killing standards. Extrapolating from the survey data, using a stochastic simulation, we estimate approximately 26,000 dogs (95% CI 20,000-33,000) are culled annually nationwide. Culling was difficult to reconcile with evidence-based international guidance on dog population management and rabies control, national animal welfare legislation, and One Health principles, underscoring the need to understand and address the factors sustaining it. Addressing culling will require engaging with the wider concerns motivating the practice, and with the sectors and communities involved.

articles_hidden.title: Accountability Among Allies: Intra-Party Competition and the Electoral Cost of Scandal
articles_hidden.authors: Stefano Sangiovanni; Giovanna Maria Invernizzi; Andrea Ceron
articles_hidden.abstract: When do voters electorally punish politicians for scandals? We argue that a scandal changes votes only when it can tip voters who are near indifference between candidates, and that intra-party contests place far more voters in that position than inter-party contests. We formalize this argument in a model of electoral sanctioning and test it in a pre-registered conjoint experiment on 3,000 U.S. adults. The scandal penalty is about 57% larger in intra-party contests, and, as the model predicts, the amplification appears even when both candidates come from the party the voter opposes. Inter-party choice settings may therefore understate how strongly voters punish misconduct when credible co-partisan alternatives are available.

articles_hidden.title: Industrializing Eastern Slovakia and Its Post- Socialist Legacy: The Cases of the East Slovak Ironworks in Košice and the Metal Working Factory in Medzev
articles_hidden.authors: Tereza Juhászová
articles_hidden.abstract:
This article explores patterns of post-socialist reindustrialization in Eastern Slovakia—a region
deeply shaped by heavy socialist industrialization and subsequently exposed to the tumultuous
“manager’s privatization” of the 1990s. Bridging social and economic history, it argues that
inherited industrial legacies—in know-how, infrastructure, workforce, and export orientation—
persisted even after a sharp decline in the first decade following the fall of socialism. Through
two case studies—the “giant” East Slovak Ironworks near the regional capital Košice and a
smaller metalworking factory in the nearby town of Medzev—the article shows how foreign
investment, limited state intervention, and local agency jointly enabled the partial revitalization
of regionally significant industries, despite the absence of a coherent industrial policy and the
dismantling of state coordination after 1989. Drawing on archival records, contemporary press,
and biographical interviews, the study traces the long-term trajectories of these sites within both
socialist development agendas and post-socialist restructuring. By demonstrating how
industrial continuity and reactivation emerged largely in the absence of strategic governance
and industrial policy, the article contributes to broader debates on post-socialist varieties of
capitalism, state capacity, and the uneven geography of industrial transformation. By
foregrounding continuity and reinvention, this nuanced perspective challenges binary accounts
of post-socialist change.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Employment in Mothers’ Careers After First Birth: A Comparison of South Korea and the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Wonjeong Jeong
articles_hidden.abstract: Upon parenthood, women face pressure to reorganize their paid work and careers. In this process, self-employment can offer a distinct option, with a different set of risks and benefits than wage work. Yet research on mothers’ employment trajectories rarely examines self-employment as a distinct option. This paper examines how self-employment fits into mothers’ careers after their first birth and how this pattern differs between two institutional contexts: South Korea and the United States. Using the Korean Labor and Income Panel Study and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, I track mothers’ employment history from their first birth through the following ten years. Descriptive and sequence analyses show that one in five mothers experiences self-employment at least once, but the way they leverage it differs by institutional context. In South Korea, self-employment more often follows nonemployment, is primarily full-time, and occurs within trajectories leading back to paid work. In the United States, mothers more often enter self-employment from wage work, while part-time self-employment appears intermittently in wage-centered trajectories. Thus, self-employment occupies different positions across these two contexts, where mothers’ counterfactual career options vary. As technology shifts, the potential importance of diverse forms of self-employment, including contract-based gig work, may increase, raising the need for future research to examine how self-employment fits into one’s career.

articles_hidden.title: Data Report:   Anchoring International Law’s Dynamism (ANCHOR)  project
articles_hidden.authors: MOBILE - Center of Excellence for Global Mobility Law; Anouk Lamé; Sarah Scott Ford; Nora Stappert
articles_hidden.abstract:
How are interpretive shifts at international courts accepted or resisted within the day-to-day work of domestic legal systems? Over the past few years, several international courts have faced critique by policymakers for developing international law too dynamically. Consequently, scholarly literature has argued that we are entering a period of backlash, with states actively trying to hedge against the domestic impact of international rulings. Yet, little is known about how – and under what conditions – interpretive shifts are received within the day-to-day work of domestic legal systems, especially at lower and specialized courts. 

This data report describes the data used for the research conducted as part of the research project entitled “Anchoring International Law’s Dynamism: Tracing Denmark’s Reception of International Rulings” (ANCHOR). Focusing on international refugee and migration law as a critical test case, the project analyses case data from the Danish Refugee Appeals Board (RAB) to examine the domestic reception of international rulings. The data report begins by describing the data collection process across its different data sources, after which it turns to data processing. The report then outlines the extraction and qualitative coding of citations to international rulings, ending with a brief discussion of the choices made for the data analysis.

articles_hidden.title: “It’s Hard to See It Through Clinical Eyes When It’s Yourself”:    General Practice and Community Healthcare Professionals’ Experiences of Domestic Abuse, Disclosure, & Help-Seeking
articles_hidden.authors: Sandi Dheensa; Rebecca Cox; Judith Worthington; Paula Whittaker; Gene Feder; Alison Gregory
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Domestic abuse is highly prevalent and causes wide-ranging harms. Healthcare professionals are especially likely to receive disclosures and international policies call for a robust healthcare response to abuse.  But the needs of affected healthcare professionals (HCPs) have been sidelined. Globally, 42% of female HCPs report lifetime experience of domestic abuse. Our study aimed to explore how experiencing domestic abuse affects HCPs to understand the safety and support interventions needed. 
Methods
We used semi-structured interviews with 18 National Health Service primary and community HCPs and used Framework Analysis, drawing on four interrelated concepts: problem recognition, stigma, candidacy, and professional identity.  
Results
Perpetrators used HCP-survivors’ roles against them and domestic abuse had wide-ranging consequences for work. Remaining themes mapped onto HCP-survivors’ trajectory towards support, including problems with recognising and/or naming domestic abuse, the impact of recognising and naming it, reflections on different support options, consequences of workplace disclosure, support experiences, and reflections on what needs to change. Professional identity and profession-related factors affected each aspect of this trajectory, delaying recognition of domestic abuse and making help-seeking and positive support experiences less likely.  
Conclusion
Building an effective and compassionate healthcare response to domestic abuse will be impossible without attending to HCP-survivors’ needs and the inadequate responses of fellow HCPs. HCP-survivors are likely assets in improving responses to patients, colleagues, and students; but without support may experience trauma symptoms. We recommend improved first-line responses to HCP-survivors in workplaces and a move towards a recognition of HCPs as potential survivors in domestic abuse education, funding, and interventions.

articles_hidden.title: From Berberism to Kabyle-Nationalism. Historical Analysis of Berberism in Algeria between 1930 and  2005.
articles_hidden.authors: Christoph Novak
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines the historical development of Berberism in Algeria from the emergence of Algerian nationalist movements in the 1930s to the aftermath of the Black Spring of 2001. It argues that Berberism should not be understood as a stable political ideology with a fixed substantive meaning, but rather as a changing political practice through which the idea of a distinctive Berber identity has been mobilised in response to particular political contexts. The analysis distinguishes three phases in the development of Berber activism. The first, exemplified by the Berber Crisis of 1948–49, was largely an elite struggle within the Algerian nationalist movement over the definition of the Algerian nation and the recognition of its linguistic and cultural plurality. The second, crystallised in the Berber Spring of 1980, transformed Berberism into a broader social movement centred on cultural recognition, linguistic rights and opposition to state Arabisation. During the subsequent period of political liberalisation and civil war, Berber activism became increasingly institutionalised through political parties, social movements and transnational networks. The third phase, associated with the Black Spring of 2001, marked a significant reorientation. The declining legitimacy of established Berberist parties and the emergence of the Citizens’ Movement shifted political mobilisation toward territorial, socio-economic and increasingly Kabylia-centred claims. Drawing on concepts of political identity, recognition, nationalism and imagined communities, the article argues that this development contributed to the emergence of a specifically Kabyle nationalism. Whereas Berberism provided a broader cultural and transnational identity, it lacked a clearly defined territorial project capable of consolidating a common political community. The post-2001 mobilisation in Kabylia, by contrast, increasingly linked cultural identity to a specific homeland, territorial political structures and demands for autonomy. The article therefore conceptualises the transition from Berberism to Kabyle nationalism not as a linear transformation, but as a reconfiguration of political actors, strategies, territorial imaginaries and claims to collective self-determination. The article was written in 2012.

articles_hidden.title: Closure without Resolution in European Prison Oversight
articles_hidden.authors: Nasrul Ismail
articles_hidden.abstract: Compliance with judgments of the European Court of Human Rights is conventionally recorded as a terminal status: a case is open or closed, a judgment executed or pending, an obligation met or unmet. These measures enable scholarly comparison, but they cannot show how a state engages with the supervision of a judgment or whether reform of prison conditions endures. As such, this article treats compliance as conduct and asks whether the closure of supervision reflects durable improvement in the conditions a judgment addressed. Drawing on the documentary record of Committee of Ministers supervision in three pilot-judgment jurisdictions (i.e., Italy, Romania, and Hungary), with two contextual comparators (i.e., Spain and England and Wales), it codes state disclosures for opacity and stance and reconstructs responsiveness descriptively from the dated supervisory sequence. Two independent coders reached strong agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.88 for stance and 0.90 for opacity, on small, well-specified eligible data sets). The cases did not form a single compliance scale but displayed distinct configurations. Specifically, Italy was transparent but shifted in its stated position before closure in 2016; Romania combined continuing engagement with capacity explanations; and Hungary combined formal but insubstantial engagement with selective disclosure. Set against current prison occupancy, the state that had completed supervision was the most overcrowded: Italy recorded 120.7 occupants per 100 places, exceeding Hungary's 114.5 and Romania's 111.2. Because the occupancy snapshot postdated Italy's closure, it could not reveal whether closure caused the later overcrowding, but it did manifest that closure did not secure lasting improvement in reforms. The article frames this durability gap as a problem of means-ends decoupling and offers a reproducible method for distinguishing compliance conduct from the substantive conditions oversight exists to change.

articles_hidden.title: Contagion or substitution? Experimental evidence on spillovers in trust between legislative and judicial institutions
articles_hidden.authors: Michal Ovadek; Stuart Perrett
articles_hidden.abstract: Does information about one branch of government affect trust in another? We show that institutional trust is neither institution-specific nor uniformly system-wide. In a survey experiment embedded in the British Election Study Internet Panel, respondents received information about the UK Parliament, the UK Supreme Court, and the European Court of Human Rights that varied the policy content of decisions, party framing of these decisions, and the conduct of individual officeholders. Policy decisions conflicting with respondents' preferences reduce trust well beyond the institution responsible, while congruent decisions leave trust unchanged. Spillovers are strongly asymmetric: parliamentary decisions depress trust in the courts more than in Parliament itself, whereas court decisions produce little spillover beyond the judicial domain. Criticism from parties offsets rather than deepens the penalty, regardless of how much respondents like the cueing party. Information about conduct of officeholders moves trust neither within nor across institutions. We conclude that institutional trust is selectively contagious, shaped above all by the policy decisions institutions make.

articles_hidden.title: The Self-Destruction Hypothesis of Consumerism: The Inflation of Consumption Standards and the Mismatch with Household Income
articles_hidden.authors: ZY Liu; Di Yuan
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper proposes and develops a theoretical proposition concerning the endogenous evolution of consumerism: consumerism may not necessarily come to an end because of “excessive consumption”; rather, by continuously raising the consumption standards associated with “normal life,” it may make an increasing number of ordinary workers unable to participate in the consumption patterns it has itself constructed, thereby eroding the demand base on which it depends. Consumer demand has a positive expansionary effect during the early stages of economic development. The paper then explains why social consumption standards may continue to rise through three channels: firm competition; positional goods and social comparison; and the diffusion and amplification of cultural products and social media. On this basis, it argues that under conditions of market competition, firms simultaneously need to expand effective demand on the consumer side and have an inherent incentive to control labor costs, creating a structural mismatch between the growth of workers’ incomes and the rise of consumption standards. When consumption standards grow persistently faster than the actual disposable incomes of ordinary workers, consumption behavior may shift from “keeping up with the standard” toward “reducing, postponing, or even exiting consumption,” with particularly concentrated effects in marriage and family formation. Using the decline in China’s marriage and birth rates, the rising consumption standards associated with wedding photography and housing, and the adjustment of the real-estate sector as illustrative empirical cases, the paper distinguishes two post-turning-point adjustment paths—“structural consumption downgrading” and “aggregate-demand-driven consumption contraction”—and discusses the possibilities and limits of external trade as a substitute for domestic demand. The paper further constructs a conceptual income–consumption-standard mismatch model to characterize the pressure generated by the divergence between income and consumption standards and its transmission to consumption behavior, family formation, and future demand. Finally, it proposes four policy directions: optimizing social-media algorithms, establishing a Departmental Employment Quality Index (DEQI) for higher education, reducing the minimum cost of basic living, and limited government intervention in consumption externalities.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond compensation: Climate politics, mobilization, and transformative statecraft
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Braun; Leah Downey
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments have pursued decarbonization through a combination of subsidies for capital and compensation for people. Political scientists have identified the compensation of those who incur losses from climate policies as the the central challenge in building green coalitions and achieving a just transition. However, a decarbonization path aimed at limiting global warming to 2 degrees Celsius entails transformative change for virtually everyone. We argue that, under such conditions, a compensation-based approach reduces green backlash to pocketbook concerns; citizens to bundles of fixed preferences; and evaluation to policy-by-policy assessment. Proposing to move beyond compensating existing preferences, we contend that transformative statecraft reshapes preferences through political mobilization. From this perspective, a technocratic approach—focused on calculation and compensation—constitutes a binding constraint on green statecraft. We defend this mobilization-based approach against the objections of manipulation and deprivation of freedom and suggest that a democratic version of transformative statecraft is possible.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Load and Moral Strain: Situational Demands and the Experience of Carrying Them
articles_hidden.authors: Chase Crossno
articles_hidden.abstract: People often recognize that something morally significant is happening before they can name what they are experiencing. Existing vocabulary, including moral distress, moral injury, moral residue, and moral resilience, describes important forms and consequences of moral difficulty. This paper develops an analytic distinction among moral demands, moral load, and moral strain. Moral demands are the morally significant claims, obligations, risks, or consequences present in a situation. Moral load names how those demands bear on a particular person through roles, relationships, commitments, foreseeable consequences, and available agency; moral strain names the internal experience of carrying that load. Load is therefore neither a property of the situation alone nor a subjective reaction to it. Prior uses of moral load have addressed moral sensitivity, clinical decision-making, and moral deliberation. The contribution here is a relational architecture that separates situation-level demands, person-specific load, and internal strain. Demands, tasks, authority, resources, and support may be redistributed, thereby changing the load borne by particular people; support may also alter strain even when underlying load remains. Consequences including moral residue and moral injury can generate new obligations and shape later load and strain, making the relationship recursive rather than linear. Implications for education, team practice, and research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Observed Shifts in the Health Equity Research Landscape: Results of a National Survey of Health Equity Researchers April-July, 2025
articles_hidden.authors: Clair Kronk; Sima Rabinowitz; Denise Milstein; Devin Madden; Nita Vangeepuram; Dinushika Mohottige; Timnit Berhane; Andrew Maroko
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives. To assess changes health equity researchers have made or anticipate making to their research in the context of the current federal administration’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusion. 
Methods. We shared an electronic survey link with health equity researchers at academic, non-academic non-profit, non-academic for-profit, and governmental institutions in the U.S. between April and July 2025. 634 responses were received; 381 completed. The survey assessed demographics, occupational and institutional characteristics, perceptions of job security, experiences of stress, collaborations, censorship, and funding sources. 
Results. A large majority of respondents (96.6%) reported having made or anticipated making changes to their health equity research. Changes included: using different language (83.7.%), adapting or altering research questions (56.4%), pivoting to new health equity topics (49.6%), developing new health equity projects (50.4%), seeking new collaborators (31.0%), stopping health equity research activities (18.9%), and withdrawing from existing collaborations (8.9%).
Conclusions. A significant number of health equity researchers have made or anticipate making fundamental changes to their research. These changes have critical implications for health equity research, public health, research teams, and the communities most impacted by this work.

articles_hidden.title: Patient-reported experience as audit evidence: a new perspective on governance in integrated care
articles_hidden.authors: Ilona Ogurcova
articles_hidden.abstract:
Patient-reported experience can identify problems in integrated care, yet feedback alone does not show whether organisations address them. This Perspective argues that experience data can inform internal audit evidence and person-centred healthcare governance when their quality, context and interpretive limits are examined. Developed within the author's doctoral research programme, the argument draws on a purposively selected set of scientific publications and official documents; it does not report a literature review or analyse the programme's empirical datasets. The conceptual method compares the purposes and units of patient-experience measurement, SCIROCCO integration maturity assessment, value-based healthcare implementation assessment and professional internal audit. An illustrative crosswalk then connects five coordination and participation concerns with contextual domains, candidate audit questions, corroborating information and management follow-up. The proposed cycle moves from patient-defined priorities through evidence evaluation to accountable action and repeated assessment of experience. It preserves management ownership of controls and distinguishes a reported concern from a demonstrated organisational failure. Neither the crosswalk nor the combined framework has been empirically validated. Patient involvement, feasibility assessment and comparative evaluation are needed to establish usefulness, burden and effects. The contribution is a testable governance proposition, not evidence of improved clinical outcomes or economic value.
Keywords: patient-reported experience data, internal audit, audit evidence, integrated care, SCIROCCO maturity model, healthcare governance, person-centred care

articles_hidden.title: Post-growth policies and business transformation: A mixed-methods expert assessment of perceived relevance
articles_hidden.authors: Josefine Henman; Manuel Suter
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines how different policies are perceived by researchers regarding their relevance in supporting the transformation of traditional businesses toward reducing ecological footprints, securing well-being, and increasing social equity. While post-growth scholarship has discussed a wide range of policy proposals, their implications for business transformations remain underexplored. To address this gap, the study combines a quantitative survey of 1,734 sustainability policy researchers with qualitative focus group discussions with post-growth business scholars. The survey results indicate that the majority of policy instruments are perceived as at least moderately relevant for supporting a business transformation towards post-growth. Descriptive analyses show that respondents with a degrowth work-orientation tend to perceive the instruments as more relevant than growth-indifferent or green growth-oriented respondents, with differences particularly pronounced for more structurally disruptive interventions. The qualitative analysis explores how post-growth business scholars perceive key tensions, barriers, and enabling conditions associated with three previously highly ranked policies: transitioning ownership structures, banning planned obsolescence, and introducing declining resource caps. Two central topics emerge from these discussions: the role of businesses’ profit orientation as a structural factor that may shape responses to policy interventions, and the importance of combining policies in order to address anticipated tensions and wider societal implications. The article bridges post-growth policy and business research by suggesting how different policy instruments and mixes may support business transformations in line with post-growth objectives.

articles_hidden.title: Geopolitical Influence & Peace: Tracking the trends shaping international relations
articles_hidden.authors: Sascha Nanlohy; Paulina Pijacka
articles_hidden.abstract:
This report asks whether the world has entered a "new Cold War" and what intensifying great power competition means for peace, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Using datasets including SIPRI, ICEWS, UCDP/PRIO, the Correlates of War and the Foreign Bilateral Influence Capability (FBIC) dataset, it compares today's international system with the Cold War and post-Cold War periods.

Geopolitical risk now exceeds Cold War levels and is nearing the peaks seen after 9/11. Global military expenditure reached a record US$2.43 trillion in 2023, the largest annual rise since 2009. Nuclear disarmament has stalled, and the UN Security Council has become less effective, with fewer resolutions passed and more vetoes since the 2010s. Bilateral sentiment between the US, Russia and China has deteriorated since 1995.

The current system nonetheless differs from the Cold War. It is multipolar and economically interdependent, although trade has plateaued at around 60 per cent of global GDP. It is also shaped by technological competition and global challenges such as climate change. The number of countries holding more than 10 per cent influence in five or more other states has almost tripled, from 13 at the end of the Cold War to 34 in 2024. This reflects the rise of middle powers such as Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, South Africa, Vietnam and Indonesia, alongside China and India.

For LMICs, competition for influence is intensifying, notably in the Sahel, West Africa, South Asia and South America. The US holds more than 10 per cent influence in 74 LMICs and China in 65. China is dominant in sub-Saharan Africa and the US in Latin America. Internationalised intrastate conflicts have increased nearly threefold since 2010. The Sudan and Syria case studies show how external backing for warring parties can prolong conflict and raise the risk of mass atrocities. Proxy wars also drove many of the Cold War's deadliest conflicts.

Economic pressures compound these risks. In 2024, 3.3 billion people lived in countries where debt interest payments exceeded spending on health and education. Aid is also shifting from multilateral to bilateral channels, which further constrains development and Positive Peace.

The report concludes that competition for influence can undermine local governance and divert attention from climate change, food insecurity and peacebuilding. A nuanced understanding of these dynamics is needed to support long-term stability and development in the developing world.

articles_hidden.title: No King, and Other Matters—America’s Perspectives in Mid-2026 on Democracy, Authoritarianism, and Election-Related Violence:  Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Garen J. Wintemute; Bradley Velasquez; Sonia Robinson; Krista Neumann; Shaina Sta Cruz; Aaron Shev; Daniel Joseph Tancredi; Elizabeth A. Tomsich; Mona A. Wright; Veronica Pear
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Political violence and the rise of authoritarianism are emerging threats to the nation’s health, stability, and future as a representative democracy. To inform and facilitate prevention efforts, we present new and updated findings on the public’s views on authoritarianism and its support for and willingness to engage in election-related and pro- or anti-government violence. 

Methods: Findings are from Wave 5, conducted May 15-June 15, 2026, of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of adult members of the Ipsos KnowledgePanel that was initiated in 2022. Findings are for the cohort as a whole and for subgroups defined by political party/Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliation. Year-to-year change for items included in 2025 and 2026 is estimated using mean change scores. Cross-sectional findings for 2026 are presented as weighted prevalences and item scores.

Results: The completion rate was 90.7%; there were 7,552 respondents. Nearly 90% of respondents continued to consider it very or extremely important that the US remain a democracy (change 0.01, 95% CI -0.00, 0.03). Agreement with expressions of authoritarianism was much less common; it decreased for the statement, “having a strong leader for America is more important than having a democracy” (change -0.04, 95% CI -0.07, -0.02) and others. In 2026, 2.1% (95% CI 1.6%, 2.7%) of respondents agreed strongly or very strongly that President Trump should be made king, but nearly half (47.7%, 95% CI 46.2%, 49.2%) agreed strongly or very strongly that he should be impeached and removed from office. 

There was little agreement with 5 actions the federal government might take in 2026 that employed violence to enforce its policies or suppress its critics in the US; the prevalence of strong or very strong agreement ranged between 4.4% and 9.6%. Across 12 items, there was very little agreement with actions—including violence—the federal government might take to subvert elections; strong or very strong agreement ranged between 2% and 4%. Willingness to commit violence was rare. For example, only 1.6% (95% CI 1.2%, 2.1%) were very or completely willing to use violence “to make sure that President Trump remains in office after his term ends.” Decreases from 2025 to 2026 in support for expressions of authoritarianism and for government-initiated violence were common across the spectrum of party/MAGA movement affiliations.

Conclusions: With national elections a few months away, Americans remained strongly supportive of democracy, did not endorse authoritarianism, and rejected the use of force by the current federal government to enforce its policies or subvert elections. They were deeply unwilling to engage in violence. These hopeful findings can inform and guide efforts to preserve democracy and prevent political violence.

articles_hidden.title: Effective Anti-Corruption Strategies for Public Organizations: Insights from Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
articles_hidden.authors: Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller
articles_hidden.abstract: Fighting corruption remains one of the most pressing management challenges in public organizations worldwide. While different organizational approaches to anti‑corruption exist, evidence of their effectiveness and the conditions under which they reduce different forms of administrative corruption remains limited. Drawing on a meta analysis and meta regression of 174 effect sizes from 34 empirical studies, this study shows that both integrity based and compliance based anti corruption strategies have a significant, positive, small to moderate effect on public organizations’ ethical performance, although their effectiveness varies across contexts. Compliance based strategies, particularly formalization and accountability mechanisms, are more effective in addressing multiple forms of administrative corruption, whereas integrity‑based strategies, such as ethical leadership, primarily reduce collusion, demonstrating that ‘one-size-fits-all’ approaches are ineffective. The findings highlight the conditional effectiveness of organizational anti‑corruption strategies and the importance of context‑sensitive ethics management. These findings carry important implications for public administration theory, research, and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Co-creating change in agriculture and food systems: A systematic review of co-creation processes and approaches for evaluating their contributions to sustainability transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Delaney; Sophia Alami; Maria Busse; Bonnie Averbuch; Fanny Boeraeve; Pauline Cassart; Valéria Csonka; Graeme Dean; Cedric Gossart; Bienvenu Kambashi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Co-creation is widely proposed to address complex sustainability challenges by bringing together diverse forms of experience and expertise. Yet practical, evidence-based guidance on how co-creation processes can support sustainability transformation remains fragmented and insufficient, including for agriculture and food systems. We conducted a systematic literature review to characterize scholarly work on co-creation for environmental sustainability and to identify process insights relevant to Living Labs and related participatory initiatives. Following a four-stage screening procedure, we reviewed 5,291 articles and retained 266 studies describing multi-stakeholder, action-oriented, experimental processes; 51 agriculture- and food-focused articles were subjected to in-depth qualitative analysis. We combined bibliometric and descriptive analyses, including co-authorship network mapping, with framework-guided qualitative coding of co-creation inputs, processes, outcomes, impacts, and evaluation practices.
Publications on this topic increased substantially over the past decade, but relatively few studies documented action and experimentation in sufficient methodological detail. Agriculture and food studies constituted a moderately self-contained segment of the broader literature. Across the qualitative sample, five enabling factors were most consistently associated with productive co-creation: participant alignment, institutional support, strong facilitation, inclusive participation and trust, and sufficient time for iteration. Studies also identified recurring trade-offs between diversity and alignment, resource-intensive engagement and scalability, and place specificity and transferability. Frequently reported outcomes were new knowledge, communication and networks, empowerment or efficacy, and skills. However, evidence of longer-term sustainability impacts was limited: most articles described intermediate outcomes rather than demonstrated transformation. Only sixteen articles evaluated the co-creation process itself, and participatory development of evaluation criteria was rare. Co-creation efforts can build the practical and relational capacities, and “social infrastructure” needed for sustainability transitions, but stronger methodological reporting and participatory, longitudinal evaluation are needed for validation of criteria and proxies for impact and establishment of how these processes contribute to lasting transformation.

articles_hidden.title: От «светоча нации» до «педагога-тирана»: как русскоязычные Telegram-медиа конструируют образ учителя, 2020–2025
articles_hidden.authors: Munira Vassilova
articles_hidden.abstract: Исследование анализирует, как профессия учителя конструируется в русскоязычном новостном Telegram-корпусе за 2020–2025 гг. Исходный архив был получен из открытого набора ResearchData.kz (dataset 233) и включал 653 170 публикаций; после ограничения периода осталось 551 880 сообщений. Лексический поиск по основам «учител*», «педагог*» и «преподавател*» дал 5 721 кандидата, после скрининга сформирован рабочий корпус из 5 256 размещений в 19 каналах. Семантическое кодирование выявило 4 440 содержательно валидных упоминаний и 816 нерелевантных совпадений. Кодбук, сформированный абдуктивно из литературы и повторяющихся паттернов корпуса, различает F0 — присутствие учителя без самостоятельного профессионального фрейма — и семь содержательных фреймов. F0 составляет 32,2% валидных публикаций. Среди содержательных фреймов наиболее распространены поддержка/инвестиции и уязвимость — по 15,1%; экспертность/агентность составляет лишь 6,2%. Это показывает, что медиа чаще говорят об учителе как об объекте поддержки, ограничений, регулирования или оценки, чем как о самостоятельном производителе профессионального знания. Временные различия невелики: доля экспертности/агентности возрастает с 3,8% в 2020 г. до 7,3% в 2025 г., а уязвимости — с 11,6% до 17,6%. Среди казахстанских источников медиа регионального охвата значительно чаще используют фрейм экспертности, а государственные — признание и поддержку; негосударственные чаще проблематизируют профессию и показывают уязвимость. Работа показывает, почему для анализа статуса профессии важно различать простую видимость, профессиональную репрезентацию и распределение символической агентности.

articles_hidden.title: Resistance to Backsliding: The Role of Democratic Conceptions
articles_hidden.authors: Noam Gidron; Yotam Margalit; Lior Sheffer; Itamar Yakir
articles_hidden.abstract: We examine who mobilizes against democratic backsliding, focusing on mass protests against the judicial overhaul advanced by the Israeli government in 2023. As contemporary subversion of democracy is often driven by governments that won an electoral majority, we posit that protesting against the government's actions requires people to have a thick conception of democracy that goes beyond majority rule. Drawing on panel data collected before and after the overhaul's announcement, we show that citizens vary substantially in their conception of democracy, and that a thick conception not only predicts protesting against backsliding but also moderates the role of other key factors in mobilizing against democratic erosion. The findings highlight the role of small-d democrats in safeguarding democracy.

articles_hidden.title: Your AI Knows Your Story. Should It Die With You?
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Seifert
articles_hidden.abstract: Personal conversations with AI assistants increasingly contain memories, reflections, and records of changing judgment that may outlive their users. This commentary argues that selected exchanges could form a digital legacy: not a posthumous replica, but a personal testimony curated while the person is still able to correct it. Such legacies may be especially meaningful for people who wish to pass on their experience beyond their immediate family. Their creation, however, requires explicit consent, designated recipients, durable access, and a clear separation between the user's own words, the system's contributions, and any interpretations generated later. Whether such archives transmit wisdom or support bereavement remains an open question.

articles_hidden.title: Social Networks and Unequal Income Returns to Education: Gender Differences and Cross-National Context
articles_hidden.authors: INVEST Flagship; Emmi Mäkeläinen; Aki Koivula
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines how social networks are associated with unequal income returns to education and whether these associations vary by gender and across national contexts. Using data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 from representative samples in 15 countries, the study analyses the interrelations between educational attainment, social ties, and personal income. The analyses distinguish both the status of social contacts and the type of ties to the upper middle class, while also examining variation by gender and country-level income inequality. The results show that access to upper-middle-class contacts is associated with wider educational differences in income, and that close ties, especially family members, relatives, and close friends, are more strongly associated with income than weaker ties. These patterns also vary by gender, with educated men’s income more strongly associated with upper-middle-class ties than educated women’s. In addition, educational differences in the association between social networks and income are more pronounced in countries with higher levels of income inequality. The study contributes to research on social stratification by showing that income returns to education are socially embedded and also vary by gender and national context.

articles_hidden.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles_hidden.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles_hidden.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The Electoral Costs of Exclusion: Women’s Candidate Placement and Party Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Iris E. Acquarone; Alba Huidobro
articles_hidden.abstract: Political elites continue to behave as if including women in electable positions is electorally risky, despite growing evidence of voter support for gender-inclusive representation. This paper advances a theory of the electoral costs of exclusion, arguing that continued exclusion can become electorally costly when parties fail to adapt to changing electoral responses to women's representation. Using data from Spanish local elections (2003-2019) and a difference-in-differences design, we show that parties increasing women's representation in electable list positions gain votes and seats relative to parties that do not; this divergence coincides with gains among parties increasing women's representation and losses among those maintaining or reducing it. These consequences grow over time and are strongest where inclusion is voluntary rather than quota-mandated. Our findings challenge the idea that underrepresentation persists because inclusion fails electorally, pointing instead to a changing electoral constraint some elites may fail to recognize: exclusion has become costly.

articles_hidden.title: Daily Dynamics of Urban Racial Segregation in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Cody Arlie Reed
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines racial segregation changes across the day and week to assess three perspectives in urban sociology: social isolation, compelled mobility, and cosmopolitanism. I link mobile phone tracking data collected on 18 days in January 2020 to 2020 Census data on the racial composition of estimated home tracts. Using the Theil multigroup segregation index, I estimate hourly racial segregation in 18 large U.S. commuting zones. Racial segregation is highest overnight, declines during weekday work hours, and is generally higher on weekends than weekdays. These patterns are most consistent with the compelled mobility perspective, under which lower racial segregation is expected when residents travel beyond their neighborhoods to access employment and other resources. Relatively high weekend racial segregation offers only weak support for social isolation. Friday and Saturday nights and the following early mornings have lower racial segregation than Wednesday at the same hours, offering clearer partial support for cosmopolitanism. Although the data do not identify why people travel, they show that the clearest declines in racial segregation coincide with the workday. Measuring racial segregation across hours and days thus helps distinguish theoretical accounts of how racial segregation persists or diminishes beyond residential neighborhoods.

articles_hidden.title: The Promise: A Breakthrough for Social Science
articles_hidden.authors: Bruno Sérgio Dias Oliveira
articles_hidden.abstract:
[SSRN has the latest version of this preprint at https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4982428 ] 

Sociology has long wrestled with theoretical fragmentation, hindering a unified understanding of social life. This paper unveils the General Social Theory of Compromises (G-STOC), a bold framework that reimagines social phenomena through the lens of promises and their reciprocal arrangements, termed compromises. G-STOC posits that all social interactions — whether mundane exchanges or transformative societal shifts — hinge on promises, broadly defined to include not just explicit pledges but also tacit expectations, norms, and imposed duties. These promises knit together into compromises, forming the essential fabric of social relationships. The theory advances several key insights: (1) social behavior springs from actual and virtual agency, with virtual agency rooted in anticipated promises; (2) emotions like anger and disappointment reveal breaches of these promises, highlighting their omnipresence; (3) compromises unify individual actions with broader social influences; and (4) sociological insight arises from tracing these compromises across time. Emphasizing the future-oriented nature of social action, G-STOC sidesteps perennial debates like agency versus structure, offering a potent, streamlined tool to decode human interactions. This paper urges scholars to engage with G-STOC, testing its potential to revitalize social science and deepen our grasp of society’s complexities.

articles_hidden.title: Health system and hospital utilization in Chile, 1952–2020: trends, reforms, and inflection points
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective. To collect and analyze longitudinal data on hospital discharges in Chile between 1952 and 2020, both at the national level and within the public subsystem. Patterns of change were identified in relation to the following key institutional milestones: the Curative Medicine Act of 1968, the creation of the National Health Services System in 1979, and the implementation of the Universal and Guaranteed Access Reform in 2005. Methods. A first-of-its-kind time series was constructed using official sources from the Ministry of Health and institutional documents. Indicators were calculated for the total number of discharges, discharge rates per thousand population, and comparisons with the United States. The analysis included exploratory graphics and construction of segmented regression models. Results. Hospital discharges rose steadily, with two periods mirroring robust expansion of the private sector: between 1982 and 1987 and between 2006 and 2019. Public provision of hospital services slowed or decreased with the 1979 reform and with the 2005 reform, although not with the 1968 reform. Conclusion. This study provides empirical evidence on the long-term trajectory of Chilean hospital services and confirms a structural contrast between the country's major health system models and the differences in their reforms. It also underscores the need for long-term information to analyze the impact of health reforms.

articles_hidden.title: Mind the Gap: Elite Preferences for Redistribution and How they Differ from the Mass Public
articles_hidden.authors: Mogens K. Justesen; Marko Klašnja; Sara B. Hobolt; Robert Klemmensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Increasing inequality has raised concerns over the disproportionate influence of the rich on public policies. Central to such concerns is the assumption that elite policy preferences are unified and differ significantly from the general public. We theorize economic elites as fiscal constituencies, highlighting intra-elite differences in policy preferences based on elite sources of affluence and therefore fiscal claims they face from the state. 
Employing high-quality administrative and survey data, including conjoint experiments, from Denmark, we compare tax and spending preferences in the general population with the largest samples to date of the top 1% by income and wealth. While elites are more economically conservative, they are not uniformly anti-redistribution; the asset-rich are less conservative than the income-rich; and their preferences often differ over tax policy. These findings highlight elite group differences based on their relation to the fiscal structure of the state and offer new insights into the micro-foundations of unequal representation in advanced democracies.

articles_hidden.title: Ranking Data in Political Science
articles_hidden.authors: Yuki Atsusaka; Shubhangi Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Across scientific disciplines, researchers have used ranking data to study people's comparative judgments, preferences, and decision-making over a range of items. While existing data-sharing infrastructures in statistics and machine learning, such as PrefLib, offer a rich collection of ranking datasets, including those related to politics, they are not necessarily designed specifically to support cumulative research in social science. In this work, we introduce the first large-scale database of political rankings based on various studies from leading political science journals. Our first release covers 52 datasets from 27 original studies published between 2005 and 2025. Our database demonstrates notable variation in substantive topics and forms of ranking data that go well beyond canonical examples of candidate evaluations and value orientations, enabling researchers to perform comparative analyses, replication, reanalysis, methodological evaluation, and new substantive research with real-world political rankings. Along with validating our database, we illustrate it by replicating key findings in four selected studies, including those of multiple identities in American politics, the representation of Muslims in India, factional leaning in the Syrian civil war, and legislative accountability for affordable health care.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Inference in the CLS Cohort Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Liam Wright; Georgia D Tomova; Martin Nejedly; George Ploubidis; Richard J. Silverwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Correlations between variables in cohort and other observational studies do not necessarily indicate causal effects and may instead reflect bias due to confounding, sample selection processes, or measurement issues. Thankfully, multiple statistical methods, frameworks, and research designs have been developed that – when used judiciously – can aid making causal inferences with observational data. This is especially the case with CLS’s cohorts, which have several properties (e.g., longitudinal assessment and rich and varied data collection) that that can make the assumptions of these methods more plausible or provide ample opportunities for each method’s use. In this guide, we provide an overview of the possibilities for causal inference in CLS’s cohorts. Specifically, we: (1) provide background on the problem of causal inference in observational data, (2) detail the attributes of CLS’s cohorts that can support causal inference, and (3) outline an extensive set of methods and research designs that – assumptions permitting – can be used to estimate causal effects in CLS’s cohort data, illustrating each with existing applications and highlighting opportunities for further work.

articles_hidden.title: FRAGMENTED GOVERNANCE AND THE FAILURE TO EXECUTE URBAN PROJECTS: THE LARGO DA BATATA COMPETITION (2001-2022)
articles_hidden.authors: Leticia Takeda Lodi
articles_hidden.abstract: Architecture and urban design competitions are often defended as democratic selection mechanisms, yet many fail during implementation. This article argues the failure stems from fragmented governance: semi-autonomous sectoral authorities operating without a coordinating hierarchy. Through a 21-year documentary analysis of the National Competition for the Urban Reconversion of Largo da Batata (São Paulo), comparing the winning, basic and executed projects (2001-2022), we show each authority discharged its mandate competently, yet the absence of coordination fragmented the outcome. This mechanism, pockets of micro-regulation practices, moves the debate from describing competition failure to explaining it, with implications for governance research.

articles_hidden.title: What influences the time to reach a tenured university professorship? Insights from machine-learning
articles_hidden.authors: Jasmin M. Kizilirmak; Frauke Peter
articles_hidden.abstract: The race to professorship is influenced by many factors, ranging from individual achievements to systemic structures. Prior research has underscored the significance of aspects such as academic productivity, institutional affiliations, and personal choices in shaping academic careers, but comprehensive analyses in specific contexts remain limited. The last two decades have seen strategic shifts within the German academic system, most notably with the introduction of junior and tenure-track professorships intended to offer a more secure career path. Yet, uncertainties persist regarding the determinants of career trajectories to tenured university professorship. Addressing this gap, this paper uses unique and novel longitudinal data of German professors to elucidate the various pathways to professorship. Based on a sample of individuals who successfully secured full university professorship, we estimate comprehensive models using machine learning to determine relevant factors that predict the time needed to reach this position. Key correlates are obtaining a habilitation, having held positions with leadership responsibilities, and disciplinary fields.

articles_hidden.title: Women and AI: A Large-Scale, Validated Mapping of Women’s Under-Represented and Under-Recognized Contributions to AI Research
articles_hidden.authors: Chiara Binelli; Elena Cossu
articles_hidden.abstract: Participation in AI research shapes which type of AI is built, whose societal needs it addresses, and how it is used in society. Despite increasing attention to gender diversity in AI, we lacksystematic evidence on the research topics, methods used, and collaboration structures associated with female AI researchers. This paper addresses this significant gap by developing the first large-scale, validated mapping of women’s contributions to both generative and non-generative AI research across data science and the main social science disciplines (economics, political science, and sociology). Using a sample of over 500,000 papers published between 2023 and 2026, we document three key findings. First, women are under-represented among academic AI authors across all four disciplines and recent years, and least represented in data science. Second, conditional on participating, women’s AI research is thematically distinctive: it is more applied, social and purpose-driven, concentrated in health, education and fairness, and, in data science, oriented towards using rather than building AI. Third, this distinctive work is heard less: conditional on working on the same AI topic women and men are cited equally, but the topics women disproportionately work on are themselves cited less, so women’s ideas receive systematically fewer citations. This voice gap is therefore a topic-composition penalty rather than a same-topic penalty, and it reduces efficiency by giving a distinctive, society-oriented research agenda too little voice in how AI develops.

articles_hidden.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles_hidden.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles_hidden.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Social Exclusion, Institutional Support and the Perceived Criminal Involvement of Waste Pickers: Evidence from a Stakeholder Survey in Rawalpindi–Islamabad, Pakistan
articles_hidden.authors: rabail ghazanfar
articles_hidden.abstract: Informal waste pickers (rag-pickers) are among the most marginalised urban groups in Pakistan, yet they are often linked in public debate to petty crime, substance use and sex work. This study surveys 300 frontline stakeholders (78 police personnel, 175 NGO staff and 47 other residents) in Rawalpindi and Islamabad to examine which offences they attribute to waste pickers and how these perceptions relate to perceived social exclusion and perceived support from government and NGOs. Substance use (80%) and prostitution (79%) were the offences most often attributed; murder rarely (5%). Perceived social exclusion was strongly associated with perceived criminal involvement (r = .73, p < .001), while perceived institutional support showed a weak negative association (r = -.17, p = .004). In a regression model (R2 = .53), exclusion was the only significant predictor (beta = .75); the association of support with criminal involvement operated indirectly through lower exclusion (indirect effect = -.23, Sobel z = -5.27, p < .001). The findings suggest that support reduces perceived criminality only insofar as it reduces exclusion, and argue for inclusion-oriented policy: integrating waste pickers into municipal waste systems, making social protection reachable, and protective rather than extractive policing. Based on the author's MPhil thesis (National Defence University, Islamabad, 2020).

articles_hidden.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS
articles_hidden.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles_hidden.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles_hidden.title: Autonomy, Adolescents, and Artificial Intelligence
articles_hidden.authors: Michael J. S. Beauvais
articles_hidden.abstract:
In this essay, I explore the potential implications of adolescent use of AI assistants on the development of adolescents’ capacities for autonomy. Thinking through these issues from the perspective of first principles is, I believe, needed in order to sharpen our understanding of some of the issues AI assistants pose for young people. A clear analysis will suggest which legal or policy prescriptions should follow. 

I first give an overview of adolescent use of AI assistants, noting their popularity and the variety of use contexts. Drawing upon the work of Catriona Mackenzie, I then outline a relational conception of autonomy that conceives of autonomy as having three distinct dimensions: self-determination, self-governance, and self-authorization. The precision of Mackenzie’s conception allows us to more carefully consider how different uses and contexts of technological use can affect individuals’ capacities for autonomy. Using this three-dimensional conception of autonomy, I propose three potential interventions for law and policy: thinking beyond harms, substantive privacy protections, and autonomy impact assessments.

articles_hidden.title: Estados, DF e municípios também podem regulamentar o SICX - Sistema de Compras Expressas?
articles_hidden.authors: Felipe Dalenogare Alves
articles_hidden.abstract:
O artigo examina a competência dos Estados, do Distrito Federal e dos municípios para regulamentar o Sistema de Compras Expressas (SICX), introduzido na Lei nº 14.133/2021 pela Lei nº 15.266/2025. A análise parte da autonomia federativa, da reserva legal das normas gerais de licitações e contratos e da doutrina do congelamento do grau hierárquico normativo. Sustenta-se que a remessa do detalhamento do SICX a regulamento federal evidencia o caráter específico e operacional da matéria, permitindo sua disciplina pelos demais entes, ou, caso se trate de norma geral, configura degradação normativa incompatível com a reserva de lei. Defende-se, assim, uma interpretação conforme a Constituição que preserve a competência dos entes federativos para editar regulamentos próprios, observados os parâmetros gerais previstos na legislação nacional e as particularidades administrativas locais.

Palavras-chave: Sistema de Compras Expressas; SICX; autonomia federativa; competência regulamentar; licitações e contratos administrativos.

Publicado originalmente em Migalhas, seção Migalhas de Peso, em 3 de dezembro de 2025. Disponível em: https://www.migalhas.com.br/depeso/445405/estados-df-e-municipios-tambem-podem-regulamentar-o-sicx. Acesso em: 27 set. 2026.

articles_hidden.title: Analysis of the Social System in Post-Capitalist Society
articles_hidden.authors: 周勇
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to enhance productivity is pivotal in determining the success of a social system. Beyond scientific and technological advancements, productivity primarily hinges on workers' production enthusiasm and labor quality, the scale of production within each unit, and the pattern of resource allocation. Under given productive forces, the scale of production per unit is determined by the rate of exploitation imposed by owners upon laborers. As productive forces advance, new production models emerge. To boost productivity, the rate of exploitation diminishes, elevating the political and social standing of the populace, thereby giving rise to new social formations. Undifferentiated human labor constitutes the origin of goods value, while interest and capital gains represent the outcome of value distribution. Goods prices in the market are primarily determined by supply, with the labor value of goods serving as the equilibrium point of supply—thus constituting the market's equilibrium price. The labor theory of value can explain the Equity Risk Premium Puzzle. The higher the automation level of enterprises, the lower the value of goods, and in the long run, the lower the profits of enterprises. After the highly developed productive forces in capitalist society, the vast majority of industries will become low-profit public infrastructure services, making it difficult for private entities to continue operating. Public ownership will replace private ownership. The future social structure will be a “communist society” characterized by public ownership and distribution according to need as the mainstay, supplemented by private ownership and distribution according to work under a free-market economy. In the historical development toward communist society, there exists no so-called transitional stage of socialist society. In this communist society the state will persist, giving rise to a united human government where selfless dedication becomes the socially advocated moral standard. Under current productive forces, public ownership impedes both productive and economic development. Marxism is mistaken about the reasons and timing for the inevitable collapse of the capitalist system. Contemporary society faces issues such as welfare systems, nationalization, unified currencies, and China's economic and political structures.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing and identifying special protection needs among refugees in the EU: Overview and Synthesis of Evidence and Policy Recommendations
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Nutsch; Maren Hintermeier; Andreas W. Gold; Clara Perplies; Nils Robson; Veronika Wiemker; Till Bärnighausen; Sven Rohleder; Kayvan Bozorgmehr
articles_hidden.abstract: The EU’s Reception Conditions Directive requests member states to identify special protection needs among asylum seekers and refugees, but assessment practices remain inconsistently implemented across Europe. We systemically searched scientific and grey literature and synthesised evidence of 81 eligible documents to identify recommendations for assessing special protection needs and their implications for policy and practice. The evidence indicates that vulnerability, which may necessitate special protection, is multidimensional, intersectional, and dynamic. This requires early, continuous, and multimethod assessment rather than one-off screening. Effective assessment systems combine standardised procedures with individualised assessment, referral pathways, and multidisciplinary collaboration. We identified 51 screening tools, however, no single tool was universally accepted and used, highlighting that implementation depends less on individual tools than on coordinated, person-centred systems supported by rights-based documentation, informed consent, and secure information sharing. These findings provide evidence-informed directions for strengthening assessment of special protection needs systems across the EU.

articles_hidden.title: Provisioning for human needs at low resource use: institutional lessons from Cuba, Costa Rica and Ecuador
articles_hidden.authors: Chirag Dhara; Gustav Cederlöf; Viviana Cordero; Carolina Mauri; Tannya Pico; Soumyajit Bhar
articles_hidden.abstract: In the pursuit of sustainable development, Global South countries face the challenge of advancing wellbeing without breaching environmental limits. A central question for development policy is what institutional and policy configurations can deliver high levels of human need satisfaction at low ecological cost. We address this through structured comparative case studies of Cuba, Costa Rica and Ecuador: three middle-income countries achieving health and educational outcomes comparable to  higher-income nations with considerably lower environmental impacts, while also differing widely on the political-economic spectrum. Situating them within a social provisioning framework, we analyse the exogenous endowments, external conditions, structural-institutional configurations and concrete policies that account for their performance. Five cross-cutting patterns emerge across otherwise divergent political contexts: 1. sustained public investment in health and education, protected from fiscal volatility even during economic crises has been the foundational mechanism of needs satisfaction among all three; 2. periods of institutional stability have been preconditions for transformative legislation; 3. land tenure reform and food system restructuring have functioned simultaneously as instruments of ecological governance and social equity; 4. organised civil society has proved facilitative for sustaining provisioning gains across political transitions, although in Cuba such organisation has occurred within the politicised framework of the state; and 5. low energy and material throughput has been induced at least partly by resource constraint rather than by design. For the Global South, these cases offer a spectrum of configurations that can enable the satisfaction of human needs at moderate levels of affluence.

articles_hidden.title: Living Arrangements, Going Outdoors, and Well-Being Among Older Persons: Examining Their Associations in a Swedish Population
articles_hidden.authors: Jeanette Melin; Marie-Louise Möllerberg; Marit Preuter; Kristofer Årestedt
articles_hidden.abstract:
Aim: This study examined associations between living arrangement, frequency of going outdoors, and well-being among older persons in Sweden, with particular attention to their interaction.
Methods: Community-dwelling older persons (n = 1,727) across nine Swedish municipalities participated in a cross-sectional survey. Well-being was assessed using the Older Persons’ Well-being Scale (OPWELLS). Linear regression models examined associations and interactions.
Results: Living alone was associated with lower well-being compared to cohabiting, whereas going outdoors more frequently was associated with higher well-being. The association between living arrangement and well-being differed by outdoor frequency.
Conclusions: Frequency of going outdoors was strongly associated with well-being irrespective of living arrangement. However, the association between living alone and well-being varied with outdoor frequency. Thus, living alone should not be considered an isolated indicator of lower well-being in older age and highlights the importance of considering living arrangements within the broader context of older persons’ everyday lives.

articles_hidden.title: An Assessment of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report on Sociology
articles_hidden.authors: Julian Go
articles_hidden.abstract: The Sociology portion of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report (VWUR) claims to have studied the discipline of sociology and asserts that sociology’s search for truth has been compromised by what the author calls “politicization.” I find that the VWUR’s claims are unsubstantiated and based upon fundamental errors. The problem is not lack of data but rather that the author, Dr. Ashley Rubin, misunderstands and misrepresents the data she does have while failing to check her own biases. She mistakenly reads politicization into everything she sees, reaffirming a thesis she had already held before her supposedly impartial study without taking the appropriate steps to suspend her bias. The VWUR violates the very social scientific standards that it purports to defend while distracting us from other problems facing social science.

articles_hidden.title: What the World Studies, Invents and Reports About Urban Heat
articles_hidden.authors: Narendra Kumar
articles_hidden.abstract: We assemble 20,422 scholarly papers on urban heat islands (1990–2025), read the 17,101 that carry an abstract sentence by sentence, and join them to 96,726 news articles (2021–2025), 4,123 patent families, 14,576 recorded heat incidents, registers of companies, funding rounds and government funding events, and the annual accounts of Indian companies. Eight results stand out. (1) The field grew about 9 times faster than the scholarly literature as a whole, and in 2015–2019 titles naming "extreme heat" overtook those naming "heat island". (2) Of 2,409 papers that attribute urban heat to a cause, 48% name urbanisation and land-use change; attribution to anthropogenic heat fell from 18.4% to 7.7%. (3) Research and news describe different problems: at equal text length, 28% of research openings raise mitigation against 1.6% of news leads, while 22% of news leads are forecasts or warnings against 1.4% of research. (4) They also describe different places: China accounts for 31% of the research and 2.3% of English-language coverage, and Delhi receives 7.4 times the coverage its research share would predict. (5) Invention has outrun science: patent families for cool and permeable pavements grew 12-fold in a decade against 2.4-fold for the research on them. (6) Across 194 studies the median reported cooling from urban trees is 2.0 °C (air temperature 2.0 °C, surface temperature 2.9 °C). (7) Between 2021–22 and 2024–25 news coverage moved from the hazard to the people exposed: workers, schools, the elderly and hospital patients each rose 1.4- to 2.4-fold as a share of heat articles while wildfire and drought fell by about half and climate change — raised in about one article in ten — fell by a quarter. (8) The market record is thin: 140 of 5.05 million companies state a heat or cooling purpose, and recorded capital is $2.7 billion of cooling-infrastructure finance against $48 million of venture funding; larger Indian cooling companies grew revenue 25% a year over three years against 16% for Indian companies generally. Every cause category extracted from the research was tested against an independent second reader; three failed, and no result reported here rests on them.

articles_hidden.title: A POLÍTICA DE EXPANSÃO ECONÔMICA SIMBIÓTICA PULSANTE DOS ESTADOS UNIDOS: MECANISMOS DE INFLUÊNCIA GLOBAL E EXPLORAÇÃO DE RECURSOS ESTRANGEIROS
articles_hidden.authors: Juliano Paniago de Alcântara
articles_hidden.abstract: O estudo propõe o modelo da “Política de Expansão Econômica Simbiótica Pulsante” para descrever a projeção de poder dos Estados Unidos como sequência recorrente de coerção, reestruturação e extração, e o submete a séries temporais, a um painel país×ano e a quatro estudos de caso (Iraque, América Latina, Ucrânia e Golfo Pérsico). Na série 2000–2024, a associação entre gastos militares e renda de investimento direto no exterior é, no longo prazo, absorvida pelo ciclo de renda mundial; em primeira diferença, a precedência dos gastos militares tem o sinal previsto e significância marginal. Em painel país×ano com cerca de oito mil observações, a presença militar americana associa-se a maior comércio e a maior participação americana nas importações do hospedeiro, sem precedência estabelecida. No Golfo, o acesso americano ao mercado iraniano colapsa após a ruptura de 1979 e as sanções subsequentes. Formaliza-se a “pulsação” como construto temporal falseável, distinto do smart power.

articles_hidden.title: Does Carbon Pricing Outperform Command-and-Control Regulation? Firm-Level Evidence from Korea’s Dual Regulatory Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Pyung Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: This study compares the effects of carbon pricing and command-and-control regulation on firms’ environmental performance. I leverage a unique dual-policy setting in South Korea, where a carbon pricing scheme (the Emissions Trading Scheme, ETS) and a command-and-control program (the Target Management System, TMS) operate in parallel. Because each firm is regulated under only one of the two, the setting allows a direct comparison of the two approaches.
